###### **1. INTRODUCTION** 

###### **1.1.   GENERAL** 

The Weda Bay nickel and cobalt deposits are located in the central part of Halmahera in Eastern Indonesia. Figure 1 shows the location of Halmahera within Eastern Indonesia and Figure 2 shows the concession area within Halmahera. The area is held as a Seventh Generation Contract of Work (COW) by PT Weda Bay Nickel (WBN).  WBN is jointly owned by Strand Minerals (Indonesia) Pty Ltd (Strand) (90%) and PT Aneka Tambang (Antam) (10%).  Strand  is a  wholly owned subsidiary of Weda Bay Minerals Inc. (WDA), a company listed on the Toronto Stock Exchange in Canada and Antam is an Indonesian mining company, owned 60% by the Government. 

The extensive areas of laterite discovered at Weda Bay have developed over serpentinised harzburgites and dunites forming part of a larger ophiolite basement complex which extends from central Halmahera some 400 km eastward through numerous smaller islands to Waigeo off the north coast of Irian Jaya.  The Weda Bay project region occurs at the western margin of this ocean floor sequence, and weathering of these rocks has produced laterite profiles that are enriched in nickel and cobalt.

###### **1.2.   PROJECT BACKGROUND** 

Application for a COW over 120 500 Ha of Central Halmahera was made in April 1996 with exploration beginning soon after under an interim exploration license (SIPP).  These preliminary investigations quickly revealed the presence of potentially economic nickel and cobalt mineralisation in several coastal laterites. 

Reconnaissance drilling began in December 1996 with the objective of establishing a resource base of sufficient magnitude to support a nickel mining and processing operation. The results of this drilling indicated that the Weda Bay coastal resources were predominantly limonitic or transitional in nature and preliminary metallurgical tests conducted during 1997 showed all laterite types were amenable to metal recovery through the high pressure acid leach (PAL) process.  Subsequent studies therefore sought to increase the understanding of these resources, their metallurgy and site logistics to enable the concept of an integrated mining and PAL processing facility to be developed.  The results of these studies were input into a Project Evaluation Study (PES) in mid-1998 which confirmed the economic potential of the project. 

Several agreements were signed in early 2000 with OM Group, Inc. (OMG), a US based company involved in the refining of nickel and cobalt metal and the manufacture and 

2 

ALTA Free Library  www.altamet.com.au 

marketing of specialist nickel and cobalt chemicals and

products.  These agreements provided the funding for ongoing work and included a take or pay sales and purchase agreement for the output of the initial phase of production.  Since mid-2000, ongoing work has further defined the resources, metallurgy and site logistics for input into a pre-feasibility study (PFS) to form the basis for further detailed metallurgical testing and engineering and ultimate development of the project. 

###### **2. RESOURCE DEFINITION** 

###### **2.1. EXPLORATION HISTORY AND GENERAL METHODOLOGY** 

A systematic approach to exploration was adopted with the initial aim to demonstrate that sufficient resources were available to support future development.  This resource development program began in late 1996 with the evaluation of the regional potential of the COW and was carried out using a combination of the interpretation of remotely sensed data (aerial photographs, Landsat TM and Radarsat imagery) to provide targets for aerial reconnaissance mapping.  This targeted the identification of the rounded landforms which are generally indicative of economic laterite development and was followed by a helicopter survey to enable visual confirmation by identifying the distinctive red-orange colouration of the laterites.   These methods proved to be very successful.  The task was made considerably easier in the cleared and settled coastal regions and areas of logging activity due to the presence of an extensive network of disused forestry tracks. These not only exposed the laterites from beneath the sometimes thick jungle canopy, but also provided 4WD access to areas of laterite development. 

A series of airborne surveys were conducted between late 1996 and mid 1998 that identified five major lateritic provinces and regions within the Weda Bay COW  (Figure 3). These occur over large and widespread areas of the COW and include the following: 

- -- The Coastal  Province, where laterites are characterized by relatively small, discrete, elongate ridge bound deposits near the coast.  These occur in the vicinity of the company’s field base at Tanjung Ulie on the Weda Bay coast. 

- -- The Big Kahuna (BK) Province in the central-western region of the COW. Resource definition has taken place in the Jira River and Big Kahuna deposits which occur in the southern region of this province.  A series of additional interpreted laterite bodies extending to the north-east from this region have not yet been subjected to detailed evaluation.  In common with the Jira River and Big Kahuna deposits, these appear to be large, dissected lateritic plateaus. 

- -- The Santa Monica region, is a large dissected plateau located in the south-central region of the COW in the northern part of the Coastal Province.  Preliminary evaluation of Santa Monica began in 1999 and confirmed it’s the potential.  A portion of this deposit has recently been classified as a measured resource. 

- -- The Sagea Province in the eastern region of the COW is characterized by

a series of large, interpreted lateritic plateaus. In the largest of these, Pintu, a preliminary drilling program has already defined additional resource. Regional geological traverses have also confirmed the development of economic nickel/cobalt mineralisation in other areas of this province.

- -- The Central Province, which is comprised of a series of narrow, ridge bound deposits extending in a belt parallel to the Big Kahuna laterites.  No road access exists but preliminary helicopter supported regional traverses have established the presence of economic nickel and cobalt mineralisation in several areas. 



Figure 3   Location of Laterite Occurrences 

Initial resource definition was commenced in areas serviced by the network of forestry roads in the Weda Bay region and the southern regions of the Big Kahuna province. Evaluation was conducted by means of hand-excavated test pits and reconnaissance diamond drilling along the major access tracks to determine general profile characteristics and grade so that different areas could be ranked in terms of prospectivity. The more prospective regions were systematically gridded, mapped and diamond drilled on 100 m x 200 m patterns using man-portable drill rigs.  This work was completed in December 1997 and defined indicated and inferred resources of approximately 90 Mdt. 

4

Having established the presence of extensive, accessible areas of laterite mineralisation, the company increased this resource base by drilling in more remote, but still reasonably accessible areas such as Big Kahuna.  Continued improvement in the understanding of the various resource characteristics and estimates was also sought through a series of specialized programs during 1998.  These included detailed studies on the density variations through the laterite profile by the excavation of a series of test pits and the collection of undisturbed samples through drilling with hollow (Shelby) tubes for detailed laboratory tests.   Alternative resource evaluation techniques were also trialled during this period, including Ground Penetrating Radar (GPR) which is a geophysical technique used to continuously map variations in and through the laterite profile. 

Activities in 1999 concentrated on Santa Monica and included gridding, mapping, excavation of a series of test pits and limited reconnaissance drilling which confirmed the size and potential of this region. 

Exploration and resource evaluation activities since late 2001, have concentrated on improving  confidence in the estimation of known resources rather than increasing the global resource base.   The Santa Monica resource data, compiled by the Company over the past three years, has been comprehensively reviewed by an independent geological consultant, International Mining Consultants Pty Ltd (IMC). IMC have constructed a computer based block model of the resource and completed an independen

t resource estimate that includes the first measured resources at SM. The estimate for SM provided by IMC at 1% nickel or 0.1% cobalt cut off is given in Table 1.

###### **3. METALLURGY** 

###### **3.1.   COASTAL ORE METALLURGY** 

The majority of the Coastal resources are limonitic or transitional in nature or consist of saprolite and are unsuited to pyrometallurgical treatment processes. 

Batch scale metallurgical tests in the second half of 1997 demonstrated that all laterite types from Coastal regions were amenable to treatment by the high pressure acid leach (PAL) process.  High recoveries of both nickel (98%) and cobalt (94%) were obtained for all laterite types at a temperature of 250<sup>o</sup> C.  Leaching kinetics were fast with extraction completed after around 30 minutes, indicating the high reactivity of Coastal ores.  Acid consumption increased from 250 kg/tonne for limonite to 750 kg/tonne for saprolite. 

Coastal limonites and saprolites thickened satisfactorily, with solids densities in the 34-40% w/w range, but transitional ores which comprise a significant proportion of the Coastal laterites, exhibite poor settling and thickening behaviour, reaching only 25-30% w/w solids density.  Composite samples representing likely plant feed from Coastal regions tended to behave like the transitional material. 

The pulps of leached residues from these Coastal composites also thickened and settled poorly and indicated that the application of the PAL process to these ores required further development. 

###### **3.2.   SANTA MONICA METALLURGY** 

As the exploration program progressed, it became evident that the plateau deposits, in particular Santa Monica, were much larger, and of more consist

ent composition than the Coastal laterites. Furthermore, the Santa Monica deposit contained more saprolitic laterite with the ratio of saprolite to limonite being close to 1:1, and only minor amounts of transitional material.  By 1999, metallurgical testwork had focused on Santa Monica ore with Coastal and Big Kahuna resources treated as potential supplementary ore. 

###### **3.2.1.  Feed Thickening** 

Following a series of preliminary tests, systematic feed thickening tests were carried out using a selected flowsheet with different laterite types at ambient temperature, with an initial pulp density of 3% w/w solids and ore ground to -212-m. 

6 

ALTA Free Library  www.altamet.com.au 

In summary, the results of these tests were as follows: 

- -- Solids densities of 30-40% w/w for limonite with acceptable settling rates for all samples. 

- -- Solids densities of 45-50% w/w for saprolite with fast settling rates but some residual cloudiness in the liquor. 

- -- Solids densities of 27-40% w/w for transitional material with generally slow settling rates. 

- -- Grinding finer than -212-m had a significant negative impact on saprolite settling behaviour. 

These tests on individual laterite types were followed by tests on composite blends made up by adding saprolite to limonite containing minor amounts of transitional material, to increase the MgO content to around 9-10%.  The selection of this MgO level was based on the behaviour of the leached pulp (see section on leach residue thickening) and these blends are referred to as PAL feed blends (PFB’s).  The feed thickening characteristics of these blends indicated that a satisfactory pulp density of 36% w/w solids could be obtained using high rate thickeners.  Liquors from PFB thickening were generally clear. 

###### **3.2.2. Pressure Acid Leaching** 

Separate PAL testwork was carried out on limonites (3-6% MgO) and PFB’s (9-10% MgO). The following conditions were selected based on the results of initial evaluations: 

- -- Leach temperature : 250-255<sup>o</sup> C 

- -- Initial solids density : 26% w/w solids 

- -- Leach time : 60 minutes -- Ore grind size : -212-m 

A series of tests on samples from different parts of the deposit showed consistently high extractions of nickel (96.5%) and cobalt (94.5%) for all samples tested.  Some general observations from the testwork were: 

- -- Leach kinetics were good generally requiring around 60 minutes. 

- -- Higher temperature and higher acidity improved leach kinetics. 

- -- Finer grinding had a minor positive impact on leach kinetics. 

- -- Impurity pickup (iron and aluminium) was minimal but increased with higher acidity level. 

Overall, the leaching behaviour of Santa Monica limonites and PFB’s in the PAL test program was very encouraging.

Leach Residue Thickening** In a series of scoping tests, it was demonstrated that leach residue thickening characteristics deteriorated with increasing MgO content in the feed. Up to approximately 9-10% MgO the settling behaviour was satisfactory, but above this level the deterioration was rapid. This led to the limitation of 9% MgO content for PFB’s. Leach residue thickening tests were carried out on limonites and PFB’s at ambient temperature with an initial pulp density of 4-5% w/w solids using a selected flocculent and a simulated barren liquor wash. Final thickened solids densities of 40-50% w/w were obtained with limonite samples and 37-47% w/w on PFB’s. In practice, it appears that that 40% w/w solids densities can be readily achievable for limonite but represents an upper limit for a PFB. The unit settling areas increase with higher MgO content. Leach residue settling tests were also carried out with blends of the Santa Monica PFB and Coastal composites at blending ratios of both 1:1 and 3:1. With the 3:1 blend, the thickening behaviour was similar to a 100% Santa Monica PFB, but at 1:1 there was a 8 ALTA Free Library www.altamet.com.au significant negative impact. These tests confirm that there is scope to blend moderate amounts of Coastal ores with Santa Monica ore in PAL plant feed. ###### **4. ATMOSPHERIC LEACHING OF SAPROLITE** Studies in 1998 had indicated the potential of atmospheric leaching for high magnesium content ore (saprolite). SAPROLITE NEUTRALIZATION (SN)** Tests have confirmed that Santa Monica saprolite is highly reactive and is suitable for neutralization of PAL pulps. With a slurry prepared by the pressure acid leaching of a PFB, up to 80% of the nickel and 95% of the cobalt were recovered from saprolite used to neutralize the excess acid at a PAL/SN neutralization feed ratio of 4:1. The final discharge acidity after SN was typically 5 g/l H2SO4, confirming the high degree of reactivity of the ground Santa Monica saprolite. There was a low degree of iron and aluminum coextraction. Tests were also conducted on leach pulps after neutralization to determine the impact of SN on leach residue thickening. These tests indicated that solids densities in the range of 40-47% w/w could be obtained at reasonable settling rates. The data indicated that coarser saprolite material fed to SN resulted in faster thickening kinetics although the final solids densities were generally independent of the saprolite grind size. 9 ALTA Free Library www.altamet.com.au However, flocculent only tests generally produced poor quality supernatants. This was resolved by the use of commercial coagulants, which resulted in only slightly slower thickening rates but clear supernatants. ###### **4.2. COMBINED SAPROLITE NEUTRALIZATION (SN) AND ATMOSPHERIC LEACHING (ATL)** Combined PAL/ATL/SN circuit trials were also undertaken on Santa Monica samples. The key results of these trials were: - -- A separate ATL circuit can recover 95% of the nickel and 85% of the cobalt from Santa Monica saprolite at 90ºC in leach times of 2 hours or less. High co-extraction of iron with the nickel and cobalt was observed, and the acid demand was typically one tonne of acid per tonne of solids feed. - -- Approximately 80% of the nickel and over 70% of the cobalt was recovered from saprolite fed to a subsequent SN stage (PAL:ATL:SN feed ratios of 4:1:1) with no significant impurity pickup. - -- Leach residue thickening tests on the subsequent pulps indicated that final solids densities of 40% w/w solids or higher can be achieved at acceptable settling rates. These preliminary integrated metallurgical trials indicate that a combined PAL/ATL/SN system has potential to further optimize nickel production through greater utilization of high grade saprolite resources. ###### **5. THE PROJECT CONCEPT** The key factors affecting the

developing project concepts are: 

- -- The nature of the resource 

- -- The metallurgical characteristics 

- -- The choice of the product 

- -- The logistics of the resource location 

The first two of these factors have been described in some detail in the previous sections, together with their impact on the development of a project concept.  The remaining two factors impacting on the project concept are discussed below. 

###### **5.1. CHOICE OF PRODUCT** 

The alternatives are to produce an intermediate product for refining elsewhere, or to produce metal directly. 

Of the projects currently operating with the PAL process only one, the Moa Bay project in Cuba, was designed to produce an intermediate product.  All the Australian projects were designed to produce metal, although the Cawse operation has recently been modified to produce an intermediate product. 

For the Weda Bay project, an early decision was made to produce an intermediate product. This decision was influenced by several factors.

Firstly, a PAL based operation involves complex chemical processes, many of which are sequential and interdependent.  If metal is produced, the number of steps and their interdependency is greater, adding to the potential for difficulties during startup and operation. There can be little doubt that this factor has been contributory to the prolonged startup difficulties of the Australian PAL plants.  The Weda Bay project is located on a remote island in East Indonesia where such problems would be magnified. Hence it was decided to limit the complexity of the initial phase of development by deferring the metal refining stage. 

Secondly, there is currently an excess of nickel refining capacity around the world and many refineries are seeking a long term secure supply of intermediate product.  These refineries are already operating efficiently and can offer payment terms based on high recovery factors, eliminating the ramp-up impact of a new refinery.  Historically, many of these refineries utilized nickel sulphide concentrates as feed, but a shortage of suitable concentrates has been developing for some years, and a sulphide intermediate product from a PAL process is an excellent substitute. 

Finally, and in Weda Bay’s case, it has been possible to write a sales contract which also guarantees revenue from the significant cobalt content. 

###### **5.2. LOGISTICS** 

One of the significant advantages of the Weda Bay project is its excellent logistics.  While the location is remote, it is easily accessible and other important logistic features are equally favourable.  These include: 

- -- The main resources (including Santa Monica) are close to the coast and are generally accessible by road. 

- -- There is a relatively flat coastal strip suitable for the construction of a processing plant and support facilities. 

- -- No people live in the resource areas or in the areas identified for the processing pl

ant site. 

- -- There is a plentiful permanent fresh water supply available from several rivers. 

- -- There is deep, sheltered bay suitable for a port located immediately adjacent the proposed plant site. 

- -- An airstrip has already been constructed. 

- -- Quality limestone deposits suitable for use in the process plant exist within the COW. 

- -- There are plentiful sources of rock suitable for aggregate and road building. 

- -- A deep trench, suitable for Deep Sea Tailings Placement (DSTP) has been located within 3 kilometers of the treatment plant.

ABSTRACT** Mineral projects have had a very chequered history as regards their economic and technical success. Project developers and owners all have very optimistic views when it comes to their project development, construction, commissioning and operation. Project financiers, especially over the past decade, have become more circumspect and are now taking a more conservative view of new project performance by factoring into their project financial analysis longer periods of ramp-up, higher capital costs and higher operating costs. There are many philosophical and perhaps psychological reasons why these two parties, both keenly interested in being associated with a successful project, have such disparate views. An even greater point of concern is “Who is correct and how do we get both parties thinking along the same correct manner?” This paper briefly discusses this problem by referring to many projects known to the author and including some previous studies that looked at this very problem. The projects studied are a mixture of those that have had difficulties along with some that have been successful. The paper attempts to take these experiences and present a project development and implementation approach that will allow at least a better degree of success both economically and technically. It should be emphasised that many of the opinions stated within the paper are strictly those of the author and subject to much debate. ###### **2. INTRODUCTION**

Over the past decade a number of large mineral resource projects in Australia and worldwide have been developed and are now operating. Many of these projects have undergone very severe commissioning “difficulties’ while others have been successful. With respect to the less successful projects financiers have had to reorganise their financial support or have exited ignominiously. The financial problems have evolved due to insufficient working capital necessary to cover shortfalls because of the need for a much longer time period than originally estimated to the attainment of full design throughput and metal production. Commissioning periods are naively estimated and initial operating costs are underestimated. Many of these projects have had difficulties allegedly because of the use of “new technology”. Plants have difficulties because of poor design of equipment and processing circuits. Materials of construction are often poorly specified or unknown. Because of poor quality control/quality assurance vendor supplied equipment and packages fail. Capital costs are invariably underestimated and, in order to reduce the overrun, shortcuts are taken in design and equipment quality. Many of the problems noted above evolve from a poor understanding of the process used to extract the metals. This poor understanding arises from impatience of the owner, unwarranted confidence in the process and poor initial testwork used to develop the flowsheets. In addition, the owner is often forced, by financial needs, to undertake specific engineering and construction contracts that are either unfavourable or are such that the owner expects not to have to supervise the performance of the chosen engineer. ###### **3. ###### **4. RECENT PROJECT PERFORMANCE** What does the data presented above tell the reader? Essentially, the lesson to be learned is that starting up processing plants is very difficult and that we in the industry do not appear to have learned much from history. We are now blessed with tools to design flowsheets, P&IDs and layouts far easier than ever before. We have models to allow our mass and energy balances to be more accurate and more precise than ever before. Piping drawings are so much easier to produce and isometrics can be produced almost at the drop of a hat. Engineering companies now possess large data-bases to support capital costs and most of the design needs. Nevertheless, we still make mistakes. Even with the best design and most prudent project development approach complex projects can not be expected to reach design until the end of the second year after construction has been completed and commissioning commences. The two studies discussed above were conducted in 1979 and 1998 both using historical data from 1 to 15 years old. The overwhelming din of protest can be heard from new project developers that new projects will not be as bad as the previous projects. Almost every one associated with the mining and minerals industry is aware of recent projects that have been implemented and have performed poorly. There have been some projects that have started well and continue to perform well. Human nature being what it is seems to focus on the failures and the successes continue unabated and unheralded. In addition to this list of self inflicted problems some almost all of the operations suffered from failures of packaged plants or plants that were provided from the vendors as proprietary installations. At the risk of being too critical the quality controls and quality assurances purported to be the basis of the vendor’s claim to being ISO-9000 certified often were non-existent. Common “off the shelf” pieces of equipment such as compressors, packaged boilers, water treatment circuits, and reagent production plants failed. Not surprisingly, the general response by the vendors to the owners was “You are the first to have such a problem!” To be really cynical one could take the view that vendors who advertise ISO 9000 should be viewed with suspicion. Regarding the lack of owners input with the engineer this is unforgivable but understandable in today’s project financing environment. The financier’s are their own worst enemies when they require all new projects be developed and built with lump sum fixed price contracts. In the first instance the fixed price never is fixed. A recent project had a major fixed price component which, when the dust settled had been increased during the construction period by almost 15%. At the same time the owner still didn’t get what was initially in the scope of work. two main protagonists, the owner and the engineer/constructor are operating with two differing and often horizontally opposed agendas.  This author thinks that a reimbursable type of contract is the best method for both parties to complete a project with success 

We are well aware of the statement that “Don’t worry about the front end.  It is simple and will cause no problems”.  There have been a number of recent projects that have suffered because insufficient attention to detail was devoted to the design and specification of the first part of the mineral resource plant that involves crushing, materials handling, grinding or scrubbing and storage of slurry.   McNulty highlighted this problem and so did CRAI. We continue to make the same mistakes and the only answer to at least reducing the incidence of failure is to be more diligent in the design of this part of the plant. 

The inclusion of new technology in flow sheets has been quoted as the main problem affecting these new plants and the recent difficulties with the PAL plants has further confirmed the problems of new technology.  However, we have to incorporate new technology into our operating plants if we wish to continue with the idea of better efficiencies, lower costs and the ability to exploit lower quality resources.  It is interesting to note that after a period of learning the PAL circuits have, generally speaking, settled down and it has been the other parts of the plants that have given problems.  Some of these problem areas can be classified as “conventional”.  Many of the difficulties experienced can be traced to either shortcuts taken by the engineer and/or the owner and to poor quality control during construction. 

What has to be done in concert with the use of new technology is to follow many of the points McNulty tried to emphasise. 

- -- Thoroughly understand the technology. 

- -- Thoroughly test the technology on the Project ore types including the use of extensive pilot plant studies. 

- -- Design the plant with a high degree of flexibility and an appropriately set safety factor. 

- -- Allow for lengthy start-up times and significant amounts of capital to cover over-runs and modifications/rectifications. 

There is not much to say regarding understanding the use of new and innovative technology other than to ensure you know what the technology does, what you want to do with it and what affect does your material have on the technology as well as what effect the technology has on the material. 

Mineralogy generally is not afforded the attention it deserves although some of the projects illustrated conducted detailed mineralogical classification.  Interestingly, these projects are the ones that performed most successfully.  Closely associated with mineralogy is the actual mineral extraction testwork.  It is this author’s experience that project developers tend to conduct sone very detailed tests on composite samples that do not really reflect the material that was to

be mined.  This is especially for the first five years of planned production.  Composite samples are suitable for some testwork but it is absolutely imperative to test individual ore types and to test in detail some well-chosen individual drill hole intersections.  Additionally, it is also imperative that the ores to be mined in the first 3 to 5 years should be tested specifically.  This implies that the project developer has to have a well thought out mining plan.  This author suggests that almost all new projects do not have a mining plan before implementation.  As a corollary it is unlikely that sufficient variability testwork has been completed.  As a result the plants often start with ores that differ significantly from the ores tested pre project implementation. 

One of the lesser problems with project development but one that does occur is the translation of the testwork to process design.  The means for the owner to reduce the incidence of this problem is to use the best people available and ensure there is significant

The subject of materials of construction warrants a paper of its own.  In all mineral extraction projects proper specification of materials of construction is very important. Many of the new projects implemented recently have suffered from a surprisingly large number of design “stuff ups”.  Everyone is familiar with these events and they seem to be happening far more frequently than engineering companies would care to admit.  One unintentional benefit from these “stuff-ups” is the extra income a myriad of lawyers gain for extended periods of time.  It vis this author’s opinion that most of the stuff-ups are closely related to the financier’s overwhelming desire to finance projects that are being built with fixed price, lump sum contracts.  In an attempt to win the job these contractors bid quite close and subsequently, in an effort to improve thin margins these contractors start to take short cuts.  Reduction of equipment redundancy, low or non-existent safety factors on piping calculations, choice of poor or lesser quality equipment and often the elimination of ancillary plant that are essential to the smoot

h operation of the process.  In addition many engineering companies tend to want to provide “self perform” services.  The idea of an engineer awarding contracts to itself is tantamount to conflicts of interest.  However, the real problem that causes these stuff-ups relates to the inexperience of the engineers themselves especially with operating plants and the operation of real life processing plants. Engineering companies have to be more honest with the pricing, Owners have to recognise that they have to pay fair price for their plant and they also have to recognise that the engineering company has to make a profit.  Finally, the Owner has to be prepared to have a strong operating team very early in project implementation that will sit with the engineering team and ensure that the plant is what they wish or at least what they expect. 

The subject of taking short cuts to save capital is one that is near and dear to all operators. In order to ensure the plant eventually performs as expected the operator or subsequent operators have to expend large sums to correct and rectify the problems created by the initial compromises.  Everyone has had the opportunity to be involved in the development of new projects and to assess the economics of these developments.  Invariably, when the sensitivity analysis is completed the project’s development is least sensitive to capital expenditure.  This author continues to be amazed at the lengths Owners go to “keep capex down”.  Not surprisingly, one of the parameters that project value is more sensitive to is the operating costs.  We all are aware that the operator has to endure higher than expected operating costs to accommodate poorly engineered and design compromised plants. 

###### **5. CONCLUSIONS** 

The conclusions that can be drawn from this brief assessment of ramp-up for new mineral processing projects are generally self-evident.  However, self evidence like common sense is neither self evident or common.  Below is a very brief summary of conclusions and action this author thinks owners and project developers have to consider. 

- -- It is prudent and, indeed, necessary to include in all project analyses a suitable ramp-up period in the financial analyses.  This ramp-up period should be no less than eighteen months and most likely twenty-four months. 

- -- The problems associated with the commissioning of green field projects seem to be the same over the past 3 to 4 decades at least.

###### **ABSTRACT** 

The hydrometallurgical processing of nickel laterite ore has reached an interesting period, the historically dominant Caron process favored in the 1970’s and early 80’s has been sidelined by the three PAL (pressure acid leach) plants in Western Australia and other PAL projects now in the pipeline. 

Atmospheric pressure ammonia leach (Caron) and high pressure acid leach (PAL) have been the only two commercial hydrometallurgical laterite ore processing options for the past 40 years. The Freeport Minerals company of the U.S.A. built the first commercial plants of both processes, a Caron plant at Nicaro, Cuba in 1944 and then a PAL plant at Moa in 1959. 

A third processing option has been developed by BHP Billiton, whereby an acid leach is undertaken at atmospheric pressure, thus negating the requirement for autoclaves and associated equipment. This process has been designated as AL. 

It has been further proposed that AL  can be used either as a stand alone operation, or in association with a PAL plant, wherein the saprolite fraction of an orebody is used for neutralization of PAL discharge liquor. 

The three Western Australian PAL projects have now been in operation for more than three years, thus providing sufficient operational and cost data to allow a reasonable assessment of PAL performance relative to operating Caron plants. 

The importance of ore characteristics in determining the preferred processing option is a significant consideration. 

###### **1. BACKGROUND** 

When Freeport constructed the world’s first commercial nickel laterite hydrometallurgical processing plant at Nicaro, Cuba, during the later part of WW II, the requirement was to achieve production quickly. At that time much of the industry in Cuba was US owned and operated. 

Not surprisingly, the process chosen was reduction roast and ammonia leach, which had been researched by Professor Caron at Delft University, Holland since the 1920’s, as much of the fundamental work had already been done. 

Another attraction of the “Caron” process was that the equipment required for: 750<sup>0</sup> C ore roasting, atmospheric pressure leaching, ammonia distillation and re-absorption and nickel carbonate calcination to oxide, was essentially available off the shelf, having been previously developed for other metal processing applications in the US. 

As part of the war effort, the Nicaro plant construction was funded by the US government and at the end of the war was auctioned off. Freeport were not successful in the bidding and the plant passed into the hands of National Lead. 

Freeport retained leases to laterite ore at Moa Bay, along the coast from Nicaro, and in the mid 1950’s looked to construct another plant to process this ore. At the time Freeport were a major sulphur producer f

rom sub-sea deposits off the Louisiana coast and had a research laboratory near New Orleans investigating new uses for sulphur. They were attracted to sulphuric acid leaching under pressure, which was made more attractive by the Moa ore being 

2

very low in magnesium content (limonitic) resulting in low acid consumption. Most other known laterite ore bodies had significantly higher magnesium contents, requiring more acid. 

The reasons for Freeport’s choice of pressure acid leaching (PAL) for the Moa project can be summarized as follows: 

- They could supply the sulphur for acid production from their own deposits off the Louisiana coast. 

- The acid consumption was low, only about 0.25 t/t ore. 

- The nickel and cobalt leach extraction would be significantly higher than in Caron processing (eg Ni >90% vs 83%, Co >90% vs no Co recovered at Nicaro). 

- Freeport would build a refinery in Louisiana (Port Nickel) so that a dedicated ship could transport molten sulphur from Louisiana to Moa and then return with a load of nickel-cobalt sulphide slurry. 

At that time the state of development of pressure reactor vessels to operate at 250<sup>0</sup> C was relatively primitive and Freeport avoided the requirement for agitators, gland seals etc, by using the pachuca principle. Steam was injection into a central vertical riser tube in the lead and brick lined carbon steel pressure vessels to induce slurry movement. The use of lead lining for corrosion protection of the vessels was the only practical option in the 1950’s and limited the upper operating temperature to about 245<sup>0</sup> C. 

The 35 gpl acid in the pachuca slurry discharge was partly neutralized, to pH 2.5, with coral mud and the nickel and cobalt precipitated as mixed sulphide, with hydrogen sulphide, The untreated acidic barren liquor was discharged to the sea and the thickened mixed sulphide intermediate shipped to Port Nickel for refining. 

The plant commenced production late in 1959, but following the revolution, the Freeport personnel were expelled and the plant expropriated. The mixed sulphide product of Moa was refined in Russia until the 1990 collapse of the USSR. Refining then changed to Sherritt’s Fort Saskatchewan plant. 

The Caron plant at Nicaro was also expropriated (from National Lead) following the revolution and continued to operate under Cuban management. 

The nickel shortage and price boom of the late 1960’s again sparked Freeport’s interest in the metal, leading to the construction of a plant at Yabulu, Queensland, to process laterite ore from the Greenvale orebody, 200 km inland. The Greenvale ore did not have the low magnesium content of Moa and this, in combination with environmental concerns relating to the acidic effluent, influenced Freeport (in partnership with Metals Exploration) to select the Caron process route that they had installed at Nicaro. 

At the same time that Freeport was building the Yabulu plant, Sh

erritt was also building a Caron plant (in partnership with Marinduque Mining) at Nonoc Island in the Philippines. At Nonoc, Sherritt used an in-house hydrogen reduction back end to produce nickel briquettes, whereas at Yabulu, Freeport produced partially reduced nickel oxide rondelles. The Nonoc plant closed in 1986, following a protracted period of low nickel prices. In the 1970’s and 80’s, the Cubans commenced two new plants, Punta Gorda and Las Camariocas, both based on the Caron design of Nicaro, but only Punta Gorda was completed and commissioned (in 1986). 3 ALTA Free Library www.altamet.com.au The only other leach plant built prior to 1998 was at Niquelandia (Tocantins), Brazil by Votorantim in 1982. Again, this plant is based on the Caron process, but with an Outokumpu designed electrowinning refinery in Sao Paulo producing nickel and cobalt cathode. Prior to the construction of the three PAL plants in Western Australia in 1998, there was a 16 year interval during which no hydrometallurgical nickel laterite plants were built anywhere in the world (39 years since the Moa PAL was commissioned). A notable feature of the three new WA PAL projects was that the owners were newcomers to the nickel industry, mostly having a background of gold production in Australia. ### **2. CARON PROCESS** 

###### **2.1 PROJECT STATUS** 

The Caron process has been around for a long time and as outlined in the previous section, was the first nickel laterite hydrometallurgical process to be commercialized. 

Freeport made some enhancements to the Nicaro design when they built the Yabulu plant and in the 28 years since, further enhancements have been implement. 

The most significant was the 1989 installation of a solvent extraction circuit (ASX) following leaching of the reduction roasted ore. The ASX circuit installation produced a number of benefits as listed below (attained with minimum further capital expenditure). 

- Efficient separation of nickel and cobalt. 

- Reduction of impurity levels in both nickel and cobalt products. 

- Ability to increase metal production, nickel by 50%, cobalt by 100%. 

- Reduction in energy consumption. 

- Reduction in hydrogen sulphide consumption. 

- Reduction in product shipping costs. 

There was also a reduction in nickel carbonate sulphur levels, which allowed the carbonate calcination step to be undertaken under reducing conditions. The calciner produced partially reduced semimetallic nickel, rather than the previous nickel oxide granules and dust. 

Two new ore roasters were installed in 1996 taking the total to 12. The current production capacity is about 30,000 tpy Ni and 1,800 tpy Co. 

At Niquelandia the Tocantins, Caron plant has also changed significantly since the first two roasters were installed in 1982. Two more roasters were added in 1992 and another three in 1997 to make a current total of seven. During this period the ore throughput per roaster was progressively increased from 22 tph to near 30 tph, without sacrificing the nickel and cobalt reduction efficiency. 

The current production capacity is about 17,000 tpy of nickel and 800 tpy cobalt. 

The original Nicaro plant in Cuba is still operating and the newer Las Camariocas plant is now approaching 30,000 tpy Ni, after a long ramp-up. 

###### **2.2 COST OF ORE** 

The cost of supplying ore to any plant (per unit of nickel produced), is largely a function of; 

- proximity of the plant to the mine, 

- proximity of the mine or plant to the sea, 

- ore grade and 

- overall nickel recovery. 

Only grade and overall recovery have a bearing on the ore processing cost, but proximity to the mine and sea transportation can have a large impact on the total project cost. This point is illustrated by comparing the ore supply cost at Yabulu and Niquelandia. At Yabulu all ore is imported (from New Caledonia, Indonesia and the Philippines) whereas at Niquelandia the mine is situated only 6 km from the plant and ore is delivered by overhead tramway. As a consequence, the delivered ore cost to Yabulu is about US$1.25/lb Ni (varies with currency

###### **2.3 PLANT OPERATING COST** 

An aspect of Caron processing that has to be taken into account when comparing costs is that each plant uses a different back end refining circuit to process the intermediate mixed Ni-Co carbonate precipitate (Yabulu is unique in that the ASX allows pure Ni carbonate precipitate). It will be pointed out later that the PAL operations also have different refining circuits. 

In ore reduction roasting, all the Caron plants use sub-stoichiometric firing of fuel oil in the combustion chambers of vertical, multi-hearth roasters, furthermore both Yabulu and Niquelandia mix 2 to 2.5% fuel oil with the roaster feed ore to aid reduction.  Fuel oil is the single largest consumable cost in Caron plants and profitability is sensitive to the oil price. 

At Yabulu, coal is used for power and steam generation and most ore drying, whereas at Niquelandia fuel oil is used in ore drying, power and steam generation as well as in the roasters. 

The ore grade at Yabulu is higher than at Niquelandia and oil consumption is lower per tonne of ore treated. 

The costs quoted below are at a point in time and change with exchange rates, oil cost, production, etc and will thus vary month to month. 

The total cost of processing ore to carbonate intermediate at Yabulu is about US$1.08/lb Ni, whereas the Niquelandia cost has been about US$1.55/lb, some US$0.50/lb higher than Yabulu because of  the combination of: greater oil dependence, oil road freight from Sao Paulo (1,300km) and absence of an ASX circuit. 

At Yabulu, one of the advantages derived from the ASX circuit is that the refining cost of the nickel carbonate intermediate and the cobalt sulphide intermediate, respectively, is lower than for the Tocantins, Sao Paulo releach, purification and the nickel and cobalt electrowinning circuits. 

The Yabulu refining cost of nickel and cobalt are: 

- nickel carbonate to saleable nickel compacts, about US$0.20/lb Ni and 

- • cobalt sulphide to “chemgrade oxide-hydroxide”, about US$0.07/lb Ni. 

The total refining cost for both nickel and cobalt is thus about US$0.27/lb Ni. 

The mixed nickel-cobalt carbonate produced at Niquelandia is filtered, dried and transported 1,300 km by road to Sao Paulo for refining. The refining cost is nearly double that at Yabulu. 

The processing and refining cost at Yabulu is about US$1.35/lb Ni (before cobalt credit) The processing and refining cost at Niquelandia and Sao Paulo is about US$2.00/lb Ni. 

The aggregate total cost for the Yabulu project, including ore purchase and product marketing costs (before cobalt credit), is about US$2.70/lb Ni while Tocantins is about US$0.30/lb Ni lower, because of the lower cost of the delivered ore.

###### **2.4 FUTURE CARON DEVELOPMENT** 

The basic equipment and technology used in the Caron plants, such as roasters, calciners etc, was developed prior to the 1970’s. If a greenfield plant was to be designed today it

is likely to be significantly different to the previous generation of plants, notwithstanding the ASX and other developments that have been incorporated into existing plants. 

Some of the developments that could reduce capital and operating costs for a new greenfield Caron plant are listed below: 

- Reduction roast in rotary kilns (as used in several Fe/Ni operations) instead of multi hearth furnaces. Whereas many multi hearth furnaces are required to process a given mass of ore (12 at Yabulu for 2.5M tpy dry ore) these could be replaced with 2 or 3 rotary kilns. 

- Resin in pulp technology to complement the existing leach and CCD circuit. The underflow slurry from the final wash thickener could be directed through resin to allow nickel and cobalt recovery from the solution component of the slurry as well as the absorbed cobalt and nickel from the solid. Such a resin circuit would allow the reduction in the number of CCD thickener washing stages to possibly less than four. 

- Direct hydrogen reduction of basic nickel carbonate slurry instead of re-dissolution and reduction from solution. The nickel carbonate produced from the ASX loaded nickel strip stream at Yabulu is cobalt free and low in impurities, thus making it amenable to direct reduction to nickel metal. 

- Overall nickel and cobalt recovery enhancement can be expected from the combined benefits of the changes outlined above. It is expected that nickel recovery could be increased from the current 82% to 85% and cobalt from 55% to 65%. 

###### **3. PAL PROCESS** 

###### **3.1 CAPITAL COST OF WA PAL PROJECTS** 

The financial difficulties of all three W.A. projects have been well documented and can be attributed to a combination of : 

- escalation of capital costs, 

- an inability to achieve design production rates, and 

- operating costs significantly higher than anticipated. 

Historically, the single greatest barrier to entry to the nickel industry has been the capital cost of a greenfield plant. This had been the main deterrent to new plant construction since about half a dozen plants (Caron and smelters) were commissioned in the 1970’s, as a result of the nickel price boom of the late 1960’s. The Yabulu and Nonoc Caron plants were part of this construction surge and suffered for many years from low cash flow, exacerbated by the “oil shock” and an inability to repay interest and capital, with Nonoc shutting in 1986. The laterite smelters built at the time suffered a similar fate of capital cost escalation and debt repayment problems. 

The enthusiasm to build the three WA PAL plants was partly based on the mistaken belief that the construction cost would be about US$5.00 per annual lb of nickel and cobalt produced. It was well known from the Yabulu and Nonoc experience in the early 1970’s that a Caron plant would cost more than US$10.00 per annual lb to build. Similarly, the cost of greenfield

more than US$10.00 per annual lb by the 1990’s, so the PAL process looked very attractive in comparison. 

One reason why the US$5.00 /annual lb figure for the PAL plants was generally accepted as achievable, was the lack of a benchmarking commercial plant and unrealistic expectations of newcomers to the nickel business. Moa had been built 40 years previously and the design and technology was in many ways quite different, a point not fully appreciated at the time. The people who had built Moa had retired. 

As it turned out, the three WA projects ended up costing >US$10/annual lb Ni, a figure not too different to the expectation for a greenfield Caron plant or smelter. 

The higher than anticipated capital cost has again raised the old nickel industry problem of generating sufficient cash flow to service the construction debt. Even if the three WA PAL plants reach design production rates in the future, the sale proceeds required to provide a reasonable return on the capital employed is more than double that anticipated at the time construction commenced. 

Since 1974, it has essentially been concern about capital that has dissuaded existing nickel producers from building an integrated green-field plant anywhere in the world. 

###### **3.2 PROJECT STATUS** 

Advances in autoclave and flash design and materials of construction since Moa’s construction have been partly driven in the past decade by the gold industries use of oxidation pressure leaching (POL) for treating sulphide concentrates (and ore). The gold industry have not used titanium clad autoclaves, only because of concern about fires. 

The three WA PAL plants have autoclaves essentially of the same design, although the four at Murrin Murrin are of larger diameter and length. The change to mechanically agitated, six compartment, horizontal vessels was a dramatic move from the vertical pachucas installed at Moa. One of the unanticipated benefits of this change was a lower rate of scale formation on the vessel walls, due to greater scale nucleation in the slurry. This caused some initial problems, but following minor modifications has allowed longer than anticipated autoclave campaigns. 

The use of explosively bonded titanium alloy, while in use since the early 1970’s, in large autoclave construction has been pioneered in the three WA PAL plants. At the autoclave discharge, the use of staged flashing from 250<sup>0</sup> C (about 4,200 kPa) was a move away from the Moa mode of operation (initial heat exchange cooling of discharge slurry to 135<sup>0</sup> C) and had been partly pioneered in the gold and alumina industries.

###### **5.1 STATUS OF DEVELOPMENT** 

BHP spent 10 years developing new technologies for the recovery of nickel and cobalt from laterite ores, largely based on their involvement with the Gag Island deposit, before their merger with Billiton. The initial work started with pressure acid leach as a base and focused on the treatment of the complete laterite resource of both limonite and saprolite. In 1997 the focus changed from high pressure leach to the development of an atmospheric pressure leach process, but again with the aim of processing both the limonite and saprolite components of an orebody. 

The merger of BHP and Billiton in 2001 prompted an investigation into the applicability of atmospheric leach for treating Ravensthorpe ore, which Billiton had been testing with PAL. 

The driver for the atmospheric leach (AL) development was the elimination of the technically complex and high maintenance autoclave systems required in the 250<sup>0</sup> C PAL processing. 

For an AL process to be competitive with PAL the following would be required; 

- give good recoveries, 

- allow acceptable acid consumption and 

- produce low residual iron in solution. 

In late 1999 BHP built an atmospheric leach pilot plant in Reno, Nevada, which was run for 3 months with Gag Island ore. The limonite component of the ore was leached for several hours before saprolite was added and the leaching continued. The pilot plant was moved to Newcastle in late 2000 and further testing undertaken on Ravensthorpe ore in 2001. 

AL is conducted at a nominal 95<sup>0</sup> C and the key to the technology was the realization that acid can be regenerated by iron jarosite precipitation and the resultant excess acid used to leach the saprolitic ore at atmospheric pressure. By using sea water for ore slurry preparation there is sufficient sodium as sodium chloride present to allow the formation of sodium jarosite. Other sodium salts are a suitable alternative if only fresh water is available. 

The limonitic ore is pumped to the first of a series of agitated leach tanks as a slurry (approximately 35% solids) and acid added in a ratio of about 1:1 to ore. After the acid addition the solids content falls to about 25% and the heat of reaction raises the temperature close to the desired 95<sup>0</sup> C. Steam is used to maintain temperature at that level. 

By undertaking the leach at 95<sup>0</sup> C, rather than 250<sup>0</sup> C, as in PAL, the reaction rate is considerably slower and the required residence time much longer. The testing undertaken by BHP indicated that a residence time of 10 to 12 hours is required to achieve >90% nickel and cobalt extraction. 

AL can be used in combination with PAL, whereby it may be deemed advantageous to process the limonite and saprolite ore components separately by PAL and AL, respectively. BHP Billiton have designated this combination as Enhanced PAL. Alternatively it is possible to process

a lower nickel grade middlings stream from a limonite beneficiation circuit by AL and the upgraded product by PAL.

###### **5.2 STRENGTHS AND WEAKNESSES** 

The strengths and weaknesses of AL are listed below. 

###### **Strengths** 

- Process equipment is simple. 

- Ramp-up should be rapid. 

- Maintenance should be low and on-stream availability high. 

###### **Weaknesses** 

- Acid consumption is higher than for PAL. 

- Overall nickel and cobalt extraction marginally lower than for PAL. 

- The leach residence time is higher than for PAL, about 12 hr vs 1.5 hr. 

- Tailings contain more jarosite than for PAL, which produces mainly hematite. Jarosite is more chemically unstable than hematite and may present long term environmental problems. 

###### **6. MATCHING PROCESS WITH DEPOSIT** 

###### **6.1 LATERITE ORE PROFILE** 

Laterite ore bodies typically consist of a profile ranging from high iron, low magnesium and silica (limonite) at the top to low iron, high magnesium and silica (saprolite) at the bottom. The limonite ore is unsuitable for smelting and the saprolite ore relatively unsuitable for hydrometallurgical processing (high acid consumption for PAL and low Ni extraction for Caron). Historically, the two ore types have been treated by different processes, Caron (with the exception of Moa) for limonite and smelting for saprolite. Attempts to develop a single process for both limonite and saprolite (such as by AMAX in the 1970’s) had not resulted in a commercialized technology. 

This has led to a situation, as in New Caledonia and Indonesia, where limonite is mined and shipped to the Caron plant at Yabulu and the underlying saprolite then mined and shipped to smelters in Japan. The Doniambo and Pomalaa ferronickel smelters in New Caledonia and Indonesia respectively, are also fed with saprolite ore. 

A typical laterite ore profile from ground surface to bedrock , with the portions of limonite and saprolite ore that are generally suitable for the processing options of Smelting, PAL, EPAL and Caron, is shown in Fig. 8.

###### **6.2 CARON PROCESS** 

. 

The ideal ore for Caron processing is a high iron limonite with silica and magnesia levels as low as possible, not because the latter consume excess reagent or cause particular impurity problems, but because the silica level is roughly inversely proportional to Ni extraction achieved in the roast and leach. For example a limonite ore with <3% silica may achieve >90% Ni extraction, whereas 20% silica ore may achieve only 60% Ni extraction. 

It has been demonstrated at both Yabulu and Niquelandia that up to 30% saprolite can be economically co-treated with limonite in the Caron ore feed. 

###### **6.3 PAL PROCESS** 

The ideal ore for PAL processing is essentially  the same as that for Caron, but for a different reason.

In PAL, the Ni extraction may not be too different for both low and high silica and magnesia ores, but the acid addition required for saprolite ore is much higher, principally because the magnesia is an acid consumer. To compare the same ore with the Caron process above, the acid consumption for 3% silica (1% MgO) ore would be about 0.25 t/t ore, but for 20% silica (8% MgO) ore >0.50t/t ore. 17 ALTA Free Library www.altamet.com.au ###### **6.4 AL PROCESS** Atmospheric leach, as developed by BHP Billiton has not been installed in a commercial operation and consequently definitive statements about economics and operability can not be made. BHP originally developed the AL process as a simple, but elegant way out of the dilemma of building a PAL plant in a location without ready access to the skilled labor required to operate such a sophisticated circuit. It is particularly applicable to resources that have significant saprolite or nontronite components, such as those at Gag Island, Indonesia and San Felipe, Cuba, respectively. The biggest drawbacks of the AL process is that acid consumption can be more than twice that of PAL (depending on iron content of ore) and the nickel and cobalt extractions marginally lower. In summary, recognizing the slow ramp-up and higher than anticipated operating costs (particularly maintenance) of the three WA PAL producers, the higher acid costs and lower recovery of AL were seen as a reasonable trade off for rapid ramp-up and lower maintenance. ###### **6.5 EPAL PROCESS** The use of saprolite ore for neutralizing PAL autoclave discharge liquor from limonite, as in the EPAL process may give the best of both worlds for many laterite deposits. ###### **7. ###### **ABSTRACT** 

Atmospheric leaching (AL) of laterites is a technology receiving increasing attention.  It can potentially be used in place of High Pressure Acid Leach (HPAL) or in combination with HPAL. 

Qualitatively the technologies can be compared as follows: 

|**HIGH PRESSURE ACID LEACH**|**ATMOSPHERIC LEACH**|
|---|---|
|High capital|Low capital|
|High maintenance|Low maintenance|
|Low acid consumption|High acid consumption|
|Predictable downstream hydrometallurgy|Some solutions difficult to treat|
|Shortresidence time|Moderateresidence time|
|High Extractions|Variable Extractions|



Quantitatively, with operating experience of HPAL gained at the Bulong Nickel Operation, it has been estimated that AL enjoys a capital and commissioning advantage over HPAL in the order of AU$65 million for a 10,000 tpa operation. 

Preston Resources Limited (“Preston”) and Western Minerals Technology (“WMT”) have conducted preliminary AL testwork with encouraging results; achieving greater than 90% nickel extraction on a Serpentinite component of Bulong ore. 

Preston and WMT are conducting further work in a Syndicated Research Initiative aimed at providing junior explorers/producers with alternative process routes for the exploitation of nickel laterite orebodies. 

###### **1. INTRODUCTION** 

Preston Resources has been involved in the development of two lateritic nickel projects, the Bulong project in Western Australia (presently producing at 85% of design capacity) and the Marlborough Project in Queensland (currently on hold).  Both of these projects were designed as high-pressure acid leach facilities.  Although this was a logical choice to ensure plant operation conditions catered for all ore types, investigation has shown that a number of ore types present in each of these deposits leach adequately at atmospheric pressure. 

Atmospheric leaching of nickel laterite is not a new concept but it has remained largely in the realms of research and development for a number of reasons. 

Recently, as the commissioning and financial woes of the three WA High Pressure Acid Leach (HPAL) plants have become apparent, there has been renewed interest in the idea. 

Jervois have been conducting research into atmospheric leach for potential use at their Young’s deposit in NSW using TTS technology developed by Duyvesteyn [2] [3]. 

BHP/Billiton have patented technology in atmospheric leaching and have presented an outline of their process [4].  This technology was targeted for use at Gag Island, but is also being incorporated int

###### **3. LATERITE CHARACTERISTICS** 

The nickel industry, as a whole, is characterised by a plethora of technologies, flowsheets and cost drivers.  As a subset of the nickel industry, the laterite industry is every bit as complex. 

Canterford [16] and Whittington and Muir [17] have reviewed the treatment of laterites and from these, other sources and the Bulong experience some general comments can be made: 

- Laterite orebodies are extremely complex and despite much mineralogical study are not well characterised. 

- The mesh between mineralogical understanding and metallurgical treatment is poorly developed. 

- Laterite orebodies, whether characterised as “wet tropical” or “WA dry” are significantly different even at the pit to pit level. 

- The nickel values (and cobalt to a certain extent) are relatively evenly disseminated throughout the orebody. 

- Treatment routes are many and diverse including both pyrometallurgical and hydrometallurgical options, with downstream processing variations resulting in the production of both intermediate and/or final products. 

- The whole orebody, above an economic cut off grade, can be subjected to processing or specific mineralogies can be subjected to processing or any combination of the above.

###### **3.1 THE NATURE OF LATERITIC OREBODIES** 

Notwithstanding the above generalities the following description is offered, based primarily on the Bulong orebody. 

Orebodies developed within the lateritic profile show a range of lithology and, within each lithology, a range of mineralogy.  The Bulong oxidation profile serves as a good example, which may simplistically be considered as ferruginous laterite at the surface, grading to clay zones, saprolite and fresh rock (Figure 2).  The ferruginous zones are generally depleted in nickel with most of the nickel grades occurring within the clay zones (which have n

o relict host rock fabric) and the saprolites (which do have remnant host rock fabrics).  These units overlie fresh basement rocks of ultramafic composition. 

Mineralogy of each of the major lithological groups is variable and hence the chemistry of the ore is also variable.  Nickel occurs as cationic substitution in silicates and as solid solution in various oxide phases.  Within individual lithological groups, there is strong partitioning of nickel and cobalt.  This partitioning appears to be a function of development of the new mineral phases during weathering as the nickel is released from minerals in the fresh rock and precipitated and accumulated in the weathering products. 

Insufficient work has been undertaken to date to determine whether the partitioning observed in some of the Bulong orebodies is a general feature of the development of lateritic nickel ores; however the following comments can be made based on observations undertaken at Bulong to date: 

- Nickel is contained within a number of phases including hydrated iron oxides, Fe/Mn oxides, nontronite, saponite, septechlorite and serpentine.  Background levels of nickel decline from ore grade to less than 0.1% nickel within the silicate phases of the fresh rock. 

- Nontronite contains ore grade levels of nickel (greater than 1% NiO) in the absence of other mineral phases.  However in the presence of septechlorite (which may commonly contain >5% NiO), the nickel partitions into septechlorite which coexists with low nickel (0.1% to 0.2%) nontronite.  Similarly nickel may preferentially partition into oxides which coexist with nontronite.  These oxides commonly contain nickel levels in excess of 5% NiO. 

- Some silicates contain small amounts of cobalt however cobalt is more commonly found within manganese oxides which may contain up to 20% CoO. 

- Serpentine, which occurs in abundance towards the base of the profile in the saprolite zone commonly contains ore grade nickel 

The characteristics of the ore and, in particular, the structure of the mineral components (i.e. the nature of the silicate lattice and the arrangement of constituents within that lattice, in particular hydroxyl groups, nickel and cobalt) affects the ability to leach. 

Samples examined to date show some minerals are much more susceptible to atmospheric leaching than others.  In a qualitative sense it appears that minerals with hydroxyls exposed on the outer surfaces (e.g. in brucite layers or serpentine like structures) show good atmospheric leaching characteristics. The nature of the products in solution, and the nature of products precipitated control the acid consumption and to a large extent it becomes an economic decision as to whether high <u>pressure acid leach (generally consuming less acid) or atmospheric leach</u>

covery. ###### **3.2 BENEFICIATION AND SELECTIVE MINING** The varying physical properties of the minerals and partitioning of nickel within those minerals, provides the opportunity for beneficiation by separating nickel rich and nickel poor phases within the ore. Bulong has achieved an average 15% upgrade in head grade through silica rejection based on size. Whilst various beneficiation factors are quoted on laterite orebodies, these are all very modest in comparison to, say, flotation on a sulphide orebody. While the search continues for the “holy grail” of laterite concentration, selective mining has the ability to separate minerals favourable to atmospheric leaching. Figure 2 shows some of the variations exhibited within a single orebody at Bulong. Although these variations are somewhat simplistic they demonstrate the distribution of phases containing much of the nickel. The upper zones tend to contain nontronite with smaller amounts of septechlorite, the two phases are intimately associated and it is impractical to separate these. As the nontronite generally exhibits poor extractions under atmospheric leach conditions, and as it is not possible to separate the higher-grade components (interstitial septechlorite), the ore type is best suited to high-pressure acid leach. With this type of mineral processing no separation is required and good nickel extractions are obtained from the ore when processed in bulk. Below the clay zones the content of serpentine increases and relict textures of the primary rock can be identified. The structure of the minerals contained within this zone (the saprolite zone) is such that they have exposed hydroxyls on the mineral surfaces and are much more prone to acid attack. This type of mineralogy is ideally suited to atmospheric leaching. This configuration is common towards the base of the lateritic profile at Bulong and leads to situations where such material can be selectively mined towards the top of the saprolite profile but may be bulk mined close to the transition from saprolite to fresh rock, leading to the possibility of parallel processing flow sheets (utilising high-pressure acid leach for the more difficult material high in the profile and atmospheric leach for material lower in the profile). ###### **6. ATMOSPHERIC LEACH TESTWORK** 

The first leach tests undertaken on Bulong ore were atmospheric leach tests [19].  These tests indicated good extractions could be obtained from the material treated.  No further work was undertaken on downstream processing as it was considered the chemistry of the solutions would result in processing problems for the preferred solvent extraction process flow sheet.  The samples leached were composites in which most nickel was contained in limonite and serpentine, with these two phases occurring in different proportions in each sample.  The samples were ground and subjected to a range of acid concentrations (up to 1kg/kg) and temperatures (up to 95°C) and leached for 24 hours. ###### **7. DEVELOPMENT STRATEGY** 

It is clear that there is a place for atmospheric leaching of laterites, and Preston is keen to develop technology applicable to its own deposits as well as other deposits. 

In broad terms, the strategy is being shaped by the following factors/observations. 

- Location.  In general it is expected that AL will be more applicable to WA type dry laterites as opposed to wet tropical laterites.  However, as has been pointed out, the mineralogy of laterites and particularly the mineralogy/metallurgy interface is not well understood.  As such the applicability of AL and/or a combination of AL/HPAL should not be discarded, out of hand for any orebody. 

- History.  Conditions which made HPAL favourable for Moa Bay in 1960, high iron ore and high acid prices [20] were not necessarily transferable to WA in 1990.  Certainly, with acid constituting the single biggest operating cost element, the current sulfur prices are a major factor in considering AL in 2002. 

- Experience.  Our own experience at Bulong, and the well documented experience of the other WA producers, has highlighted the fact that the capital costs, ongoing maintenance costs and commissioning/ramp-up times for HPAL plants were greatly underestimated.  There is no doubt that pioneering work has been achieved, but as a bold debatable statement we offer the following:   Engineering is still playing catch-up to the process concept of HPAL. 

- Downstream processing.  The HPAL/AL debate is one of degree.  With HPAL experience under our belt, the disadvantages of AL such as iron and silica control and solid/liquid separation do not loom as large as previously.  There are technologies available or in development to deal with the above and other industries to learn from.  Iron hydrolysis at elevated temperature has been practised for many years in the nickel sulphide [21] and zinc industries [22] [23].  The milder processing conditions (150C – 180C) compared to HPAL at 250C (and rising) is a quantum leap in the right direction in terms of engineering simplicity and reliability. 

15 

ALTA Free Library  www.altamet.com.au 

- Flow

sheet Development.  As with sulphide operations there is not one best laterite flowsheet.  The best flowsheet for a particular orebody is dependent on a myriad of factors including mineralogy, geography, infrastructure, power, fuel, reagent and transport costs, labour skills base, etc. 

- Economic Decision.  The above factors emphasise the fact that ultimately the choice of HPAL, AL or a combination thereof must be an economic one.  Why treat the whole orebody through an expensive process if it is not necessary?  Can we learn from the gold industry where the bulk of the ore is leached atmospherically and refractory ores are pressure oxidized? 

- Global Trends.  It is our view that further rationalisation will take place in the nickel industry leading ultimately to fewer, larger players.  As part of this, we envisage greater movement of concentrates to refineries in Europe, Asia and Australia.  As such there will be increased scope for juniors to process and sell intermediates to the large companies with hungry refineries.  Clearly if this can be done with a low capital plant the economics should stack up; a laterite equivalent of the small nickel sulphide mine and concentrator. 

###### **8. CONCLUSIONS** 

Preston and WMT have come to the conclusion that there is a need to develop atmospheric leaching technology and that the correct strategy is as follows: 

- Conduct further testwork on the atmospheric leaching of nickel laterites to develop an improved understanding of the technical and economic factors impacting on the technology.  A specific aim of the testwork will be the generation of data, sufficient in quantity and quality, to facilitate optimisation of laterite orebody exploitation. 

- Develop relevant downstream processing leading to the production of economic intermediate and/or final products.  The optimum process and product form is orebody dependant and project specific, encompassing all the factors already mentioned.  WMT has particular expertise in this area and has developed and piloted a variety of nickel/cobalt flowsheets, including a number of product forms. 

- Seek support from junior explorers/producers who do not have access to expensive R&D programmes to join Preston and WMT in a Syndicated Research Initiative.  A specific objective of the SRI is to provide each participant with project specific data aimed at optimum process selection.

Resin-in-pulp (RIP) technology was developed for the recovery of valuable metals from high volumes of low grade pulps, as is the case with gold processing.  More recently, the application of this technology has been evaluated for the recovery of soluble losses of valuable metals from solid residues in base metal plants.  For this type of application, the RIP process will improve overall plant recoveries, especially where solid-liquid separation proves difficult as a result of poor filterability or settling characteristics of the solids.  An added benefit of the RIP process is a reduction in the environmental impact of the solid residues contaminated with entrained base metals from the plant. 

Mintek investigated the metallurgical and economic feasibility of using RIP technology for the recovery of soluble cobalt, nickel and copper from thickener underflows on behalf of Anglovaal Mining.  Laboratory and mini-plant investigations included the recovery of copper with RIP, followed by simultaneous nickel and cobalt recovery using a second RIP circuit.  Recovery of copper, nickel and cobalt in a single RIP circuit was also investigated. 

###### **1. INTRODUCTION** 

The development of the resin-in-pulp (RIP) process at Mintek was initially targeted at the recovery of metals from large volumes of low-grade leach pulps, as is the case in the gold processing industry. Mintek’s RIP expertise culminated in the development of a resin-inpulp process, MINRIP<sup>TM</sup> , for the recovery of gold from leached slurries. Mintek has subsequently evaluated the applicability of this technology for the in-pulp extraction of copper, zinc, nickel, cobalt, vanadium, manganese and cyanide [1,2,3]. 

The main application of the RIP process in the base metal industry will be the scavenging of soluble metals from leach residues, precipitation residues and other solid wastes that have poor filterability or settling characteristics. However, this technology can also be applied to the recovery of metals from the leach slurries when low-grade materials are treated.  The major advantages of the resin-in-pulp pr

ocess are as follows: - It is effective for the recovery of soluble metals from pulps. The fact that the process operates in a pulp medium means that the upstream solid-liquid requirements may be reduced or possibly eliminated. In addition, it may be possible to significantly reduce wash water requirements associated with conventional solid-liquid separation steps. - The RIP process may be able to achieve lower discharge metal concentrations than those possible with the more conventional filtration or solid-liquid separation systems, hence reducing the potential for problems associated with the disposal of wastes containing soluble metals. - The overall metal recoveries on the plant can be improved. - Co-precipitated and adsorbed metal species can generally be recovered with the RIP process, which will further improve the overall metal recovery. Anglovaal Mining commissioned Mintek to evaluate the feasibility of a RIP process for the recovery of soluble cobalt, nickel and copper from a thickener underflow. This paper outlines the process development, from the batch laboratory testwork to the continuous mini-plant campaign. Based on these results, full-scale plants were sized and preliminary techno-economic studies were conducted on three flowsheet options. ###### **2. PROCESS DESCRIPTION** A RIP plant could either be operated in a carousel counter-current mode where resin handling can be limited and the resin inventory is accurately controlled in each stage, or in a continuous counter-current mode. Although inventory control may prove more difficult during continuous operation, a substantial capital expenditure (CAPEX) saving is possible. For the recovery of base metals with RIP, typical upgrading ratios vary between 10 and 50, in comparison with 1000 or more for gold as applied in the CIS and MinRIP-. Hence, in 1 ALTA Free Library www.altamet.com.au order to achieve barren specifications on a base metal plant, resin inventory control across the adsorption train will be critical. Consequently, a carousel mode of operation was chosen for the mini-plant evaluation for the recovery of cobalt, nickel and copper from the Anglovaal Mining slurries. After the resin has been passed counter-currently through the adsorption plant, the resin will be loaded predominantly with the valuable metals together with lower concentrations of other metals.
