The loaded resin exiting the adsorption circuit is separated from the pulp by means of a linear belt, sieve bend or vibrating screen, and the pulp is returned to the repulp tank. The loaded resin is then rinsed with water to remove any particulates, after which the resin is transferred into an elution column. During elution, the metals are stripped from the resin with sulphuric acid (this could be fresh acid or any acid-bearing stream), producing a concentrated metal sulphate eluate. Excess acid and entrained eluate solution are washed from the resin bed with water, and the eluate, and possibly the wash water, are returned to the relevant unit operation in the primary process flowsheet. The eluted, washed resin is returned to the adsorption circuit during the next transfer. Elution and washing of resin in a fixed bed are established operations, therefore the miniplant investigation focused on the adsorption circuit. ###### **3. ###### **4. CONTINUOUS MINI-PLANT CAMPAIGN** 

The mini-plant consisted of a four-stage cascade of contactors, each with an active volume of 960mL. The resin-pulp mixing in each stage was achieved with mechanical overhead stirrers. Resin was retained in the contactor by means of a 200 µm peripheral screen, and pulp gravitated through the screens from one stage to the next. During adsorption, the pH was controlled at the desired set point in each stage. Lime slurry, limestone slurry or any other alkali may be used for pH control. 

In order to minimise the CAPEX associated with the adsorption circuit, pulp and resin residence times are minimised, whilst resin loading is maximised to limit the OPEX of the operation.  For a carousel operation, physical constraints often restrict the design, e.g. the time required to drain the first adsorption stage and separate the loaded resin from the pulp.

###### **2. PURITY SYSTEMS INC. TECHNOLOGY PROFILE** 

"Conventional" ion exchange resins are totally organic polymeric beads that incorporate active functional groups that are attracted to or bind with metals or other species by chelation, ion exchange, or other phenomena.  The basic improvement of **_PSI_** technology over "synthetic" (organic) bead resins is that it is primarily an inorganic core that has been coated with a nominal layer of organic polymer, functionalized to provide the active sites that attract and separate the metals. **_PSI_** has overcome so

me of the structural and material deficiencies of the organic bead resins whereby the core, or inactive inorganic component, is not subject to the same degree of physical and chemical (even radiolytic) trauma that a totally organic substance may encounter.  In addition, **_PSI_** inorganic substrates with active organic functionality can be made in kinetically superior size ranges. To achieve this feat for organic bead resins, extraordinary process control in the emulsion polymerization process in their production would be required, making any such materials very expensive to manufacture. 

The patented **_PSI_** materials are generally made by conditioning silica gel to accept an organic polymerized coating.  This coating completely covers the gel core and strengthens it to make it rigid.  This polymer is in itself a mass of active functional sites, and can be further reacted to form other functionalized sites with different properties for a variety of metals separations.  Other inorganic substrates can be similarly treated. 

This coated inorganic material is not so subject to the ionic strength of the solution in which it is immersed, exhibiting minimal osmotic properties, as opposed to totally organic resins. The **_PSI_** product does not shrink or swell with loading or eluting as with synthetic bead resin.  Because water adsorption is not an expected physical feature as it is for bead resin, it can be stored and shipped dry - more product per unit of weight - and has dramatic shelf life - which cannot be said for other totally organic resins.  Because it does not swell, smaller columns can be used than for synthetic resins, with precautions for tank ruptures avoided due to potentially expanding packing.  Suspended solids, if present, will need additional freeboard space in order to remove. 

Solvent extraction lixiviants that are made up of amines, oximes, phosphines, hydroxyquinolines, etc., have limited shelf life or require special storage and handling, and may in themselves be toxic, and must be combined with hazardous and volatile solvents for removing metals from a leachate.  The **_PSI_** material has no volatile component as do these extraction materials and as many ion exchange synthetic organic bead resins do have, contaminated with monomer and decomposition products. 

In contrast to solvent extraction/liquid ion exchange, the **_PSI_** material is readily isolated whether in virgin or loaded form.  It can be fluidized, pumped in an aqueous environment as well as sluiced, and can be utilized in a fixed or fluidized bed and does not require volatile/flammable solvents that must be recovered.  In high elevations and remote situations solvent make-up can be problematic.  Also dilute raffinates can be treated with **_PSI_** materials effectively where the limitations of diminishing returns of dilute metal recovery by solvent methods is readily overcome. 

Comparing the **_PSI_** materials with the _SuperLig_<sup>_®_</sup> products, t

he main difference is that those products may be totally synthetic organic structures like conventional bead resin and, in those cases, subject to some of the same thermal, structural, chemical and radiolytic limitations.  These host/guest "clathrate" products are also relatively expensive active sites.  This clever technology is also suitable for removal of monovalent ions in some of its forms, however, the **_PSI_** materials are only polyvalent/transition metal ion removers, limiting the load on the exchanger and with relative selectivity.  Precipitated or potentially colloidal substances like Fe will not block or foul the **_PSI_** material by entering a pore or cavity.  Some applications allow for the removal of various iron species from solution. Many applications allow for dramatic pH ranges, extreme acid environments and using

The profitable recovery of metals from low value ore deposits has for time in eternity posed difficulties, and, whilst technological advances have gone some way towards making life a little easier, the challenge still remains.  As an example, the use of improved bacteria inoculums, such as the Pacific Ore Technologies proprietary bacteria offering improved kinetics and higher operating temperatures, has gained wide interest and do certainly improve the process economics.  For comparatively high value metals, such as cobalt and nickel, these improved bacteria offer considerable potential for resource exploitation.  The real challenge lies in the lower value metals such as copper where, in many cases, even if the copper is solubilized with other high value metals during the leach process, there is simply not enough value there to pay for the industry accepted recovery methods such as solvent extraction – electro winning (SX-EW). 

Some advances in alternative technologies such as the EMEW<sup>®</sup> direct EW cells, produced and marketed by **_Electrometals Technologies Limited_** have been made and have gained some acceptance when the economics are suitable. **_Purity Systems Inc._** , in conjunction with **_Ammtec Limited_** , have quietly over the past 12 months or so devoted very considerable effort in the evaluation of the PSI resins to the profitable recovery of value metals, such as cobalt, nickel and copper, from low value ore deposits.  By their very nature these deposits tend to lend themselves to heap leaching processes.  These processes can work well, for example the **_Titan Resources NL_** Radio Hill project, but the problem remains of how to economically recover the metals once they are brought into solution.  We believe the **_PSI_** family of resins offers a very compelling and attractive solution to this problem.  The selectivity and low cost of these resins, coupled very high flow rate capability translating into lower comparative pressure drops withi

n the columns, can provide very significantly improved comparative CAPEX (capital costs) and OPEX (operating costs).  Obviously you still must have sufficient metal value there to pay for the recovery system but the **_PSI_** resins do open up profitable recovery for many deposits which previously have been written off as non economic.  So why do we say this and what are we basing it on?  The simple answer is the comparatively **lower cost** of the **_PSI_** resins to the available resin alternatives (typically 40% cheaper). 

All of the new generation resins offer significant advantages in technology and, at the end of the day, they do function in basically the same way, however there are some differences in the way they go about it.  Detailed examples are given later in this paper on maximizing the unique properties of these resins, such as selective elution and recycle of the elution stream to increase target metal tenors to open up some interesting and innovative recovery possibilities. 

**_Purity Systems Inc._** do not intend to offer products for every application, even if technically feasible, rather we are targeting specific areas where we know that our products work well and offer significant economic advantages such as nickel, cobalt and in some instances copper recovery.  This said, two very pertinent comments must be made. Firstly, for any application, flows and metals tenor will dictate the economics of any recovery system be it IX, SX, precipitation and so on.  You must look at all of the available recovery options and make an economic and technical assessment.  Most often one or two of the possibilities will stand out.

###### **3. RESIN BATCH TESTING** 

For any process application there are often several competing or complimentary technologies available which are capable of carrying out the required task.  As would be expected, these technologies may vary in the way they achieve this and also in the costs associated with them, both operating and capital. 

The majority of the technology suppliers, including most ion exchange resin suppliers, are now capable of generating an indicative capital cost estimate (in conjunction with systems suppliers) based on solution flows and solution matrix.  It may be prudent to obtain this information prior to embarking on a test program. 

Once the decision has been made to have a closer look at the technology, the next step is to conduct a batch test program which should be designed to confirm expected technical performance and, additionally, to provide sufficient data to allow a more detailed estimate of capital costs to be supplied. 

Any ion exchange batch test program must consist, at a minimum, of the following essential steps: 

- Comprehensive analysis of the process liquor 

- 

   - Selection of resin 

- Determination of loading resin loading capacity 

- Determination of resin loading kinetics 

- 

   - Determination of co-loading elements for product and by-product selectivity. 

- Determination of wash ratios 

- Determination of elution kinetics for product and by-products.

- Determination of the effect of recycle streams 

- Comprehensive analysis of the final elute product 

It is important to remember that mixtures of metals will behave differently to each of the elements tested individually. 

Each of these points when combined will provide sufficient information to enable a preliminary system design and system cost estimate to be made. 

###### **3.1 ANALYSIS OF PROCESS LIQUOR AND RESIN SELECTION** 

A preliminary technical assessment based on client supplied analysis data will have already been conducted, and a resin capable of carrying out the duty selected.  During this process particular attention would have been paid to the following: 

- Process pH 

The resin selected must be able to not only operate at the advised pH but additionally, <u>at the very least, must be capable of operating over the pH range</u> expected to be experienced during normal process operation.  To reduce technical risk the resin should ideally be capable of operating at pH’s outside of the expected range to allow for any abnormal process occurrences

.  pH is important as the metal selectivity and loading will vary in line with the variations in pH. 

- Loading Elements 

An assessment of the resin’s selectivity for the target metals would have already been conducted.  The resin would have been selected for its ability to load the target metals at process pH.  It is important, at this stage, to consider the remaining elements in the liquor and their deportment during the load cycle.  Coloading elements will normally deport to the elution streams thereby contaminating the final elute liquor.  If recycling is used, for example to increase the metal tenor in the elute liquor, then the level of contaminants in the elute liquor will increase with each recycle.  It is essential to have a thorough understanding of what specification is required for the final elute liquor.  Removal of some of the contaminants may be achieved by the use of selective elution or, alternatively, by taking advantage of differing binding affinities of elements to the resin during the load cycle. 

Other sources of contamination that should be considered are the contaminants used in the acid expected to be available on-site and any further down-stream processing of the elute liquor, for example pH adjustment. 

Finally, the resin testing facility should also request a sample of the process water from the site.  This will enable an assessment to be made on its possible use during the **rinse – wash** cycles.  Whilst the resin may be capable of rejecting all of the contaminating elements in the process water, highly saline process waters do impact on the system materials of construction and in the final analysis it may be more cost effective to install a reverse osmosis, or similar, plant.

Prior to conducting the program a decision must be made as to whether to feed the process streams to the top or bottom of the column. The choice of which system to go with, in most cases, is governed by the resin inventory versus systems cost. Generally speaki

ng, fixed bed columns will be cheaper to manufacture than a carousel type system but will require a greater resin inventory. For those applications where the cost savings in resin inventory outweigh the increased system costs of the carousel equipment, the carousel system should be seriously considered. Carousel systems should provide lower operating costs and steady state product concentrations may be higher. For fixed bed columns there are two primary considerations in the sizing of the columns, the first being resin kinetics and resin loading capacities, whilst the second is hydraulic limits (liquor flow rates and their effects on channelling within the column). It may be possible if the resin kinetics are fast enough to reduce the resin inventory by using smaller, but more, columns coupled with a shorter comparative cycle time. Offsetting the reduced resin inventory, in this case, is the comparative increase in valving complexity and increased auxiliary and pumping equipment. In sizing a fixed bed column we are aiming to minimise the pressure drop within the column at the optimum flow rate. It is important to use a bed depth in-line with the column diameter to give a suitable aspect ratio (height/diameter), typically 1 to 2. Very shallow beds may lead to inefficient ion exchange, whilst a high bed will result in higher-pressure drops across the bed leading to comparatively more costly materials of construction and increased pumping costs. ###### **4. RESIN PILOTING** 

The batch testing has now been conducted and data evaluated, resin selection made, systems choice made, preliminary system design generated, estimated capital costs supplied and a decision made to proceed to piloting. 

The pilot principals are essentially the same for fixed bed columns and carousel systems. For fixed bed columns, normally the total height of the commercial beds are calculated and heights of seven or more metres have been designed.  For a pilot application it is not easy to use small columns of these heights, so what is commonly done is to connect several smaller columns together such that the total combined column heights are equal that of the height of the commercial bed.  For carousel systems the issue of column height is not as pronounced due to the use of a larger number of short bed columns. 

The pilot run must demonstrate that the process works metallurgically, and products and by-products meet target grades.  It is essential that that the correct feed is used for the pilot and that all recycles be used in the process.  For the piloting of resins the optimised system must be run for a sufficient period of time to ascertain any drop in resin loading capacities over time.  Normally, a minimum of sixty cycles is recommended.  If we are using fixed bed columns with a cycle time of 5 hours, this would require running the circuit for just over 12 days of continuous running.  If using carousels with a cycle time of 1 hour then a minimum continuous running time of two and a half days would be needed. 

For styrene based resins reductions in loading capacities of between 27 and 63 percent over four years have been reported by Michael Gottlieb in his paper titled “Predicting The Operating Capacity of Strongly Basic Anion Resins From Static Laboratory Tests” published in the Water Conditioning and Purification Journal May 1997.

However, the precipitation and re-leaching stages results in complexity of the process flowsheet. Reagents such as ammonia are expensive and the scrubbing and recovery of ammonia are not easy. Furthermore, the reductive stripping of cobalt from organic extractant and the re-oximation of the organic extractant cause organic degradation (Kindred 2000) and the cobalt sulphide containing zinc is a semi-product, indicating a revenue loss. Cobalt, copper, zinc and manganese are separated from nickel, calcium and magnesium by solvent extraction with Cyanex 272 (Fig. 3). This requires large contactors in both circuits, indicating higher capital cost. Furthermore, the use of sulphide precipitation, solids/liquid separation and re-leach to separate manganese and the subsequent zinc SX and copper IX make the cobalt circuit complicated and costly. The formation of gypsum in the Versatic 10 circuit causes operational problems and nickel loss. It would be ideal to separate nickel and cobalt from the major impurities (Mn, Mg and Ca) through a direct solvent extraction (DSX) process in the first SX circuit without intermediate precipitation and re-leach. The concentrated and purified nickel and cobalt could then be further purified and recovered in a second SX circuit. At Inco’s Goro mine, New Caledonia, a nickel/cobalt demonstration plant has been operated for over two years (Mihaylov et al. 2000). A conceptual flowsheet is shown in Fig. 4. After the removal of copper by IX, the leach solution is subjected to solvent extraction using Cyanex 301. Cobalt, nickel and zinc are extracted and stripped using 6 M HCl to separate them from the major impurities (Mn, Mg and Ca). Zinc is then separated by IX and cobalt is separated from nickel by SX using tertiary octyl amine (TOA). After hydrolysis, nickel is recovered as oxide and HCl is recycled for stripping. Cobalt is precipitated as carbonate. Its major advantages are - Removal of the main impurities in one SX circuit. - No intermediate precipitation and re-leach, and - No pH adjustment due to extraction at low pH. Although the Goro process is a direct SX process, its major disadvantages are - Copper has to be eliminated using IX due to its irreversible extraction by Cyanex 301, - The whole volume of the leach solution passes through two circuits (copper IX and Cyanex 301 SX), resulting in high capital costs, - High acidity HCl (6 M), high temperature (60ºC) and longer than usual stripping time (5 minutes) have to be used to strip the nickel, cobalt and zinc from the loaded organic solution, - Expensive HCl has to be recovered and recycled which would be costly due to its highly corrosive nature, and - Cyanex 301 has to be regenerated due to degradation by Fe3+ and/or O2. 4 ALTA Free Library www.altamet.com.au H2SO4 Laterite ore SO2 Limestone

DSX PROCESSES DEVELOPED BY THE AJ PARKER CENTRE / CSIRO MINERALS** The SX group of the AJ Parker Cooperative Research Centre for Hydrometallurgy / CSIRO Minerals has developed SX processes to directly recover nickel and cobalt from leach solutions without intermediate precipitation and re-leach steps. ###### **2.1 SEPARATION OF NICKEL FROM CALCIUM WITH VERSATIC 10 AND SYNERGIST CLX50** There is no highly selective extractant for nickel and cobalt as there is for copper (LIX 984 and Acorga M5640) and the development of new extractants is very expensive (Mackenzie, 2001). Even if a new extractant is successfully synthesised in t

he laboratory, the cost of commercialisation would be in the order of US$3-5 million. On this analysis, for the relatively small demand, the extractant would be too expensive to be attractive. Therefore, the use of a synergist to improve the selectivity of the existing commercially available extractants is an attractive alternative to the development of new extractants for nickel and cobalt recovery. 

Much research work has been carried out on synergistic solvent extraction to improve extraction and separation of various metals. Systematic research work on the separation of nickel in various extractant and synergist systems was carried out by Preston and du Preez (1996a, 1996b and 1996c). With commonly used extractants, nickel is extracted at a higher pH than most other metals. Extraction of nickel ahead of other metals has been a research goal for reagent manufacturers and researchers for many years. Preston and du Preez (1994) reported the synergistic effect of pyridine carboxylate esters on the extraction of nickel using Versatic 10. Two pyridine carboxylate esters, n-octyl 3-pyridinecarboxylate ester (octyl-3PC) and Acorga DS5443A (also called CLX50, a pyridine di-carboxylate ester manufactured by Avecia), were used as synergists with Versatic 10 for the extraction of divalent metals in sulphate solutions. The pH50 difference between calcium and nickel increased from 1.08 pH units (Versatic 10 alone) to 3.07 pH units (Versatic 10 and octyl3PC) and 2.24 pH units (Versatic 10 and CLX50). This would substantially increase the separation factor of nickel over calcium and may imply an industrial application.

Cole and Nagel (1997) also reported the use of synergistic solvent extraction for nickelcalcium separation in sulphate solution using a mixture of Versatic 10 and 4-nonylpyridine. The pH50 value for nickel shifted from 6.5 for Versatic 10 alone to 4.6 for the organic mixture. For calcium, the pH50 shifted towards higher pH, resulting in a much larger pH50 difference between nickel and calcium (3.3 pH units). 

In the Bulong process, the separation of nickel from calcium using Versatic 10 is incomplete, and over 10% of the calcium is co-extracted with the nickel, resulting in gypsum precipitation in the scrub stages. This causes severe operational problems and nickel loss in the SX circuit. Preliminary test work was carried out at the Parker Centre on the use of CLX50 as a synergist to improve the separation of nickel from calcium using Versatic 10. (Cheng, 2000a). The pH isotherm of nickel with Versatic 10 was significantly affected by the addition of CLX50. The pH50 value of nickel was reduced by 1.10, 0.95, and 0.60 pH units by adding 20%, 10% and 5% by volume CLX50 to the organic solution respectively (Fig. 5). The pH isotherm of calcium with Versatic 10 was not affected by the addition of CLX50. As a result, the addition of CLX50 as a synergist substantially enlarged the ∆pH50 between calcium

and nickel. The ∆pH50 between calcium and nickel increased from 0.77 pH units without CLX50 to 1.87 pH units with 20% CLX50 synergist. The addition of 10% CLX50 gave a ∆pH50 between calcium and nickel of 1.70 pH units At pH 6.4, the separation factor of nickel over calcium increased from 47 with no CLX50 addition to 258 with 5% CLX50 addition and then to 1216 with 10% CLX50 addition, indicating very good separation of nickel from calcium. Operationally, this would reduce the calcium co-extraction and substantially improve the nickel-calcium separation. A chemical stability study on the Versatic 10 and CLX50 system was conducted for 3 months at 40°C, at high temperature (60°C) and in simulated mixer/settler operation. Results showed that no noticeable chemical changes occurred in the system during the tests, indicating the system is chemically stable. The results will be reported in another paper. 100.0

SUMMARY** The SX processes of the three nickel plants in Western Australia and the Goro SX process in New Caledonia were reviewed. The use of intermediate precipitation, solids/liquid separation and re-leach in the three WA nickel plants and the use of Cyanex 301 for a DSX process in the Goro process make these processes complicated and costly in capital and operation. The research work carried out by the SX group in the AJ Parker Cooperative Research Centre for Hydrometallurgy / CSIRO Minerals has led to the invention of DSX processes to recover nickel and cobalt from leach solutions. The 15 ALTA Free Library www.altamet.com.au simplicity of the process flowsheets and the expected savings in capital and operating costs are the major advantages of the new DSX processes over the reviewed processes. By using a new synergistic system in semi-continuous tests with a pilot plant leach solution from the San Felipe Project of BHP-Billiton Stainless Steel Materials (after iron precipitation), the metal values (Ni and Co) together with zinc and copper were separated from the major impurities (Mn, Mg and Ca, together with Cl)

in the first SX circuit. The organic solution effectively extracted all of the cobalt, zinc and copper and 99.98% of the nickel and left manganese, magnesium, calcium and chloride in the raffinate. Some 96% of the co-extracted manganese, 100% of the co-extracted magnesium and 61% of the coextracted calcium were scrubbed, leaving 2 ppm manganese and 4 ppm calcium in the scrubbed organic solution. After stripping, the metal values (Ni and Co) together with zinc and copper were concentrated, resulting in a much smaller second SX circuit and equipment in the down stream processes. The extraction and stripping kinetics with the organic solution were very fast. Within 0.5 minutes, the extraction and stripping almost reached steady state. 

Semi-continuous test work with a synthetic leach solution, a cobalt bio-leach pilot plant solution from Peko Rehabilitation Project Pty Ltd and a synthetic solution to simulate a concentrated leach solution for the San Felipe Project of BHP-Billiton Stainless Steel Materials showed that manganese, calcium, copper and zinc can be effectively and efficiently separated from nickel, cobalt and magnesium by extraction, scrubbing and stripping. This led to the invention of another type of DSX process to recover nickel and cobalt from leach solutions. When the concentrated leach solution was tested, over 99% of the zinc, calcium and manganese and nearly 99% of the copper were extracted. The raffinate contained only 1-3 ppm Zn, Ca, Mn and Cu. Some 7.7% cobalt, 9.0% magnesium and 0.44% nickel were extracted. Over 93% of the co-extracted cobalt, 97.6% of the coextracted nickel and 89% of the co-extracted magnesium were scrubbed out from the loaded organic solution. Only 1 ppm magnesium, 2 ppm cobalt and 2 ppm nickel were left in the organic solution. After the separation of cobalt from nickel in the subsequent SX circuit, both metals could be recovered. 

###### **4. FUTURE WORK** 

- Although the new synergistic system is chemically stable under the test conditions, the system should be investigated for longer term chemical stability. 

- Intensive piloting using the new processes should take place to demonstrate their feasibility at commercial scale operation. 

- The proportion of the extractant and the synergist during a long term operation should be closely monitored.

###### **1. INTRODUCTION** 

Anglovaal Mining (Avmin) in conjunction with Western Minerals Technology (WMT) have developed a flowsheet for the refining of copper, nickel, cobalt and PGMs from Nkomati sulphide concentrates. For the refining of nickel, Avmin are considering using versatic acid as the extractant in the nickel solvent extraction (SX) circuit. This circuit has been tested and optimised during a previous integrated pilot-plant campaign<sup>1</sup> . 

Versatic acid is a readily available and cheap nickel extractant, but does co-extract some calcium along with nickel. The difficulties of the separation of nickel from calcium using versatic acid have been well documented over the years<sup>1, 2, 3, 4</sup> . The problem with this system is that it requires the extraction circuit pH to be carefully controlled to minimise the co-extraction of calcium. The principle of using a Bateman Pulsed Column (BPC) is that it would be possible to reduce the operating pH of the extraction circuit to minimise the coextraction of calcium. While this would require 3 - 4 additional stages, these could be added at fairly low cost to a BPC circuit, unlike a mixer-settler plant where the additional stages would be fairly costly. The BPC offers considerable capital cost advantages over a mixer-settler plant as the number of stages required increases, and it was thought that the BPC would be well suited for this application. 

With this operating philosophy in mind, Avmin approached Bateman to carry out a testwork campaign to verify the operating philosophy as well as the control of pH in the BPC. 

This paper reports the results of the pilot-plant campaign carried out at the Bateman Advanced Technologies research centre in Katzrin, Israel, during December 2001 to January 2002 to test the principle discussed above.

###### **2.2. EQUIPMENT AND PROCEDURES** 

The final nickel extraction circuit consisted of an extraction BPC, split into two columns operated in series. This was done to ensure that there would be sufficient length in the BPC to achieve the raffinate concentration of < 0.3 g/l nickel, while minimising the coextraction of calcium. Two mixer-settlers were used for the scrubbing of calcium and magnesium off the loaded organic phase, a mixer-settler for the first and a BPC for the second stage of stripping. 

A synthetic PLS solution was added to the first 7m high extraction BPC (PC01), and the exiting raffinate was stored in an intermediate tank before being fed to the second 5m high extraction BPC (PC02). Stripped organic was pumped into PC02 and the exiting, partially loaded, organic was stored in an intermediate tank before being fed into PC01. 150 g/L NH4OH was added to PC01 and PC02 to maintain a pH profile in PC01 of 6.1 at the top of the column and at 5.9 at the bottom. In PC02 the profile was set at 5.7 - 5.9 in the top of the column and a small amount of NH4OH was added to the middle of the column to ensure that a pH of > 5.6 was maintained at the sample point below the addition point. 

The loaded organic exiting PC01 was fed into the two scrubbing mixer-settlers to remove the majority of the co-extracted calcium. The pH in the scrubbing circuit was not directly controlled but the pH of the scrub liquor fed to the mixer-settlers was adjusted to 3.5 and 200 g/L H2SO4 was added to the mixers for pH control, when required. The scrub liquor flowrate was set to ensure that the calcium scrubbed from the loaded organic and reporting to the spent scrub liquor would be below the saturation level of calcium. The spent scrub liquor reported to the PLS tank. 

The nickel loaded onto the scrubbed organic was stripped, firstly by contacting the organic with strip liquor exiting the 7m stripping BPC (PC03) in a turbine pump mixer-settler (TPM), and then with weak electrolyte (WE) solution in PC03. The aqueous solution exiting the mixer-settler stage (advance electrolyte) contained the highest concentration of nickel and the lowest concentration of acid.

the BPC used for the test work, meant that pH could not be controlled at the point were the NH4OH was added, as NH4OH was injected directly onto the probe. To reduce these lag times, pH variances and to prevent any gypsum precipitation, it was decided to replace the first three by 1m contacting sections with six by 0.5m contacting sections in PC01. To minimise this co-extraction, an additional NH4OH addition port was added to PC02. This improved matters as the pH at the top of PC02 could be reduced, but the coextraction of calcium was still too high as it was found to be far more dependent on the pH at the top of PC02 than on any other variable. Unfortunately, as PC02 was only brought on line fairly late into the campaign, it was not possible to replace the 1m contacting sections with 0.5m contacting sections nor to add any additional NH4OH dosing points.

With lower pH values the extraction will probably take place in the first 2 - 3 metres instead of in the first metre of the BPC, as was the case during the BPC trial. Of course with the lower pH the calcium coextraction will also be lower. 

As the pH could be reasonably controlled with unfavourable manual operation, the control of pH in an industrial BPC should be far superior. The pH will be measured much closer to the addition point and the control will be automatic. Extraction of calcium is also expected to be reduced, as there would be no elevated pH along the length of the industrial BPC. 

Magnesium extraction was less than that of calcium as it is extracted at a higher pH than calcium. The co-extraction of magnesium did not create any problems, as its solubility limits are far higher than those of calcium are. This was not the case in PC02 due to the elevated pH at the top of the BPC when the profile was taken. 

The extraction BPCs were pulsed at a frequency of 150 cycles/minute and an amplitude of 8mm. It was found that these mixing intensity settings resulted in a bubble size of between 1 – 3 mm and dispersed phase hold-ups of approximately 11 - 20%. This ensured that adequate mass transfer was achieved. 

The average nickel recovery in the extraction circuit was 99.2%, with a variance of 93 – 99.9 %. The average calcium co-extraction in the extraction circuit was 5.4%, with a variance of 1.3 – 11.4 %. A brief summary of the results is presented in Table 3. 

No attempt was made to continuously measure the amount of NH4OH being added to each sample point in the BPC. Instead, the overall amount of NH4OH added was measured. It was found that the addition rate varied between 1.5 – 2.7 L/hr when the PLS addition rate was 9.6 L/hr. The NH4OH was thus between 16 and 28 % of the PLS flowrate. The stoichiometric equivalent for the nickel extracted is approximately 19% assuming 22 g/L nickel in the PLS.

###### **4. CONCLUSIONS** 

The pilot-plant campaign has indicated that a BPC is suitable for the extraction of nickel using versatic acid in Avmin’s Nkomati nickel SX circuit. The BPC offers an advantage over mixers-settlers in that the operating pH can be lower resulting in a lower co-extraction of calcium. The objective of >99% nickel extraction with <10% co-extraction of calcium was achieved. The average nickel extraction before scrubbing was >99%, with a range of 93% to 99.9%, while that of calcium was 5.4% with a range of 1.3 –11.4%. The co-extraction of calcium in PC02 was a result of the elevated pH at the top of PC02 and can be avoided by the measurement of pH closer to the NH4OH addition point. 

The scrubbing circuit performed satisfactorily with the majority of the calcium being removed from the loaded organic to get an average co-extraction of calcium of 4.1%, with a range of 0.8 – 12.6%. The removal of the co-extracted calcium could be improved in an industrial plant by installing a pH control on the first scrubbing stage. On a industrial plant a co-extraction of calcium of < 3% should easily be achieved. 

The stripping circuit did not perform as anticipated in the BPC. It was found that the stripping efficiency in the BPC was very strongly dependent on the mixing intensity/hold-up in the BPC. The BPC had to be run very close to flooding conditions to maximise the stripping efficiency. On the introduction of the TPM as the first unit in series with the BPC, the strippin

g efficiency increased considerably. For an industrial application it would appear that 3 TPMs or conventional mixer-settlers would be required. 

The results so far achieved have being very promising, and all of the client requirements were achieved, but further testwork will be required on a slightly larger scale to overcome some of the problems indicated in this report and to further minimise the co-extraction of calcium.

###### **ABSTRACT** 

The paper covers the application of on-line analysis to solvent extraction in nickel leach solvent extraction processes in Australia. It covers the utilization of on-line analysis in process control and two working applications. 

The paper reviews the goals of and requirements for controlling the solvent extraction stages of iron, zinc copper removal from nickel-cobalt solution and subsequently in the preparation of purified nickel and cobalt solutions for metal reduction. 

The applications at the plant of OMG, Harjavalta

, Finland and Anaconda’s Murrin Murrin operations are compared. 

The OMG plant has applied on-line analysis widely in matte leach, solvent extraction and the metal reduction process. The technology used and considerations affecting its choice are reviewed. 

The newer Murrin Murrin project uses a redesigned analyzer system specifically intended for solvent extraction and similar applications. The technology used is reviewed and design considerations are discussed. 

Requirements for on-line control and analyzer performance are compared. 

###### **1 INTRODUCTION** 

At the same time as solvent extraction has become a fast-growing technology for treating copper oxide ores  and low grade copper sulphide ores, it has become important in nickel and cobalt ore processing. Processes treating readily soluble raw material, such as the processing of nickel carbonate at Sociedad Niquel Tocantins, Sao Paulo, Brazil, have been designed around solvent extraction in the 1970’s. In enlarging its plant in the late 1980’s and early 1990’s , the then Outokumpu cobalt plant at Kokkola, now OMG Kokkola Chemicals Oy, opted for solvent extraction processes to produce solutions from which high-grade metal salts could be produced. And in the late 1990’s the then Outokumpu Nickel plant, now OMG Harjavalta Nickel, changed the purification of the liquor from matte leach and the smelting of slag in an electric arc furnace to a solvent extraction process. The already existing nickel electrowinning plant remained in use, but the additional metal content from the expanded leaching capacity was treated in a hydrogen reduction plant producing nickel and cobalt powders. 

At the same time a new approach to the treatment of laterite ores for nickel and cobalt was being developed in Western Australia. Pressure acid leach (PAL) of the laterite provided a feed that was suitable for further treatment by solvent extraction to remove iron, copper, zinc and other metals leaving nickel and cobalt in the solution. The nickel and cobalt are then separated by a second solvent extraction stage  and both recovered as powder by hydrogen reduction. The first stages of the development of three properties are now in operation in Western Australia around Kalgoorlie and Leonora. 

Outokumpu has used wavelength-dispersive X-ray fluorescence technology since the first COURIER 300 analyzer was installed in the Pyhдsalmi flotation plant in 1969. Compared with energy-dispersive, the wavelength-dispersive technology offers significant advantages in on-line analysis for metallurgical processes. The most important is the ability to distinguish the fluorescent radiation of trace elements in concentrated metal salt solutions, for instance in solutions of nickel sulphate containing 100 g/l Ni the detection limits of iron, cobalt, copper and zinc are between 1 and 2.5 mg/l.  The X-ray tube used as a source of primary radiation excites so high an intensity of fluorescent radiation that actual measuring times ca

n be 60 seconds, or even less for measuring higher contents. Another advantage is that the structure of the Johansson-type curved fixed-crystal spectrometer is so robust that after 13 years of use spectrometers from an analyzer being replaced have been transferred to the new analyzer. 1 ALTA Free Library www.altamet.com.au Since 1989 a number of on-line analyzers using the batch sampling technology have been installed in the then Harjavalta nickel plant of Outokumpu Oy. This plant is now OMG Harjavalta Nickel Oy. ###### **5 MAKING AN ANALYZER SYSTEM SPECIFICALLY FOR SOLVENT EXTRACTION** 

After the delivery of the on-line analyzers to Harjavalta the growing importance of solvent extraction processes made it necessary to rethink the approach to analysis needs and sample handling for plants of this kind. [2] 

The project to design an X-ray analyzer system aimed specifically at solvent extraction plants was originally specified with Chilean copper plants in mind. Typical copper heapleach, solvent extraction plants under construction in the Chilean copper field cover a much larger area than the various stages of plants for nickel production. Sixteen to twenty sample points are scattered over an area as large as 250 m by 150 m. Usually most of these can however be located at the edge of the tank farm area. The floor of the tank farm on larger sites is 10 to 15m lower than the level of the mixer-settlers. Sample transport for copper plants was designed to operate over the long distances and with the small head or hydraulic gradient available. 

The process streams to be sampled are all solids free, unless crud formation is a big problem, but the danger exists of blockage due to crystallization, especially at high altitudes where winter tempera

tures can be below zero. System design must counteract the tendency of solution flowing in small pipes to cool and crystallize. 

The need has also been seen to limit to a minimum the quantity of valuable solution, electrolyte that has to be discarded or recycled by pumping. In addition there are several groups of process streams that must not be mixed, to avoid the loss of valuable refined solution. In the more complicated process of refining nickel and copper cross contamination of the different organic reagents used in the two main stages must be avoided. 

A fourth goal is to provide prompt and frequent analyses. To give sufficiently frequent data for effective control of the process, whether automatic or manual, repeating analyses every ½ hour is perceived to be necessary. Since the equipment is designed for 16 sample streams this implies making a new measurement every two minutes. With a measurement time of 1 minute; that leaves 1 minute for rinsing the parts of the system intimately connected to the measurement cell or cuvette. 

Chemically the solutions are frequently aggressively corrosive. The acid content of copper electrolytes can be as high as 200 g/l H2SO4, and the REDOX potential may be 400 to 550 mV relative to the standard hydrogen electrode. 

In the design process this all led to the idea that the samples could be taken from gravity fed fast loops terminating in the tank farm area, or from process pipes in which the solution was being pumped to the mixer settlers. The flow of samples would be driven by the hydraulic gradient of 5% to 10%, or by process pump pressure, and the maximum pressure at the analyzer site would be between 1 and 2 bar. This was determined by the topography of the mixer-settler pad and the tank farm. 

The need to minimize the amount of sample taken into the sample multiplexer of the system, and the desire to keep sample handling time to a minimum, has led to a much simplified sample multiplexing system based on using small bore piping with a minimal dead volume. The total sample take-off from a fast loop or a process pipe is envisaged to be no more than 1 ½ liter for short final pipes. The design of the sampling system now designated COURIER 30SX also includes stringent rinsing to forestall the possibility of crystallization. A carefully planned rinsing sequence has been designed to meet the criterion that for a system with an X-ray analyzer alone the time between successive analyses in the sample sequence should be no more than 2 minutes. ###### **ABSTRACT** 

The importance of good rheology testwork and meaningful rheology data is increasingly being recognized by the mining industry, driven to a great extent by the introduction of high pressure acid leaching of nickel laterites in Western Australia.  Most metallurgical plants operate under continuous flow mode, and information on the flowability of various process slurries is needed to generate design criteria for mass and energy transfer processes. 

This paper covers the areas of rheological investigation that are required for metallurgical processes such as sample characterization, generation of test results, and interpretation of data. The importance of generating base line rheology during the initial stages of a testwork program is stressed, because of the impact of rheology on equipment selection and design for pilot plants. 

Examples include rheological characterization of nickel laterite slurry samples at temperatures ranging from ambient to 200ºC.  Some of these examples illustrate how effective rheological testwork can be when interpreted correctly. Entire ore bodies or isolated slurry streams displaying difficult or complex rheology may be identified readily and the unnecessary expense of high cost testwork avoided. 

Future directions that rheology testing may take are also discussed, such as process control using online rheology and the opportunity afforded to move in the direction of compact micro-pilot plants.

###### **1. INTRODUCTION** 

Rheology, the science of flow and deformation of matter is a well-established discipline with applications in several fields of engineering including the mining and metallurgical. Flow behavior impacts energy and mass transfer based unit operations such as mixing, pumping, grinding, heating, and gas transfer. Processes that involve the physical separation of liquids from solids (settling and thickening) and of solids from solids (screening and cycloning) are also slurry-rheology dependent. 

Rheological data requirements from the mineral and metallurgical industries consist of flowability assessment and generation of design criteria. A typical example of a rheology driven process is the hydrometallurgical processing of lateritic ores. While the underlying process chemistry of the high temperature (aut

oclave) acid leaching is relatively well known, the rheological behavior of various laterite ore samples still needs to be understood. Predicting the rheological behavior of most lateritic ore slurries from first principles is difficult and may carry a significant risk. This creates the need for testing in order to produce reliable rheological data needed to develop design criteria for equipment sizing.  As a result, rheology has become an integral part of metallurgical testwork programs for laterite projects.  Ore type and orebody variability increase the amount of rheological data needed for adequate characterization of the deposit and subsequent generation of comprehensive design criteria. 

This paper provides a general overview of the rheological behavior of various lateritic ore slurries. The information presented was summarized from data generated during commercial testing. Future directions such as impact of rheology knowledge on testwork design, integrated compact pilot plants, high purity materials, and nanorheology are also briefly discussed. 

###### **2. APPLIED RHEOLOGICAL TESTING** 

The concept of applied rheological testing is common to most process industries, including mining and metallurgy. Important factors that determine the quality of rheological testwork results include: 

- --Understanding of rheology fundamentals; 

- --Generation of unambiguous test-data; 

- --Interpretation of the results and elaboration of design criteria. 

Particulate fluid character dictates the most relevant rheological properties pertaining to mineral and metallurgical process slurries. Consistent application in practice of the theory of particulate fluids, in conjunction with adequate testwork procedures allow for the generation of unambiguous rheological test data. The interpretation of the results and design criteria elaboration tend to be more interdisciplinary, in the sense that these aspects are related to both rheology as well as to metallurgical and chemical engineering.

A previous paper [1] discuses aspects related to testwork protocols applied for the generation of rheological data using concentric cylinder rotational viscometry (“CCRV”). 

The Brookfield viscometer is a fairly popular device for rheological studies, including work 1

###### **3. PARTICULATE FLUIDS** 

A particulate fluid can be simplistically defined as a system composed of a discontinuous solid phase dispersed in a continuous liquid phase.  Assuming uniform distribution of the solids in the liquid phase, the particulate fluid can be considered as pseudo-homogeneous. Provided that settling is sufficiently slow, these fluids are generally considered to be “nonsettling” or “stable” (particulate) systems. 

Particulate fluids of specific interest in mineral and metallurgical processes are commonly known as “slurries” or “pulps”. These fluids can be subdivided into three main types: “NonFlocculated” (“Deflocculated”, or “Fully dispersed”), “Flocculated”, and “Fibrous” [3, 4]. 

In a broader sense, the rheological behavior of the slurries is determined by physical and physico-chemical factors [3, 4, 7, 8, 9].  Physical factors include temperature, shearinginduced hydrodynamic (liquid-particle) interactions, as well as properties related to the suspended particles, such as their shape, concentration, size and size distribution. 

Physico-chemical factors consist of attractive and repulsive interactions between the particles. Attractive interactions include Van der Waals, long range electrostatic and hydrophobic forces. Repulsive interactions consist mainly of Van der Waals, hard sphere, as well as short and long range (double layer) electrostatic forces. The Van der Waals forces tend to act as attractive forces, except when the solid particles are composed of dissimilar materials suspended in a fluid of intermediate density, such as in the case of particle-bubble interactions in water [7]. 

The zeta potential is a measure of the net result of the attractive and repulsive interparticle forces. The value of the zeta potential indicates whether the particles adher

e on collision or remain in a dispersed state. 

A non-flocculated or partly deflocculated, low particle concentration slurry (i.e. particulate fluid) tends to follow what is referred to as Newtonian behavior, characterized by a unique value of the viscosity, η, that is independent of the rate of shearing to which that fluid is being subjected [3, 4, 5]:

η = τ/γ = constant, where τ is the shear stress and γ is the shear rate. 

In these low volume fraction, “ideal” particulate fluids, the correlation between viscosity and solids density tends to obey the Einstein relation [3,4,7,8]. 

η = η0(1+2.5Φ) where η and η0 are the viscosities at volume fractions Φ and Φ=0, respectively. 

In the above situation, individual particles (or relatively small aggregates) act as flow units. At intermediate solids concentrations, the flow units tend to become increasingly larger, as a transition towards the flocculated state takes place.  Variable shearing of medium to high intensity may induce dilatant (“shear thickening”) behavior in these slurries, causing an increase of viscosity. 

In mineral and metallurgical processes, high volume fraction particulate fluids that can be assimilated to relatively stable flocculated systems are common. Under gradually increased shearing, the flocs are reduced in size, progressively releasing some of the liquid component, making it available as medium (“lubricant”) for the motion of the particles.  The net (measurable) effect is a reduction of the resistance to flow (i.e. viscosity) of the slurry.  This phenomenon is known as shear thinning. Shear thinning is characteristic for Pseudoplastic fluids. Further shearing at constant rates, for a certain period of time, can produce a thixotropic breakdown. Thixotropy is the condition whereby the flowability of a particulate fluid increases due to shearing in time.  Rheopexy (antithixotropy) is the opposite phenomenon, consisting of a build-up of the resistance to flow of a particulate fluid due to shearing in time. 

Time-dependency of the viscosity of mineral slurries is in general of a transient nature, as it usually reflects the time required for the fluid to reach a constant viscosity value (i.e. flowability). 

Being shear rate dependent, the flocculated particulate fluids do not follow Newtonian flow behavior and the relationship between viscosity and solids density cannot be expressed by the Einstein equation. 

Their inherent settling tendency renders most of the mineral and metallurgical process slurries as quasi-stable systems. Most of these materials will not flow unless a stress that exceeds a certain value, the yield stress, is applied through shearing. This is known as Bingham Plastic behavior and is widely encountered in the study of the particulate fluids. The yield phenomenon separates the quasi-solid and quasi-liquid states of the Bingham Plastic particulate fluids. The behaviour of Bingham plastic fluids tends to be t

imedependent to a certain degree (i.e. until they reach their ultimate flowability), since their shearing history generally influences their rheology. 

It should be noted within the context of this brief overview that in strict theoretical terms, time-dependent fluids cannot be characterized by non-Newtonian rheology. Timedependency may exist as thixotropy, or rheopexy (anti-thixotropy). A widely accepted practical compromise however takes into account the fact that in general, both thixotropy and rheopexy are transient phenomena. Accordingly, most mineral slurries tend to reach a final (i.e. “equilibrium” or “ultimate”) value of their flowability at which point a nonNewtonian assessment of their behavior can be made and used for engineering purposes. Furthermore, in terms of settling behavior, “ideal” particulate fluids, characterized by lack of interparticle interactions, obey the Stokes relation [10]:

Fibrous slurries are found less often in mineral and metallurgical processes. They contain long, flexible fiber shaped particles, which tend to form flocculated structures even at very low volume fractions. Therefore, non-Newtonian flow behavior is common in the case of dilute fibrous slurries. However, the suspending medium is easily displaced from the fiberflocs, causing sudden changes of rheology. These changes tend to be difficult to track experimentally, due to the development of non-uniform particle concentration profiles in the mass of the entire fluid and/or at its boundaries (i.e. wall-slip).

LATERITIC ORE SLURRIES** The influence of slurry flow properties in nickel laterite processing is perhaps the most relevant example of a rheology-driven metallurgical process. Lateritic ores (“laterites”) are developed by the weathering of various nickel-bearing parent 5 ALTA Free Library www.altamet.com.au rocks, and are widely distributed in tropical areas. Lateritic ores consist in general of goethite along with variable amounts of minerals such as serpentine, garnierite, chlorite, olivine, diopside, chromite, vermiculite and others. Laterites with high-aluminum and lowmagnesia content are generally known as limonitic, whereas the low-aluminum and high magnesia content ores are commonly identified as saprolitic. From both rheological and metallurgical perspectives, it is very important to determine the correct amount of solid matter contained in a slurry sample that is being retrieved from a process, and which is destined for rheological measurements and chemical analyses. The approach selected was to quantify the degree of cumulative interactions occurring in the slurry, regarded as a particulate fluid. It has been found that in order to achieve the required level of accuracy, it was necessary to amend the equation of the ideal mixture to reflect the properties of the real slurry, as discussed below. For the case of an ideal bi-component particulate fluid, composed of a continuous liquid phase and a dispersed solid phase, the volume of that slurry-system can be expressed as the sum of the volumes of the two imiscible phases, according to the Ideal Mixtures Law [17]: where V1 is the volume of the solid-in-slurry component (flow unit, floc, etc), V2 the volume of the liquid. 7 ALTA Free Library www.altamet.com.au For the case of non-ideal slurry, the above relation can be rewritten as: αV1+ βV2 = V where α is the correction factor that quantifies the effect of all interactions at equilibrium (i.e. interparticle and solventparticle) that affect the volume of the “quasi-solid” phase. Correction factor β quantifies the effect of all interactions (i.e. solvent-particle) that may affect the volume of the liquid phase. By definition: α = ASG/ρ1 where ASG is the “Actual Specific Gravity” and ρ1” the dry residue specific gravity. In the case of flocculated slurry, the ASG (“Actual Specific Gravity of the Solids in Slurry”) can be formally assimilated to the real density of the “quasi-solid” flow units (flocs) present in the slurry. The final form of the amended equation can be obtained after substitutions and regrouping: ρ = ρ1ρ2/(αfρ2+βρ1(1-f)) where ρ is the pulp density, ρ2 the solution density in g/L, f is the solids weight fraction of the slurry. Since pulp density and solids weight fraction are easily determinable, they allow for subsequent calculation of the ASG and implicitly of the α values. In the case of a given process slurry sample, the density of its liquid phase is a constant that includes the effect of any possible particle-solvent (chemical) interaction, such as swelling, ion exchange, etc. Therefore, provided that no interactions occur during sampling (i.e. slurry make-up, post reaction, etc.), the density of the liquid can be determined una

mbiguously, hence β = 1. Situations involving β ≠ 1 tend to be more complex, as they may involve the necessity of introducing time as a parameter. Under the conditions outlined above (β=1) and, in addition when α = 1 (thus ASG = ρ1), the equation reflects the particular case of an ideal mixture, characterized by the absence of any interactions, hence allowing for individual particle volumes additivity. In this particular case, the pulp density can be calculated using the traditional, ideal equation: ###### ρ = ρ1ρ2/(fρ2+ρ1(1-f)) > For situations when α ≠ 1, only the ASG values or, alternatively, calibration curves (pulp > versus solids fraction functions, ρ = F(f)) can be used for accurate pulp density determinations. In either case, the solids density ranges of applicability need to be defined, as some of the interactions (e.g. flocculation), could be influenced by the solids density. Thus the ρ = F(f) relationship may not always be linear. As noted above, the assumption of β=1 implies constant solution density for this scenario. Otherwise, α would become a function of time, and its quantification would require kinetic data. The objective is to provide design criteria and the example provided is related to a slurry transport application. The approach described below is applicable to other rheology dependent unit operations. Defining the optimum pumping conditions for slurry transpor

t is a typical rheological testwork objective that provides direct design criteria. Examples include pumping of highdensity, beneficiated laterite ore slurries as well as process intermediates and tailings. Rheological testwork data generated time-independent flowcurves such as illustrated by the lower (“Down”) curve are illustrated in Figure 6. At least two rheological models, Bingham Plastic and Ostwald de Waele could be applied with reasonable accuracy, based on the best-fit modeling. Pressure loss calculations [1] were carried out based on generally accepted criteria [18, 19]. The results covered the entire shear rate range tested and returned fairly similar friction loss values, except for the zero velocity fluid (Figure 7). The zero velocity exception was given by the power law-based Ostwald de Waele model, according to which, the pressure loss would be zero. The physical significance of this fact is that the fluid would be free flowing, i.e. no pump start-up power would be needed. As can be seen in Figure 6, this would be in contradiction to reality. The example illustrates the importance of understanding the system to which the rheological model is being applied, rather than examining the mathematical predictions of the model in isolation. The shear rate of application also has an important role. For example, based on the shape of the curve in Figure 6 in the low shear rate area, an insignificant yield stress would be implied, again a contradiction of physical reality. Friction pressure loss calculations under 12 ALTA Free Library www.altamet.com.au the insignificant yield stress scenario imply a Newtonian approach to the problem. Accordingly, the zero fluid velocity scenario would imply that an extremely high viscosity needs to be used for the calculation in order to obtain a realistic value of the friction pressure loss. Further application of the Newtonian model in a consistent manner would require extensive calculations over several small increments of shear rate values. This would not take advantage of the application of a non-Newtonian rheological model, which was found to be valid in the first place. The straightforward application of the Bingham model provided certainty and validity over the entire shear rate range tested. In addition, it correctly reflected the real flow behavior of the slurry tested. It is also worth noting that (Figure 7) that the concentric cylinder rotational viscometry (CCRV) data accurately models the results obtained from a pump-loop. Therefore, pump loop testing is needed only for applications where the CCRV technique is not applicable, such as in the case of fast settling slurries containing coarse and/or high specific gravity solids. This is a significant result, since pump-loop testing is usually very costly compared to CCRV testing, and requires much larger quantities of sample. 140

###### **Figure 7 Comparative Pressure Calculations** ###### **4.3 FLOW BEHAVIOR OF LATERITE ORE SLURRIES** There is extensive literature describing the rheological behavior of lateritic slurries, both in general terms, as well as with reference to specific cases, ore deposits, processes, applications, etc. [1, 13, 14, 15, 16]. The purpose of this section is to provide a succinct comparative description of the rheological behavior of various lateritic ores slurries. The data was produced through commercial testwork carried out on laterite slurries originating from several deposits around the world. The main rheological characteristics, found to be common to most laterite ore samples tested, can be summarized as follows: - --Lateritic ore slurries of practical importance for extractive metallurgy display nonNewtonian flow behavior, best described by the Bingham plastic rheological model; - --Certain lateritic ores form slurries that display poor flowability characteristics at solids densities as low as 29%, characterized by yield stress values of 30 Pa or more. These lateritic ore types referred to in this paper as type “M”, consist mainly of a variety known as “dry laterites” [20]. - --There are also lateritic ores that form slurries that display excellent flowability at solids densities as high as 42%, characterized by yield stress values of 30 Pa or less. These lateritic ore types, referred to in this paper as type “I” consist mainly of a variety known as “wet laterites” [20]. - --The relative effects of temperature, dilution and dispersants on the flowability of type “M” lateritic ores are more pronounced than on type “I” ores. However, within the temperature range of 25 to 200ºC, the overall flowability of the type “I” lateritic slurries is clearly superior to that displayed by type “M” slurries. That temperature range is relevant for the feeding and preheating stages of the high temperature autoclave acid leaching process. - --There are lateritic ores that form slurries with intermediate rheological properties between the two types defined above. The flowability of these slurries can be improved 14 ALTA Free Library www.altamet.com.au by ore blending, optimizing the salinity of the process water, controlled dilution during preheating and the use of rheological additives. **Figure 9 Effect of Temperature on Yield Stress – Slurries Type “M” and “I”** A general characteristic of type “M” laterite slurries is that they display high yield stress even at relatively low solids densities, such as the case with the 29% slurry displaying a yield stress of about 48 Pa. At higher solids densities, the “plug-flow” phenomenon is generally present. Type “M” lateritic slurries display a thixotropic tendency which allows them to dramatically increase the flowability; (even under these conditions, their flowability remains far below the flowability displayed by laterite slurries type “I”). Overall, type “M” slurries can generally be treated as time-independent, with well defined rheological properties. A general characteristic for type “I” lateritic slurries is that they display low yield stress even at relatively high solids densities as illustrated by the case with the 42% slurry having a yield stress of about 26 Pa. The degree of thixotropic breakdown is less visible in these slurries, compared to type “M” slurries. In fact, diluted slurries may exhibit an antithixotropic behavior, limiting the allowable rate of shearing during metallurgical processing. The high temperature behavior of laterite slurries is very important during the heat exchange and subsequent autoclaving unit operations. While type “I” slurries continue to display the most desirable behavior, the increase in their flowability on heating is not as dramatic as in the case of type “M” slurries. On the other hand, type “M” slurries generally need significant dilution (i.e. “M” at 29% solids) and in certain cases chemical modification (MM at 38% solids) to improve their flowability. ###### **4.4 FLOW BEHAVIOR OF PROCESS SLURRIES** Typical slurry streams produced during the metallurgical processing of lateritic ores include the autoclave discharge (ACD), counter-current decantation underflow (CCD) and various precipitate samples (NTR). As note

d above, these slurries tend to be chemically active, rendering their characterization time-dependent in a chemically-kinetic sense. From a 16 ALTA Free Library www.altamet.com.au purely rheological point of view, these slurries do not, however, present special flowability problems. The rheological properties of these slurries tend to be independent of the properties of the originating lateritic ore slurries. Maximum yield stress values displayed by typical CCD slurries, measured at a discharge temperature of about 75ºC ranged from 30 to 38 Pa, at slurry solid densities ranging from 45 to 49% by weight. The predominant rheological time-dependency consisted of thixotropic breakdown at the higher range of solids densities, in the thickener underflow discharge. Moderate rheopexy was observed in the case of more diluted slurries such as thickener feed. Maximum yield stress values displayed by typical NTR slurries, measured at a discharge temperature of about 65ºC, ranged from 1 to 6 Pa, at slurry solid densities ranging from 36 to 40% by weight. The predominant rheological time-dependency consisted of rheopexy. The extent of rheopectic build-up was found to be directly proportional to the rate of shearing and inversely proportional to the solids density. The Bingham model could not be always applied for the NTR slurries, as a power law (Ostwald de Waele) type of behavior tended to prevail at higher shear rates. More complex models such as Hershley - Bulkley and Casson seemed to better reflect the rheological behavior of these slurries. The ACD slurries displayed a fast settling behavior, rendering them unsuitable for CCRV measurements. A Metzner – Otto based testwork protocol was employed instead, allowing for the generation of baseline mixing torque data (Figure 10). The resulting power–torque curves allowed for the estimation of the power required to maintain the slurry in suspension and provide blending under a prevalent laminar regime. In addition, the approximate value of the equivalent Newtonian viscosity (mPa.s) of the slurry sample could be obtained, by comparing the torque responses to those generated by calibrated standard fluids. Flowcurves could also be produced within a relatively narrow range of shear rates, corresponding to the true laminar mixing regime. 200

FUTURE TRENDS** A wide applicability range for the test data generated, low cost and fast turn-around characterize rheological testwork. Most importantly, the rheology data have both predictive and application value, making rheology an efficient testing tool. Future trends include: - --Generation of base line r

heology data during the initial stages of a testwork program. These data can be used for the estimation of optimum parameter ranges or even for preliminary scale-up and prefeasibility studies, involving capital and operating cost estimates. Thus, the necessity (or not) of a pilot plant campaign can be determined with reduced cost. 

- --Altering the rheology of laterite slurries to enhance their flowability is a challenge facing the exploitation of type “M” laterite deposits, characterized by problematic rheological behavior. 

- --There is a need for testing rheological behaviour at high temperatures owing to the lack of relevant physical data for most feed and process slurries encountered in laterite autoclaving processes. 

- --Process control using online rheology – The main driving force is the optimization of energy utilization in plant unit operations such as slurry transport, communition, heat exchange and others. 

- --Establishing the optimum flowing conditions creates the possibility of reducing the size of integrated pilot plants, with potential reductions in metallurgical testwork duration and cost. 

- --The renewed interest in hydrometallurgical processing of sulfidic nickel bearing ores will create the need for rheological data. Gas transfer in slurry systems is rheology-dependent. The rheology of these systems is greatly influenced by the size and particle size distribution, such as in the case of low-temperature oxidative processes. In addition to the size-fraction effect, the presence of molten sulfur in these systems could render them rheologically complex. 

- --The need for increasingly pure process intermediates and final products could lead in some cases to a requirement for the production of precipitates with sub-micron particle sizing. Apart from the fact that the chemical properties of such materials may be different from those of conventionally precipitated products, their rheological behavior is not predictable. The main question is whether or not a relatively monodisperse, nano-particulate fluid would follow the trend of increasing resistance to flow in proportion to the fineness of the solid particles. Furthermore, if the flowability behavior changes at some particular fineness, it would be necessary to quantify this change and determine when it takes place. Therefore, the rheology of nano-particle slurries could be an important field of study in the future. 

###### **6. CONCLUSIONS** 

- --Applied rheology testwork is needed because flowing properties influence the economics of continuous operations involving process slurries. 

- --Unambiguous test results can be achieved through accurate sample description and detailed rheological characterization, carried out in accordance with the theory of particulate fluids. 

- --The actual specific gravity of the solids contained in laterite slurries and various derived process slurry samples has been found to be dependent on the solids

content of the respective slurries and related to their Bingham yield stress. 

- --Lateritic ore slurries are particulate fluids that display a non-Newtonian flow behavior best described by the Bingham plastic rheological model. Type “M” lateritic ore slurries typically display poor rheological characteristics and may not flow readily at solids densities as low as 29%, characterized by yield stress values of 30 Pa or more.  Type “I” lateritic ore slurries typically display excellent flowability at solids densities as high as 42%, characterized by yield stress values of 30 Pa or less. 

- --The relative effect of temperature, dilution and dispersants on the flowability of type “M” lateritic slurries is more dramatic than on type “I” slurries. However, the overall flowability of the type “I” slurries is clearly superior to the flowability displayed by type “M” slurries within the temperature range of 25 to 200ºC. 

- --Certain lateritic ores form slurries that display rheological properties intermediate between types “M” and “I”. The flowability of these slurries can be improved by oreblending, optimizing the salinity of the process water, controlled dilution during preheating, and use of rheological additives. 

- --Some of the future trends in applied rheological testing include wider application of process rheology, use of rheological data to optimize the size and scope of process pilot plants, and development of process control applications based on rheological monitoring.  Rheology data should find increasing importance in project due diligence studies.  Rheological testing techniques will probably be driven towards examining higher temperature systems, systems containing finer (nano) particles, and three-phase systems with gases, solids and liquids that can result, for example, during the oxidative processing of sulfidic ores.  Rheological data will also be used to alter and optimize the flowability of process slurries.

###### **1. ABSTRACT** 

Manganese is commonly found in acidic leach liquors of copper, zinc, cobalt and nickel, and its control is one of the challenges facing the metallurgist who has to minimise operating costs and maintain product quality. 

Techniques at the disposal of the metallurgist to effect the control of manganese are numerous but the most practised are alkali precipitation, sulphide precipitation, electrolytic oxidation and solvent extraction.  Practical examples are presented of Cu-Mn, Zn-Mn and Co-Mn separations from various acidic leach liquors; the focus is placed on the use of SO2/O2 mixtures as selective oxidant to oxidise/precipitate manganese from zinc and cobalt leach solutions. 

The same technique, with some modifications,  can be applied to laterite leach liquors, and this leads to the possibility of improving the purification process presently practised or proposed for several laterite projects. 

###### **2. INTRODUCTION** 

Manganese is frequently found in nature associated with copper, zinc, nickel and cobalt. During the processing of these metallic ores, the separation of manganese from the other metals is normally not efficient, and, therefore, manganese eventually ends up together with the other metals in leach solutions from which pure metals or compounds have to be produced.  The presence of manganese within the base metals acidic leach liquors, if not controled properly, can lead to additional operating costs or even to contamination of the final product. 

This paper aims at reviewing the current status of the manganese control strategies in acidic liquors of copper, zinc, cobalt and nickel, as they are commercially practiced, or discusses processes which have been proposed to improve current manganese control practices.  In particular, a new process, developed by Lakefield Research,

and based on the selective oxidation/precipitation of manganese using SO2/O2, has been proposed and tested numerous times on acidic liquors containing zinc and cobalt. Special emphasis is placed on the treatment of laterite leach liquors where manganese is frequently found in quantities exceeding cobalt, and here also selective oxidation/precipitation of Mn using SO2/O2 is shown to be successful. ###### **3. REVIEW OF OPTIONS TO CONTROL MANGANESE IN ACIDIC LIQUORS** The separation of manganese from base metals of Cu, Ni, Co, Zn is not easy, and procedures that can be envisaged vary considerably, depending on the relative amounts of metals to separate, and the metal to separate the manganese from. From the start, one could think of removing the manganese and leaving the metal in solution, or leaving the manganese in solution and removing the metal. Normally, one should try to remove the element present in lesser amounts, but that cannot be always done. In addition, the selection of a process will also depend on what is the intended fate of the manganese separated (discard, recycle, sell) and the metal from which it is separated from. ELECTRO OXIDATION OF MANGANESE** The electrolytic oxidation of manganous ion Mn2+ to MnO2 is well known, and the production of electrolytic manganese dioxide (EMD) is commercially practiced, both from sulphate or from chloride electrolytes. The oxidation of manganese follows the reaction: Mn2+ + 2 H2O - MnO2 + 4H+ + 2e- 7 ALTA Free Library www.altamet.com.au The standard potential for that reaction is 1.23V, nearly identical to the standard potential for the water decomposition reaction (oxygen evolution reaction), which is the typical anodic reacti

on for most electrowinning processes: 2H2O - O2 + 4H+ + 4e- Therefore, both reactions will normally occur together to a certain extent which will depend on concentration in solutions, anodic material, temperature, acidity, … In the case of EMD, other factors are also critical to the marketability of the MnO2 produced; in particular, the MnO2 must be of the - variety to be used in dry cells. Also, anodic current efficiency has to be maximized, while maintaining product specification. These constraints do not necessarily apply to processes removing manganese as an impurity. ###### **3.4.
