Whenever possible, examples of commercial application are reviewed, as well as proposed procedures. ###### **4.1. THE COPPER-MANGANESE SEPARATION** The occurrence of manganese in copper leach circuits is not rare, and it could cause operating problems. Significant amounts of manganese are present in the Gecamines (DRC, ex-Zaire) copper electrowinning circuits, and in Girilambone (Australia), for example. Manganese could originate from Cu-Mn Wads and Cu-Co-Mn Wads, and other manganiferous minerals that undergo some solubilization under Cu leach conditions. The presence of manganese could have noticeable effects on the operation of the plant: 1. the manganese does not plate with copper, but it could be physically entrapped into the copper deposit and contaminate the Cu cathode if the Mn level in solution is too high (LME Grade A copper specification is 1 g/t Mn). 2. the manganese gets plated at the anode, forming a MnO2 layer; this layer could peel off and some MnO2 flakes could be incorporated within the cathode, contaminating it. The other potential problem with MnO2 coating the anode arises for plants planning to use reactive inert anodes (i.e. DSA anodes) to replace conventional lead anodes (21): in that case, the reactive anode being coated with MnO2 behaves like a MnO2 anode, therefore negating some of the energy savings advantages of the reactive anodes. The manganese in solution is also partially converted to permanganate at the anode, and if the spent electrolyte is used as stripping solution in a conventional Cu solvent extraction circuit, severe degradation of the organic extractant will occur (22). This is the situation at Girilambone, where the spent electrolyte Eh is measured and controlled to less than 750 11 ALTA Free Library www.altamet.com.au mV (NHE). The control mechanism in that plant is to maintain a Fe2+ /Mn ratio of at least 10 (23). The possibility also exists to reduce the permanganate prior to SX. In the case of plants not using SX and where Mn build up would jeopardise cathode quality (i.e. Gecamines, for example), the Mn is controlled through the circuit bleed (24,25), as illustrated in Figure 11. THE ZINC-MANGANESE SEPARATION** Zinc and manganese are commonly associated in commercial sulphate electrolytes. The association of zinc and manganese in sulphide concentrates is not uncommon, and the typical example is that of the Gamsberg deposit in South Africa (26). The Zn/Mn association in oxidic minerals (for example franklinite [(Zn, Mn)O.Fe2O3] (27) or in recycled products (28) (Leclenche batteries, EAF dusts,…) is also frequent. In addition, typical practice calls for adding MnO2 to oxidise ferrous prior to jarosite precipitation: MnO2 + 2 FeSO4 + 2 H2SO4 - MnSO4 + Fe2(SO4)3 + 2H2O (1) 12 ALTA Free Library www.altamet.com.au The manganese sulphate follows the zinc sulphate to the cell house; part of the manganese is then re-oxidised back to MnO2 at the anode, and accumulates at the bottom of the cell to be periodically removed and recycled to the ferrous oxidation stage. Most commercial plants operate with 5 - 6 g/L Mn in the electrolyte to protect lead anodes from corrosion and insure the quality of the electrowon zinc. Steady-state levels of Mn in the electrolyte are normally easily maintained, except when substantial amounts are introduced to the system via the calcine. In those cases, excess manganese must be removed from the system. Dimensionally stable anodes (DSA) prepared by coating a titanium blank with a precious metals mixture (Pt-Ir, Ir,…) have been proposed and investigated as a replacement of lead anodes for the electrowinning of copper, cobalt, zinc. In the particular case of zinc electrowinning from sulphate solutions, it has been shown that the manganese present in the electrolyte would coat the DSA anode and increase the overpotential for oxygen evolution, negating therefore one of the main advantages of these anodes. Various options have been considered to accommodate high manganese zinc solutions. ###### **4.2.1. Co-recovery of MnO2 and zinc metal** The possibility of replacing the oxygen evolution reaction, which has high overvoltage, by a more favourable anodic reaction has always attracted researchers, since it would lead to substantial energy savings. Methanol oxidation (zinc electrolysis), and ferrous oxidation (copper electrolysis) have been proposed in the past (21), and the latter is still being investigated. In the case of high manganese zinc sulphate solutions, researchers have proposed (29,30,31) a process by which manganese oxidation replaces the oxygen

evolution reaction at the anode, and produces MnO2 (EMD) for sales, while the cathodic reaction remains the zinc reduction. Anode: Mn2+ + 2H2O - MnO2 + 4H+ + 2e- Cathode: Zn2+ + 2e- - Znº Overall: Mn2+ + 2H2O + Zn2+ - Znº + MnO2 + 4H+ Conditions favouring the electrodeposition of MnO2 are diametrically opposite to those for zinc metal. MnO2 deposition is favoured at high temperatures (>90ºC), low anodic current densities (<100 A/m2 ), relatively low acid concentrations (~0.2M), and high manganese concentrations. The deposition of zinc, on the other hand, is favoured by lower temperatures (<40ºC), higher current densities, higher acid concentrations (~0.5M) and low manganese concentrations. The overpotential for the MnO2 deposition has been measured to be very small, and therefore the cell voltage is significantly lower (2.3 - 2.7 V at 90ºC, 300 A/m2 cathodic current) as compared to traditional zinc plants (3.43 V at 526 A/m2 ). The system requires the use of an anode material that will promote manganese dioxide deposition, and the material proposed by the researchers is graphite. 13 ALTA Free Library www.altamet.com.au ###### **4.2.2. THE COBALT-MANGANESE SEPARATION** Cobalt and manganese are frequently associated in nature. In Central Africa, Democratic Republic of Congo (ex Zaire), cobalt is found primarily as carrollite (CuCO2S4) in the sulphide zones, and as helerogenite (CoOOH) in the oxide zone, together with a weathered compound named cobalt wad, a soft manganese oxide of low density. The cobalt oxide rich layer, named BOMZ (Black Ore Mineralized Zone) is characterized by its black MnO2 component. Another famous Co-Mn association is that represented by ocean manganese nodules, which contain significant amounts of cobalt. Similar land manganese “nodules” are als

o known, in Australia for example (42). The limonitic laterites have been touted in recent years as a major source of nickel. CONCLUSIONS** Control of manganese in acidic leach liquors is certainly not a new issue and various options are available to the metallurgist to raise to the challenge. Obviously, besides metallurgical performance and economic factors, the choice between the various process options will depend on other factors, such as solution composition (in particular the ratio of manganese to the pay metal(s)) and the type of pay metal compound that is being targeted (metal, sulphide, oxide, carbonate,…). In the case of copper-manganese acidic solutions with high Mn/Cu ratios (manganese electrolyte, for example), copper can easily be removed selectively from manganese by sulphide or hydroxide precipitation. If the ratio Mn/Cu is lower (for example, copper leach solutions), and no copper solvent extraction process is practiced, as in the Central African Copper Belt), manganese is controlled through a bleed, and copper is separated by a two-stage hydroxide precipitation with recycle of the second stage Cu-(Mn) precipitate. The issue arises when copper is recovered by SX/EW, because of organic degradation by permanganate ions formed at the anode. Solutions to that problem are to maintain a Fe2+ /Mn ratio of at least 10 in the electrolyte (Girilambone), or to reduce the Mn in the spent elec

trolyte prior to contacting the loaded organic. 

In the case of zinc manganese acidic liquors, excess manganese can be controlled by electrolytic oxidation to MnO2 in a sacrificial cell, or by selective oxidation/precipitation. Normally, strong oxidants (ozone, Caro’s acid, hypochlorite) have been suggested for manganese removal, but, recently, Lakefield developed a process using SO2/O2 mixtures 

35 

ALTA Free Library  www.altamet.com.au 

to remove Mn from zinc electrolytes from the Gamsberg project.  The possibility also exists to selectively solvent extract zinc from manganese and produce SHG grade zinc, as demonstrated for the Boleo project during a pilot plant at Lakefield. 

Cobalt in well separated from manganese by sulphide precipitation; on the other hand, the selectivity of cobalt hydroxide precipitation ahead of manganese is not great.  The main cobalt solvent extractant, Cyanex 272, displays little selectivity between cobalt and manganese. 

Removal of manganese away from cobalt using oxidation/precipitation normally requires strong oxidants and, therefore, cobalt losses in the manganese precipitate are usually high.  Removal of Mn from cobalt solutions using SO2/Air mixtures was also piloted successfully at Lakefield, and cobalt losses were low (<0.5% Co). 

Laterite liquors contain significant amounts of Mn, usually several times higher than cobalt. Of the 4 commercial plants using PAL to treat limonitic laterites, two (Moa Bay, Murrin Murrin) are using sulphide precipitation to produce an intermediate Co/Ni sulphide concentrate, and, in that case, Mn is not an issue.  At Bulong, Mn is extracted with Co and Zn using Cyanex 272, and the Co-Mn separation is effected later by sulphide precipitation. At Cawse, hydroxide precipitation is used to prepare an hydroxysulphate Co/Ni concentrate, and some manganese is co-precipitated with the Co/Ni. 

A new purification process, based on bulk removal of (Mn + Co) using oxido-precipitation techniques (hypochlorite, SO2/O2,...) could result in a significant simplification of the nickel recovery circuit and shows promise, in particular for Bulong-type or Cawse-type laterite plants.

###### **1. INTRODUCTION** 

Unlike other base metals such as zinc and copper, nickel recovery by electrometallurgical methods only accounts for 45% of total world nickel production (Appendix 1) 

Zinc, with its lower relative yield, and larger product material handling demands, has been economically driven over the last thirty years to large scale automated cellhouse technologies such as those developed by Union Miniere (um) and Asturiana de Zinc (AdZ). 

Over the last ten years, the copper industry has developed through the introduction of large scale and low cost heap leach solvent extraction electrowinning technology. Plants in South America have converted from the traditional and higher cost starter sheet cellhouse operations to more automated permanent cathode systems like that of zinc. In the copper industry these automated technologies are known as the ISA Process and the Kidd Process after their respective locations of development.  Other process technologies such as polymer concrete UNICELLs and rolled lead anodes have also been developed during this time. 

Recently, nickel producers have begun to focus on design efficiency and operating productivity within the cellhouse.  A number of factors have delayed this trend and these are in part due to: 

- multi-form product market (not just cathode); 

- focus on upstream nickel extraction process efficiencies; 

- absence of interest (until recently) in hydrometallurgical nickel extraction in laterite deposits; and 

- electrometallurgical purification being a relatively small part of the total nickel process extraction route. 

This paper focuses on developments in engineering design and process technologies that have recently, and may in the future, be applied to nickel electrowinning systems, both in sulphate and chloride electrolytes.  These developments can also be applied to cobalt electrowinning systems. 

They include: 

- adjacent cell configuration; 

- complex UNICELL polymer concrete cell designs; 

- rolled lead alloy and DSA anodes; 

- contact busbars; 

- • automated cathode handling machinery; and • cellhouse ventilation systems including anode bags.

###### **3. NICKEL  ELECTROWINNING  CELLHOUSE LAYOUT** 

Traditional nickel cellhouse layout designs include cells that are located in pairs with catholyte or anolyte pipework attached externally for visual inspection and operating purposes.  Individual walkways are designed to allow operator access in between each pair of cells and electrical connection of the cell pairs are by a number of copper busbars under the walkways.  This has been a typical design for both sulphate and chloride electrolyte systems so far. 

Recently a cellhouse configuration that combines anode diaphragms with integrated anolyte pipework in polymer concrete cells has led to a layout of cells that are adjacent. This eliminates walkways and busbar runs in between the cell pairs.  This engineered layout was used at Cawse Nickel in Western Australia.  A graph showing capital cost comparisons between paired and adjacent cell configurations is shown in Figure 1 and indicates that a reduction of up to 5% in capital costs with the adjacent cell configuration is possible. A layout plan comparison is shown in Appendix II. 

Adjacent cell layouts can also lead to lower overall voltage and power costs due to the elimination of the busbar runs between the cell pairs. 

Current nickel cellhouse operators may claim than an advantage of the paired cell configuration is that for cell, bag or electrode repair only two cells need to be cut out of the cellhouse electrical circuit thus minimising production losses.  However with the recent development and acceptance of integrated cell shorting frames with automatic switches, adjacent cell layouts can also be maintained and minimal production loss.  These shorting frames allow the removal of a single cell from the electrical circuit. 

For future chloride electrowinning cellhouse designs in greenfield projects, and even for expansions of existing cellhouses, there is the opportunity to investigate the 'adjacent cell configuration' in order to save project capital and operating costs. 

Other layout considerations include proximity of the starter sheet section to the starter sheet preparations machinery for efficient logistics, and whether this combination should be located at one end of the cellhouse or centrally.  In larger capacity cellhouses, centrally located machinery ensures that the starter sheets and handling machines are at equal distance from either end of the cellhouse. The liners were made of lead, fibre reinforced polyester (FRP) and plastics such as polypropylene (PP) and polyethylene (PE). Typically these liners have a limited lifespan due to operation wear and mechanical damage. The liners would then have to be replaced and acid-attacked concrete repaired, during which time production would be lost. One of the major areas of process development, and one that allows nickel cellhouse design to incorporate "adjacent cell configuration", has been the development of polymer concrete UNICELLs. Polymer concrete electrolytic cells were first tested in Zambia in the 1970s, but it was in the 90s where the UNICELL concept became universally accepted throughout the electrometallurgical industry as the leading technology available. ATHODE BAGS** The purpose of the separating bag is to protect the cathode from the low pH anolyte formed at the anode in reaction (1). ###### **6. ELECTRODES** 

Nickel electrowinning electrode design is separated into two types, anodes where the generation of oxygen or chlorine gas occurs [reaction (1)] and cathodes where the reduction of nickel cations to metal takes place [reaction (2)]. 

###### **6.1 ANODES** 

Anode design and choice of materials largely depends on what electrolyte is chosen in the nickel electrowinning circuit. 

In sulphate electrolytes, the common anode material has been insoluble lead. This has also been typical of copper, zinc and cobalt electrowinning operations. In the past the lead anodes were cast and would likely warp, damage the electrode bag, cause short circuits and reduce current efficiency.  In some cases antimony would be added to the casting to help stiffen the anode. 

Rolling technology was then introduced to the lead anode fabrication process for the copper industry.  This cold rolled anode was stronger, stiffer and straighter than the cast lead anode.  Calcium tin alloying from lead acid battery technology was also combined with the rolling to extend anode life.  The alloy forms a coherent corrosion layer and minimises particulate lead compounds in the electrolyte. Electrode (both cathode and/or anode) bags assist with the reduction of particulate contaminating the nickel cathode. 

Lead alloy anode variations exist at nickel electrowinning operations.  For example at Harjavalta, Finland, cold rolled pure chemical lead anodes are used, and at Rustenburg, South Africa, strontium tin is used.  However it has been the complete

Further reasons why cold rolled anodes are favoured over cast lead alloy anodes are: 

- Cold rolled anodes are stronger than cast anodes, so are relatively thinner and allow for more inter-electrode space between bag and electrode. 

- At higher current densities and temperature (60-65<sup>0</sup> C) cold rolled anodes will remain straight. 

- Rolled anodes produce a fine-grained corrosion product, which does not attach to bag faces, but falls to the bottom of the cell or anode bag for eventual cleaning. 

In copper electrowinning plant designs, 6 mm thick lead alloy anodes are specified for electrolyte temperatures of 35-45<sup>0</sup> C, but in nickel electrowinning 8 mm minimum thickn

ess is recommended due to the higher electrolyte temperature of 60-65<sup>0</sup> C and relatively more complex and unstable electrometallurgical process. 

In chloride electrolytes, lead or lead alloy anodes are unacceptable due to complete anode corrosion and so dimensionally stable anodes, or DSA's are chosen.  These are expensive and typically in mesh or plate form.  Falconbridge's operation in Norway uses a titanium structure coated with an electro-active layer of a noble metal oxide. 

Designs must also consider: 

- Ba(OH)2 addition to electrolyte to precipitate soluble lead in electrolyte. 

- Separation of anode face from bag (in anode bag cases) by using plastic insulators. 

- Seal of the bag around anode to reduce gas separation equipment sizing. 

- For anode bags, anodes also have plastic insulators to ensure separation from the bag. 

Future engineering opportunities include: 

- Anode bag and frame assemblies that are functional and easy to clean. 

- • Insulators and devices that positively locate the cathodes between the anode bag frames. 

- 'Shot peening' of the lead anode face to increase surface area and to strengthen it. 

- Copper hanger bar designs that do not anneal and bend under high current due to short circuits.  These designs include silver copper alloys and optimum work hardening of the hanger bar by extrusion. 

###### **6.2 CATHODE** 

Nickel cathode product can be produced from starter sheets that have been previously located on mother blanks or from a permanent masked cathode to produce 'crowns' or 'rounds'.  As yet there is no commercial technology where full sized cathodes are plated on permanent mother blank like in copper or zinc.

The typical size of a cathode is 1 m square and it is then sheared into smaller sizes between 25 and 100 mm square.  A typical nickel cathode is plated for six to seven days and should be approximately 8 mm thick. 

Starter sheet blanks are most commonly made of titanium, which is 3mm thick and sized to allow for starter sheet trimming and electrode plating overlaps (30-50mm). Stainless steel, which is cheaper than titanium, has been used at Bulong, (Australia) Bindura, (Zimbabwe) and Tocontins, (Brazil), in sulphate electrolytes. However from operational experience blank strippability of titanium is easer than stainless steel. 

Cathode design aspects to consider for optimum cathode purity and current distribution are: 

- Nickel starter sheet that is rigid and straight. 

- Copper hanger bar that has a circular profile for point busbar contact and to 

- ensure efficient contact of the rigid loop. 

- Stronger copper hanger bars that are hard extruded and alloyed with silver. These are more difficult to damage and anneal with high temperature and current from short circuits. 

For chloride electrolyte it is necessary to use titanium mother blanks or permanent and masked cathodes to produce 'rounds' or 'crowns'.

###### **8. CONTACT BUSBARS AND CELL TOP FURNITURE** 

Whilst only a small component of the overall cellhouse design, contact busbar and associated insulator design is nevertheless an important design aspect.  It is the aim of all cellhouse operators to target the equivalent current in each electrode pair throughout the entire cellhouse to ensure optimum current efficiency.  Correct electrode location, short circuit elimination and clean contacts are just some of the measures taken to strive for this target and it is all related to busbar and cell top furniture design. 

Types of busbar designs used have been: 

- triangular; 

- • dogbone; and • double contact. 

Triangular busbar designs have been used in the past and consist of a copper equilateral triangle, typically with one inch sides.  Advantages and disadvantages of the system are: 

- **ADVANTAGES** -           Low cost. - Easy to fabricate. - Easy to replace on cell and clean. - Once one contact on edge of the triangle has been worn the bar can be flipped over and another edge used. 

- - Simple cell top furniture. 

###### **DISADVANTAGES** 

- Asymmetric anode hanger bar design is required. 

- - Low current carrying capacity. 

A 'dogbone' busbar is an alternative to the triangular cross section.  The 'dogbone' is a cross section of copper busbar that connect two circular or triangular contacts and allows for a symm

etrical anode hanger bar design.  It is more expensive as there is more copper, it’s a more complicated extrusion and machining is also required.  The cell top furniture is also more complicated.  However its advantage is that it has more current capacity and better current distribution which has lead to its widespread acceptance within cellhouse designs. 

Recently busbar design developments have led to the double contact design.  The main features are equalizing bars for anodes or cathodes or both.  Because of the equalizing bars, electrodes have two contacts, which help even out current distribution between electrodes.  As a consequence the cellhouse can operate at higher current densities and higher current current efficiency. Figure 2 shows a combination of triangular and dogbone busbar  "double-double" contact as used at OMG’s Kokkola copper electrowinning cellhouse.

###### **9. AUTOMATED ELECTRODE HANDLING MACHINERY** 

Traditionally, where labour costs have been low, all electrode handling such as starter sheet preparation, cathode washing and bundling has been done manually.  As labour costs rise, and issues such as safety and occupational hygiene have become an essential consideration, automated methods of handling electrodes have been developed. 

At present machines exist that prepare and strip permanent 'crown' or 'round' nickel production.  These are typically patented by the operators. 

In full cathode starter sheet operations, Outokumpu has developed automated starter sheet cathode handling machinery.  This automation is used in plants at Harjavalta in Finland (where it was developed) and Cawse cellhouse in Australia (now shutdown) and can process approximately 150 starter sheet blanks per hour. Appendix VII shows an Outokumpu nickel starting sheet stripping machine. 

The sequence of automated handling is as follows: 

1. Titanium or stainless steel start sheet blanks are loaded by crane into the starter sheet production cells. 

2. Plating of a nickel starter sheet takes place for 24 to 36 hours. 

3. The plated starter sheet cathodes are lifted from the cells and loaded into the nickel starter sheet stripping machine where they are washed, flexed, stripped and 

12

stacked.  The washed titanium or stainless blanks are returned to the starter sheet cells for further starter sheet production. 

4. The stacked starter sheets are then transferred to the starter sheet preparation machine where they are trimmed to their specific cathode dimension, straightened, strengthened by folding or embossing and nickel loops welded.

4. Copper hanger bars are then slid through the nickel loops and the crane transfers the prepared starter sheet to the commercial cells. 

5. After four to six days of commercial production plating, the crane lifts the nickel cathodes and loads them into a machine for automated washing, bundling and weighing. 

Future developments in nickel electrode handling automation include: 

- Full deposit permanent cathode stripping which would eliminate nickel starter sheet preparation and only include the simplified functions of washing, stripping, bundling and weighing. 

- More automated methods of cleaning cells, bags and anodes depending on cell configuration (anode or cathode bags). 

- Automated unmanned cranes that are linked to the nickel electrode handling machines, as has been accomplished in copper and zinc. 

- Automated machinery carried by cranes that can detect and correct electrode short circuits. 

###### **10. MIST SUPPRESSION** 

In nickel electrowinning, nascent oxygen or chlorine gas is generated at the anode and produces acid mist.  At the cathode, if there are low (high acid) pH excursions, then there is the possibility of hydrogen gas generation.  Any mist generated also carries with it nickel which is a recognised carcinogen. Hence ventilation and mist suppression design in the nickel cellhouse is an important component of the overall design concept. 

Methods of mist suppression available in the electrometallurgical industry today include: 

- Anode bags. 

- Mist suppression foams. 

- Mist suppression balls and beads. 

- Open cellhouse designs. 

- Cell top hoods. 

- Positive flow ventilation. 

- • Combinations of the above. 

- **Anode bags** as discussed in a previous section completely capture the mists generated at the anode .  Essential for chloride electrowinning they are now becoming important in nickel sulphate systems. . 

- **Mist suppression foams** such as SLS, not only suppress acid mist but assist in the nickel cathode growth, and are very common throughout the nickel industry. Research has also shown that SLS in anode bags can assist with the equalization of liquid/gas evacuation from the individual bag compartments.

- **Open cellhouse designs** with no side walls are a cheap alternative to minimize acid mist in the operating area. This is common in some low cost copper electrowinning designs and was originally designed for Rustenburg.  Rustenburg then enclosed the cellhouse due to wind blown dust contaminating cathode in the cells.  Bulong Nickel has an open cellhouse. 

- **FRP hoods** can be placed on the cell and in fact integrated with the polymer concrete cell design to

A combination of several of the above measures is common in industrial electrometallurgical practice today, and is likely to be so in the future. 

###### **11. OTHER DESIGN ASPECTS** 

Further engineering features that are necessary for the optimum operation of a nickel cellhouse include: 

- Adequate electrolyte surge capacity between the cellhouse and the upstream process unit operations, whether this be solvent extraction, ion exchange or liquid/solid separation, to allow for process upsets and minimal affect on the cellhouse operation. 

- Adequate heating of total cellhouse and surge volume electrolyte to ensure a stable electrolyte temperature even when electrolyte is being circulated and trickle power is applied to the upstream shutdowns. 

- Back-up emergency rectifier in case of power outage (in particular in starter-sheet production area) so that galvanic corrosion of cathodes does not occur. 

- Adequate design for prevention of stray currents including electrically insulated pumps, large cell overflows (that 'splash' and break flow and provide a high resistance path) and consideration of 'null' points or electrically neutral point of the circuit. 

- Cell shorting frames with vacuum switches that minimise production loss when maintaining cells, bags, frames and electrodes.

- Conservative current density from 200-240 A/m<sup>2</sup> . 

- Nickel tenor in catholyte to be targeted at 85-100 g/L. 

- Conservative pH target of 3-3.5, controlled with boric acid (sulphate electrolyte). 

- Nickel starter sheets that are rigid and straight when loaded into the commercial cells. 

- Addition of SLS additive (sodium laurel sulphonate), a surfactant that assists cathode deposition by reducing occurrence of pre-stripping and giving a smooth dense electrodeposition. 

- Large catholyte surge and heating capacity to minimise process upsets and maintain a steady electrolyte temperature at 60-65<sup>0</sup> C. 

- Automated dual media anthracite/garnet filters be

tween electrowinning and solvent extraction circuits that removes SX organic from incoming electrolyte. 

- Hot and efficient washing of nickel cathode when removed from cell. 

- Addition of barium hydroxide to electrolyte to precipitate soluble lead so that it does not plate with the nickel. 

- Double contact busbar system that equalizes current and minimises short circuits and impurities in nickel cathode. 

- Tight tolerance positive locating spacer insulators that locate electrode hanger bars in exact positions to ensure equi-spacing and minimisation of short circuits. 

- Polymer concrete UNICELLs that do not use plastic, lead or FRP liners, and so do not contaminate the electrolyte as liners do when they fail. 

###### **13. CONCLUSIONS** 

In short there are many factors to consider in nickel electrowinning cellhouse design. These include polymer concrete UNICELLs, bag systems, rolled lead alloy anodes, cellhouse ventilation and automated electrode handling and cellhouse layouts.  It is clear that opportunities exist to improve productivity and cathode purity by use of some of the process technologies that are already in use in the copper and zinc processing industries.

INTRODUCTION** The reverse osmosis process is commonly used at remotely located nickel operations where high salinity bores are the only available water source. The reverse osmosis system is the major step in the water treatment process that provides high quality water for the nickel recovery process. Whilst the reverse osmosis process is reasonably well known, the often competing issues that drive the cost of ownership are less well understood and usually vary from site to site. Often, but not always, design initiatives that may increase capital cost may significantly reduce operating cost, lowering the whole of life cost. Reduction in cost stems from understanding all of the influencing factors, making a cost benefit assessment and ensuring that the equipment specification reflects the outcome from this assessment. ##

#### **2. CAPITAL COST** 

###### **2.1. WATER DEMAND ANALYSIS** 

Careful water demand analysis with a focus on minimising water use will result in a smaller, lower cost RO plant. Some thought should be given to the selection of “water efficient” processes downstream of the RO unit and the potential to recycle or reuse water where possible. 

State of the art water reuse technology is now available and can considerably reduce overall water consumption if applied appropriately. Often an integrated approach where a membrane based wastewater treatment system and desalination system are combined can reap benefits in overall cost of ownership. 

The rule here is: Lower desalinated water demand means lower RO capital cost 

###### **2.2. FEED WATER SOURCE** 

###### **2.2.1. Total Dissolved Solids (TDS)** 

“TDS” is the term used to describe the levels of dissolved material in water and is usually only used to provide an “at a glance” indicator of the water characteristics. When evaluating suitability for an application, a detailed analysis of the feed water is required. 

TDS is used in Table 1 to provide a basis for comparison of RO systems operating with feed waters at different concentrations.

###### **2.2.2. Feed Water Chemistry and Recovery Ratio** 

Recovery Ratio is the ratio of product water (permeate) produced to RO plant feed water. For a given permeate flow, a system with a high recovery ratio has a lower feed water flow than a system with a low recovery ratio.  Theoretically, this means that high recovery systems cost less to produce than low recovery systems due to smaller pumps, smaller / l

ess pipe work, and (perhaps) less membrane elements. In practice however, issues relating to feed water characteristics tend to skew this relationship. 

The RO process progressively concentrates the feed water as product water is extracted.  The higher the RO recovery ratio, the higher this concentration.  If this concentration exceeds the saturation level of a feed water constituent, it will precipitate within the membranes.  For this reason, it is important to understand the constituents of the feed water and concentration at which they become saturated.  Sensible design dictates a recovery ratio that either avoids saturation of feed water constituents or allows some saturation to occur but manages precipitation through use of anti-scalant chemicals. 

Additionally, higher feed water salinity dictates higher RO system operating pressure.  In this case, the benefit of high recovery ratio must be carefully balanced against the cost to produce it as the RO system operating pressure required may be prohibitively high. 

_The rule here is: Maximise recovery ratio within the bounds of the feed water characteristics to reduce capital costs._

###### **2.2.3. Total Suspended Solids (TSS) and Turbidity in the RO feed** 

“TSS” is the term used to describe the levels of suspended material in water and is measured in milligrams per litre.  Usually, TSS is considered simultaneously with turbidity, which indicates the size and the quantity of the suspended particles, when designing pretreatment to RO systems. 

Feed water to an RO system must be virtually free from suspended solids. The quantity and characteristics of the feed water suspended solids will dictate the removal mechanism. Where feed waters can demonstrate very low levels of suspended solids, minimal filtration such as disposable cartridges can be used successfully. 

As the level of suspended solids increases, more significant pre-filtration is required. This is typically a back-washing multimedia pressure filter or self cleaning strainer followed by the disposable cartridge filters described above. This adds 10 – 15% to the capital cost of the RO system with cartridge filters only described above. 

Further increase in the level of suspended solids may require the installation of a settling tank, with perhaps a flocculant addition step, prior to the other prefiltration steps. This adds 20 – 35% to the capital cost of the RO system with cartridge filters only described above. 

Finally, if the suspended material is of a fine nature and varying in quantity so that cannot be chemically settled and will pass through conventional filters, a membrane microfiltration (MF) or ultrafiltration (UF) plant may be required. This adds 60 – 80% to the capital cost of the RO system with cartridge filters only described above. 

_The rule here is: All other things being equal, decreasing feed water TSS equals decreasing capital cost._ 

###### **2.3. PRODUCT WATER

SPECIFICATION** Reverse Osmosis plants remove a proportion (usually 97 – 99%) of the feed water dissolved solids, and so some dissolved solids remain in the product water. The actual removal rate (rejection) is a function of the feed water composition, the RO membrane element type, the RO membrane configuration and the system operating conditions. Very high rejections (99.5%+) can only be achieved by using more costly high rejection membrane elements or by re-treating the product water in a further desalination step, which also adds to the cost. Conversely, if lower rejections (say 65%– 75%) are acceptable, some of the feed water can be diverted around the RO system and mixed with the RO permeate. This effectively reduces the size of the RO system and reduces cost. _The rule here is: The ability to accept lower quality permeate will reduce capital cost._ 4 ALTA Free Library www.altamet.com.au ###### **2.4. DIMENSIONAL CONSTRAINTS** It is possible to reduce the “footprint” of an RO system whilst maintaining it’s hydraulic configuration. Common strategies of achieving physical reductions are: - Reducing the length whilst increasing the quantity of RO pressure tubes. - Tighter packaging of components on RO skid. ###### **3.1.1. Energy Recovery** 

Energy recovery systems reduce the overall power consumption of RO systems by using the RO let-down energy to supplement the RO system pump drive.  Typically, this is most effective on plants that operate at higher pressure and lower recovery ratios, as these conditions make the most energy available for recovery. 

Typically, installation of an energy recovery system on a seawater desalination plant can add 30% to the capital cost but can reduce power consumption by up to 50%. 

###### **3.2. MEMBRANE ELEMENT REPLACEMENT** 

Although RO membrane elements should not be considered a consumable item, they do have a finite life-span.  This life-span has a significant impact on operating cost. 

Consider the example, in Table 2, of the RO system operating with a feed water salinity of 2000 mg/L.  This plant requires 42 membrane elements with a total value of A$63,000.  As the expected operating life of RO membrane elements is 2  - 5 years, the annual operating cost, associated with membrane element replacement can be as high as A$31,500 or as low as A$12,600.  Clearly, maximising membrane element life is essential to the overall management of operating cost. 

###### **3.2.1. Feed Water Characteristics** 

A feed water with a high fouling or scaling potential, and where inappropriate pre-treatment is employed, will result in reduced membrane element life.  Most commonly found scalants and foulants are, to some degree, removable by cleaning; however there is always a proportion that remains on the element and accumulates over time.  Accumulation of foulants/scalants reduces the permeability of the membrane elements and reduces the overall system product water flow rate. 

_Low Fouling / Scaling feedwater = Low membrane replacement cost._ 

###### **3.2.2. Membrane Element Cleaning Strategy** 

In reality, some degree of fouling / scaling will always occur.  Because of this, the an appropriate cleaning strategy should be adopted to increase membrane element life and to ensure more consistent water production. 

In almost all cases, a cleaning regime which employs more frequent cleans with less aggressive chemicals promotes increased membrane element life when compared to less frequent, more aggressive cleans. More frequent cleaning also provides the opportunity to more frequently evaluate cleaning effectiveness and, if necessary, make adjustments to and optimise the cleaning regi

me. 

_Less Aggressive / more frequent cleaning = Low membrane replacement cost._

###### **3.2.3. Membrane Element Construction** 

Although physically similar and mostly retrofittable, membrane elements from different manufacturers are often constructed differently providing certain advantages.  Some manufacturers provide models with higher membrane surface area, which allows same production rates at lower pressures. Use of lower pressures means that foulants and scalants are less likely to “driven” into the membrane surface and are therefore more likely to be removed successfully by cleaning. 

Other construction techniques focus on more evenly distributing the TMP (trans-membrane pressure) within the element.  This tends to more evenly distribute the flux within the membrane, and can increase the run times between cleans. 

###### **3.3. CHEMICAL USAGE** 

Most reverse osmosis systems make use of chemicals to pre-treat the feedwater, to clean the membrane elements and to santise the membrane elements. 

###### **3.3.1. Antiscalants / Dispersants** 

Antiscalants / Dispersants are dosed in the RO system feed water to: 

- inhibit the formation of scale on the RO membrane elements. 

- Inhibit the build up of NOM (natural organic matter) on the RO membrane elements. 

These chemicals have significant impact on operating cost and their use needs to be optimised, for a specific application, in order to reduce operating costs. 

The optimisation process involves installing a test unit on the RO concentrate. The test unit contains a small section of membrane flat sheet, which, after operating for a known period under known conditions, is removed and analysed.  The process is repeated until the appropriate type and dose rate of Antiscalant / Dispersant is determined 

###### **3.3.2. Cleaning Chemicals** 

Selection of the optimal cleaning regime impacts both membrane element life (and therefore membrane element replacement cost) and the cost of the cleaning chemical itself. 

The cleaning chemical and its’ application needs to be optimised in order to reduce costs.  Initial selection of a cleaning regime is usually based on the expected foulants from the water analysis. 

During operation, the cleaning efficiency is monitored and the cleaning regime adjusted to optimise the results. 

7

###### **3.4. CARTRIDGE FILTERS** 

Cartridge filter replacement, influences not only it’s own cost but membrane element life, and therefore membrane replacement cost. Their primary purpose is to polish the feed water prior to the RO membranes.  Usually, the optimal cartridge type is one that provides the lowest particle size cut-off whilst maintaining good dirt holding capacity. 

Here again, it is essential to try different types of filter as each has advantages in different applications.  The most appropriate selection methods is to take TSS measurements before and after the fi

lters and to measure the rate of pressure differential increase.  Weighing filters when new and when at maximum differential pressure can indicate maximum dirt holding capacity. 

###### **3.5. MAINTENANCE** 

Correct and timely maintenance of RO systems is essential.  It assists the management of the cost associated with insufficient water production.  “Maintenance” involves the chemical cleaning of membrane elements mentioned above, recalibration of dosing pumps, recalibrating of instruments, checking vibration or wear in rotating equipment and making adjustments to compensate for feed water variability. 

This ultimately reduces membrane replacement cost, optimises chemical usage and ensures consistent water production 

###### **3.6. COST OF FEED WATER** 

Due consideration must be given to the cost to deliver the feed water to the RO plant. Costs may include: 

- Establishment of bores 

- Installation, operation and control of transfer pumps 

- Civil works such as pipelines, transfer stations 

- Maintenance of equipment.

###### **ABSTRACT** 

The trend toward increasing acid and chloride levels in hydrometallurgical pressure leach processes, such as HPAL of nickel laterite ores, warrants selection of more resistant titanium alloys for equipment.  Although the Ti-Pd alloys (Grades 7, 11, 16, and 17) are traditional, technically-viable candidates for preventing crevice corrosion and/or vapor phase acid attack in HPAL equipment, these alloys are  costly due to the high and volatile price of palladium.  The Ti-0.1% Ru alloys, Grades 26 and 27, represent lower-cost alternatives to Ti-Pd alloys with similar properties. 

HPAL autoclaves are constructed of titanium-steel clad plates.  Although one should expect the same explosion-bonding behavior as the unalloyed Ti and Ti-Pd alloys, Ti-Ru alloy plate bonding to steel had not previously been demonstrated.  To formally qualify the clad product for HPAL process use, two explosion-bonding trials on 9 mm thick Grade 26 and Grade 27 Ti-Ru plates bonded to 50 mm A516GR70 steel backer plates were conducted.  These clad plates were thoroughly metallurgically characterized via destructive and non-destructive examinations, and subsequently subjected to a typical hot head-forming operation to demonstrate vessel fabricability. 

In addition to detailing results of these two bonding trials, this paper provides an overview of Ti-Ru alloy metallurgy and properties, and corresponding clad plate equipment cost implications and candidate HPAL applications. 

###### **1. BACKGROUND** 

Pressure acid leaching (PAL) ore in the presence of sulfuric acid at high temperatures and pressures provides a potentially low cost option for production of nickel metal.  The process exhibits hot oxidizing conditions under which nearly all common metals and alloys perform poorly.  Titanium is one of the only metals that has excellent corrosion resistance under the combined conditions of temperature, acid concentration, possible chlorides, and oxidizing ions present in these PAL autoclaves.   However, the high pressure, temperature, and volume requirements for the autoclaves create conditions in which monolithic titanium equipment is not economically viable

. Titanium clad steel offers the corrosion performance of titanium at much lower cost. Fabrication and operation experience demonstrate that titanium clad steel is the preferred material of construction for PAL autoclaves for nickel production. Titanium-steel clad plate for PAL construction has been manufactured exclusively by the explosion cladding process. ###### **1.1 AUTOCLAVE ENVIRONMENT** Autoclaves for PAL of nickel laterites operate around 250°C to 270°C (480°F to 510°F) and 5.0+ MPa (725+ psi), with a 5 to 7% sulfuric acid concentration. High concentrations of oxidizing metal ions, such as ferric and nickelous ions, are naturally present. Corrosion conditions in these facilities are frequently aggravated by high chloride concentrations in the available process water. Process economics demand that the autoclaves have large capacity and continuous process design. Consequently, the pressure vessels are typically large in diameter and length, and are of horizontal construction with a sequence of mechanically agitated chambers. Six PAL autoclaves have been operating in nickel/cobalt ore leaching plants in Western Australia since 1999. In recent years palladium has become a common alloy for use in a number of applications, the most prevalent being the catalytic converters in cars.   The result has been a dramatic increase in palladium usage and price.   Limited supply and world political conditions have resulted in dramatic price swings as well.  Since 1995, palladium prices have ranged between $200 and $1,200 USD/troy oz.  At present, palladium price is in the $375 USD/toz range.   In comparison, ruthenium price is currently in the $75. ###### **1.4 EXPLOSION CLADDING OF TITANIUM ALLOYS** 

Explosion clad plates of Ti-Pd Grade 11 and steel have been manufactured for the chemical process industry since the 1960’s.  The Bulong autoclave project was the first major commercial use of Ti Grade 17 clad steel.  The first significant commercial applications of the Ti-Ru alloys, Grades 26 and 27, have occurred over the past two years. At this time, commercial use of Ti-Ru clad plates has been limited to some small heat exchanger tubesheet applications.  The objective of the explosion cladding trial program discussed in this paper was to qualify the manufacture of large explosion clad plates of Ti Grade 27 bonded to steel, and to evaluate the  suitability of these plates  for fabrication into the heads and cylinders required for autoclave construction. 

###### **2. Ti-Ru ALLOY METALLURGY** 

The metallurgy of the Ti-Ru binary alloy system is fairly well defined.  Established phase diagrams<sup>(8)</sup> reveal that minor ruthenium additions act as strong beta phase stabilizers in titanium, such that as little as 0.05 wt.% Ru stabilizes a fine uniform dispersion of second (beta) phase within the alpha phase matrix, Figure 2.  As such, the fine beta phase formed is enriched with ruthenium to levels on the order of 5-10 wt.%<sup>(6)</sup> .  With a rather high solubility in beta titanium in excess of 30 wt.%, ruthenium remains in solid solution and does not form any intermetallic (e.g., TixRuy) compounds or additional phases in these alloys<sup>(6-8)</sup> . 

Since the net amount of ruthenium a

ddition to these Ti-Ru alloys is so meager (~0.12 wt.%), there is no significant solid solution strengthening and the mechanical and physical properties of Ti Grade 26 and 27 (Ti-Ru) alloys are equivalent to that of unalloyed Grades 2 and 1, respectively.  As a result, strength values, design allowables, fabricability, and weldability of Ti-Ru and corresponding base chemically pure (C.P.) alloy mill products are generally similar.  Since the ruthenium only forms a very small volume fraction (~2 vol.%) of uniformly dispersed beta phase which is metallurgically stable, Ti-Ru alloys are thermally stable, and do not exhibit thermal or corrosion sensitization (e.g., weld/HAZ effects) or aging. 



Figure 2:  Typical Microstructure of Ti-Ru Alloy Sheet at 200X mag. 

In addition to enhancing corrosion resistance, minor ruthenium additions to unalloyed titanium improve ductility and cold/warm formability in wrought mill products.  This beneficial effect stems from a significantly finer microstructure (i.e., grain refinement) induced by Ru-stabilized beta phase particles, acting as nuclei and/or grain growth inhibitors during recrystallization.  Therefore, Ti-Ru wrought products (e.g., plate or strip) can exhibit somewhat improved forming limits over equivalent low-iron C.P. titanium or Ti-

###### **2.1 EARLY ALLOY CHALLENGES** 

The development and qualification phases of the Grade 26 and 27 TiRu alloys by RMI Titanium Co. revealed two metallurgical challenges that needed to be overcome to successfully commercialize TiRu mill products.  The first stems from pure ruthenium's elevated melting point compared to titanium (or palladium), which makes it difficult to VAR and, especially, EB hearth melt fully and homogeneously into titanium ingots.  RMI Titanium Co. successfully addressed this concern through the development of a proprietary (patent-pending) master alloy, which ensures total rapid assimilation and homogenization during the melting process. 

The subsequent challenge involved the excessive directionality in strength values exhibited by TiRu plate products when processed via traditional routes used for C.P. titanium products.  The refined grain structure from the Ru-stabilized beta phase magnified the typical basal transverse crystallographic texture in C.P. titanium plate; such that transverse direction yield strengths far exceeded maximum limits specified in ASTM B- 265.  This is of significant concern for Ti Grade 27 plate to be cladded, since low and similar yield strength (flow stress) values are required in all plate directions for optimum, successful explosion bonding to steel.  RMI Titanium has since qualified a proprietary processing procedure which consistently achieves minimal L vs. T property directionality in all Grade 26 and 27 plat

e products, with strength values well within ASTM B-265 specification limits. RMI Titanium Co. has U.S. trademarks for both Ti-Ru grade products: TIRU-26TM and TIRU-27TM ; which ensure that chemical homogeneity and minimal property directionality in plate mill products are consistently achieved. More stringent internal aims on minimum ruthenium content (0.1% Ru min.) and low iron limits for optimum corrosion resistance are also inherently designed into these trademarked alloys. ###### **3. MECHANISM FOR Ti-Ru ALLOY CORROSION RESISTANCE** The mechanism for ruthenium enhancement of titanium corrosion resistance is basically the same as that of palladium and other platinum group metals, and involves alloy ennoblement. The fine ruthenium-enriched beta phase dispersed throughout the alpha grain matrix provide cathodic sites of low hydrogen overvoltage which facilitate hydrogen ion reduction kinetics(9,10) in aqueous acidic media. This depolarization of the hydrogen ion reduction reaction, or "cathode modification" phenomenon, produces a substantial shift in the titanium alloy corrosion potential towards the noble (positive) direction where the protective surface oxide film (TiO2) is stable, and full passivity can be achieved. It is, therefore, not surprising that Ti-Ru alloys exhibit very similar resistance to the Ti-Pd alloys in hot dilute reducing acid solutions as indicated in Figure 3. Similar behavior can be expected with weld and HAZ metal as shown. It is important to note that the use of Ti-Pd (ERTi-7) filler metal for welding Ti-Ru alloy components is recommended and preferred from both a corrosion resistance and commercial availability standpoint. They further indicate that this metal combination can be produced in plate sizes needed for cost effective PAL autoclave manufacture, and that the clad plates can be formed into heads and cylinders without concern of metal cracking or bond separation. BACKGROUND INFORMATION** To achieve reliable corrosion and erosion protection of a pressure vessel shell in many cases requires the use of specialty ceramics and a membrane lining system applied onto the carbon steel substrate. This paper explores a lining selection process that has proven to produce reliable ceramic linings. A properly selected lining system will subsequently aid in the availability of the PAL vessels and subsequently, increase the reliability of the overall plant. It is extremely important to have comprehensive lining design information available early on in a project to ensure proper lining design and reliable costing data. This includes, but is not limited to information such as process chemistry, variable ore composition, temperature and pressure ranges, possible upset conditions, etc. Ignoring critical information in the lining design phase and in the overall lining selection process can lead to significant lining problems that can impede a brick lined pressure vessel’s operating performance, resulting in unplanned plant shutdowns and higher plant operating and maintenance costs. Over the last few years, a number of PAL operations i

n various parts of the world have experienced unusual start-up and operating difficulties. This issue has been explored in technical papers presented at Alta Ni/Co Conferences over the past few years.  Part of the difficulties faced can be attributed to improper material selection.  This was discussed in Alan Taylor’s April 2001 Minerals Gazette Article – “MATERIALS KEY TO PAL PLANTS.” 

Another significant reason for some of the problems faced by a few PAL operators in recent years relates to design incompatibilities between their ceramic linings and the associated vessel steel shells. Unfortunately for the plant owners this issue was not properly accounted for during the lining and steel design phase. This topic was explored in more detail in an ALTA Ni/Co ‘99 technical paper titled “INTEGRATION OF PRESSURE VESSEL STEEL & BRICK LINING DESIGN.”  This paper focuses on the importance of proper timing of the project’s design and procurement schedule for the steel shell and the brick lining system. 

In recent years, it has been found on a number of HPAL and HPOX projects that there is a definite benefit to supply of the steel vessel and the ceramic lining system as a complete “unitary” system; thereby designing and supplying the vessels and their associated ceramic linings with single source responsibility.  Several significant points to consider with this approach are as follows: 

- The ceramic lining system typically encounters the process directly while the steel vessel performs as the containment enclosure for the process.

- Ceramic linings impose specific requirements on the design and fabrication of the steel vessels, which are drawn from the empirical experience of the lining suppliers.  Nozzle lining and nozzle steel designs have proven to be critical to the proper performance of a ceramic lined PAL vessel. 

- There are relatively few capable ceramic-lining suppliers for HPAL or HPOX service when compared to the number of very competent vessel fabricators. 

- A competent ceramic lining supplier who can take on the design and supply of the whole system as a package should also be able to provide a “unitary” warranty for the entire system.  Suppliers of this nature are available. 

This single source design/supply approach to PAL Vessel supply has been shown to be successful on three recent Australian projects in New South Wales, Queensland, and Western Australia.  This approach is becoming the strategy of choice for an increasing number of owners; mainly because there are significant reductions in risk to the project and demonstrable benefits for the ALL of the participants – owner, consultant and suppliers. 

The primary benefit for the plant owner for utilizing the outlined selection process is to achieve the most reliable and cost-effective PAL Vessel ceramic linings, so that the plant will operate reliably and reduce risks of production losses, reduced profits and lower return on investmen

t. 

The term Pressure Vessel Grade “PVG” ceramic brick has been initiated in the last couple of years to distinguish certain specialist ceramic brick materials that have proven performance in PAL vessels from “standard” acid brick that is typically used for corrosion applications such as floors, sulfuric acid plant towers, sumps, and atmospheric tanks.  “Standard” acid brick, which meets ASTM C-279 Type III, II or I specifications, when used in PAL Vessel lining applications, have had a history of limited performance, high maintenance, and in some cases severe degradation within only a few months of operation. 

Because an ASTM designation does not yet exist for “PVG” Pressure Vessel Grade ceramic brick, it is relatively difficult for owners and their engineering consultants to make material selection decisions.  In some cases, the decision on ceramic brick is based on material data sheet information and at times with limited performance data in similar service.  Due to the severity of the PAL service conditions, particularly in the nickel laterite industry, selection of materials based on limited information can be catastrophic to the operating reliability of the associated PAL vessels. 

It also been known for suppliers of “standard” ceramic brick to make claims that their current or “new” brick will provide long-term (several years) performance in PAL service without fully understanding the suitability of the material in the total lining design for that particular application. 

Due to lower manufacturing costs, typically “standard” acid brick can be substantially cheaper than “PVG” specialty brick.  The lower initial cost option can be somewhat deceiving to the consultant and owner who has to make a significant capital investment into the new plant and is therefore “cost-sensitive”.

###### **2. IMPORTANCE OF A PROPER SELECTION PROCESS USED FOR DETERMINING A SUITABLE “PVG” PRESSURE VESSEL GRADE CERAMIC LINING SYSTEM FOR CRITICAL HPAL OR HPOX VESSELS** 

The most important factor in selecting a suitable lining system, proven to have the greatest chance for success, relies on past experience of the lining materials and the particular lining design in similar pressure leach applications.  This experience or knowledge base can be referred to as “empirical knowledge.” 

A ceramic lining system, which has already been implemented in the severe service conditions common to PAL applications and has been monitored for several years, provides excellent information for future lining designs.  Most importantly, review of the past history of similar applications, caters for the opportunity that the lining system has had to perform in service, to provide real operating data and a track record for the lining system.  This concept would apply to most mechanical components associated within the PAL circuit. 

How the lining reacts to the service conditions found in a pressure vessel during operation and after seve

ral extended shutdowns (at least two to three years of service history is critical for a suitable performance assessment) is the true indicator of the linings potential long-term performance in another similar application. 

A pure engineering approach, which could be termed “computer modeling”, to ceramic lining design for pressure vessels, without empirical knowledge from other similar applications, has inherent technical risks.  Many variables are found in mining industry processes, likely due to the variables that changes in the ore or concentrate bring, that aretypically not the case for other major industry processes (i.e. Chemical, Pulp & Paper, Pharmaceutical, etc.).  It is easy for this important process variable situation to be overlooked, if the lining designer is not familiar with the potential problems that can occur. 

More importantly, if only material science information (material chemistry, physical properties, corrosion and erosion resistance information, etc. of the lining components) is utilized for “computer modeling” of a lining design, there is a strong possibility that the “dynamics” of a lining design such as the **_changes in material properties of the lining components when exposed to various operating and upset conditions_** could result in serious design deficiencies. 

###### **3. UTILIZING THE CONCEPT OF “PROVEN PERFORMANCE SELECTION” AS A MEANS OF LOWERING TECHNICAL AND COMMERCIAL RISK EXPOSURE FOR THE CONSULTANT AND OWNER** 

To assist the owner or associated consultant in selecting the lining system that will provide long-term, reliability, with low life cycle costs, it is critical that the performance history of the lining system in other similar applications is reviewed closely.  As mentioned, this ceramic lining knowledge base can be referred to as “empirical knowledge.” 

Following this very important procedure can substantially reduce technical and commercial risk associated with designing and constructing a PAL plant.  A suggested name for this review process for the selection of the optimal ceramic lining system for any given application can be termed “Proven Performance Selection.” Proven Performance Selection in combination with computer-aided design will typically result in the best lining design. 

Proven Performance Selection as a minimum involves the following:

- Site Visits to Operating PAL Plants to Gather Lining Performance Information for Comparison Purposes of Various Lining Systems. 

This should include the gathering of information such as destructive testing, chronological photo documentation, field service representatives written lining observation reports, downtime records, lining maintenance costs, etc. 

- Material Selection Review 

This includes not only known physical properties of available lining materials but also the properties or tested materials obtained during destructive testing. 

- Lining Design Results Review 

Includes comparing

the final lining design to previous designs currently in use along with their respective lining performance history. 

- Lining and Steel Vessel Compatibility Review 

Includes the review of how steel design incompatibility in other operations has affected lining performance; this information can be used to avoid similar problems.  This process would typically include such key elements as steel shell out-of-roundness, nozzle sizing and design, nozzle flange seal design, etc. 

- Nozzle Sizing and Nozzle Lining Review 

Includes the review of proven lining designs with those being considered. 

###### **4. EXAMPLES OF RELIABLE CERAMIC LININGS IN HPAL AND HPOX SERVICE PROOF OF SUCCESSFUL LINING SELECTION PROCESS** 

The following are a few select case histories of HPAL, PAL and HPOX applications that have successfully utilized “PVG” ceramic lined Pressure Vessels for at least three years (and in one case for over 40 years). 

- Nickel Laterite HPAL – HP and LP Flash Vessels – Two Plant Locations – New Lining Installations 

Both Projects involved PVG brick lined flash vessels – a total of six vessels.  All of these brick lined vessels have performed well for there duration of operation.  One of the projects that has two flash vessels (an HP and a LP) has operated for well over 3 years with minimal maintenance – typically minor joint re-pointing in the bottom head due to erosion from the process.  The importance of having an impingement block in the bottom head of the HP flash vessel was proven during the first week of operation in one of the cases.  All six flash vessels are proof that a PVG type brick lining (SEMCO brick to be specific) offers reliable corrosion and erosion protection of the steel shell in this type of severe service application.  The owners’ have confirmed that the lining systems are proving to be costeffective due to their long-term and reliable performance.

The lining damage consisted of spalled (delaminated) sections of the brick lining, mainly in the vapor zone of the autoclaves.  The autoclaves required continual lining maintenance to keep in proper working condition, which resulted in costly downtime and severe production losses for the owner. ognising the existence of a distinct nickel sulphide sub-sector, and of investing judiciously within that sub-sector, are considerable: 

Leverage with diversification – the sub-sector comprises small companies entirely focused on nickel.  Hence their share prices may be expected to be volatile and much more strongly leveraged to the nickel price than larger producers in general, and large diversified producers in particular.  Moreover the general risks of investing in small cap companies may be mitigated through spreading an investment through the sub-sector, so that a single large investment in the sub-sector, offering strong leverage to the nickel price, would also carry the benefits of diversification, with the risk spread among several companies, deposits and managements. 

Viewing the sub-sector as a whole, the combined share market turn-over of the companies in question is just over $9 million per month.  This seems to imply that a large institutional investor could build a position of several million dollars in the sub-sector within a month without significantly altering the share prices of the target companies, and neatly getting around the relentless and value-denying focus on sheer size. 

Unrivalled exposure to exploration – Small producers are almost always explorers at heart. Small companies in general offer very good leverage to exploration success, in a way that big companies simply do not.  Thus investments in this sub-sector offer not only the exploration focus of each of the companies, but the certainty that exploration success in any particular company will be strongly reflected in the share price of that company.  An important point is that being producers, these companies have the cashflows to consistently pursue exploration without ongoing recourse to shareholders for exploration funding. 

Financial robustness – being low cost and profitable producers, these companies offer value purely by virtue of their profit stream.  Their transparent nature means that they can be easily evaluated on the basis of independently verified profits, with the exploration upside as a powerful sweetener.  Their low costs and small size also mean that their fixed cost component (corporate overheads etc) is likely to be small, giving them a buffer against low nickel prices. 

Finally, to the companies themselves, I believe there is a real benefit to the recognition by the market of our sub-sector.  Though hard to define, it comes down to identification with a profitable and well-performing sector, getting around the financial markets obsession with size of market capitalisation, creation of a peer group for bench-marking, and leading ultimately to a reduction in the cost of capital.

###### **1. INTRODUCTION** 

The Browns polymetallic project is located some 80 kilometres south of the deep water port of Darwin in the Northern Territory.  Its location is idyllic for a mining and processing operation in Australia, being 7 kilometres north of the township of Batchelor and serviced by bitumen road from Darwin.  A 132 kV power line runs nearby as does a gas pipeline and the Adelaide to Darwin railway which is under construction runs right past the project. 

Insitu resources in the immediate Browns area contain 82 million tonnes of mineralisation, grading 2.3% lead, 0.12% cobalt, 0.76% copper and 0.11% nickel<sup>1</sup> along with silver credits.  The deposit has not been closed off by drilling. The project has been described at previous ALTA conferences (<sup>2</sup> 1998,<sup>3</sup> 1999). 

Under a Commonwealth Government R & D Start Grant to develop and prototype an innovative process circuit, a bulk sample was mined from the sulphide portion of the orebody some 25 metres below surface and 10 metres below the depth of oxidation.  A 400 tonne sample of this material was processed through a prototype bulk flotation plant at AMDEL in Adelaide and the resulting concentrates used to develop a lead fuming process with greater than 95% cobalt recovery to matte. 

The concept is to fume the lead away from the copper, cobalt and nickel early in the circuit extracting these metals into a high grade matte for their recovery by hydrometallurgy with the return of the residue to the lead fuming furnace as a flux.  The resultant matte is leached and the copper recovered by SX/EW and after purification the cobalt and nickel are recovered separately into premium products. 

The most robust economics are achieved at a throughput of around 2 million tonnes per annum.  This results in a total project capital in excess of $A500 million.  With the globalisation of the world minerals industry and the takeover of virtually all the medium sized Australian mining companies by larger groups, funding such

a project by an emerging Australian mining company is obviously difficult without a major joint venture partner.  A half million-dollar project is, generally speaking, too small to interest a major mining group to enter into such a joint venture. 

Value engineering has been undertaken in order to reduce the capital investment to below $A200 million.  This figure is believed to be financable by Compass Resources in association with other strategic partners/co-venturers.  The focus is now on the start up of a smaller incremental project.  Compass Resources has two cornerstone investors being the Doe Run Company of the US and the Australian technology company, Ausmelt Limited.  In association with these companies the scaled down incremental project is now being reviewed.  The alternatives are to scale down the pyrometallurgical process or to adopt the first commercial application of Engitec's Flubor lead leach process.  In each case, lead will be recovered from a bulk sulphide flotation concentrate leaving the copper, cobalt, nickel and silver in either a matte or a flubor residue.  These metals will then be recovered hydrometallurgically. 

In the final technology validation as part of the ongoing Definitive Feasibility Study, these two alternatives will be benchmarked against one another and various other potential circuit configurations including chloride leaching and low-pressure acid leaching. 

The DFS scope will be refined pending the technology validation in April 2002.

###### **2. HISTORY** 

The Browns Project forms part of a large mineralised belt analogous to the Central African Copper Belt.  Following some small copper production, the area is most noted for its uranium production from the Rum Jungle Mines.  Although the area was extensively explored for uranium in the 1950s, relatively little modern day base metals exploration has taken place apart from the work undertaken by Compass. 

The area is rich in carbonaceous black shale hosted polymetallics with the major mineralisation being in contact with dolomites and high grade magnesites.  Of these, drilling at Browns, Area 55 and Browns East makes them the most well defined of the many target zones in this new mining district. 

###### **3.  LOCATION AND TENEMENT STATUS** 

Compass' exploration and mining tenements cover approximately 370 square kilometres to the north and east of the township of Batchelor.  The majority of the prospective land in the area is covered by the Company's Exploration Licences and Exploration Retention Licences. 

Application for Mining Leases for ancillary purposes for the Browns operation has been made over a footprint large enough for all mining operations including the stockpiling of overburden from open pit operations. 

The comprehensive regional geology position held by Compass provides potential for similar scale deposits as Browns and Area 55 to be located as additional feed to the Browns plant or to s

Negotiations are being arranged to secure a major partner for a regional exploration joint venture, which would be conducted without impacting on development timetables at Browns. 

###### **4.  GEOLOGY** 

The Browns and Browns East deposit form a major strata bound polymetallic deposit, hosted by Proterozoic graphitic shales, dolomitic sediments and dolomite.  The minerals were deposited in a marine basin with gradually increasing water depth, in a sub-horizontal sheet.  A clear zonation pattern exists within the mineralised zone from the eastern edge of the system where a shallower water more oxygenated environment existed through to deposition under progressively deeper waters proximate to the shoreline.   Uranium was deposited and this zones into copper, then lead, then zinc as more reducing conditions were experienced under deeper water. 

Cobalt is pervasive through portions of the copper and lead zones.  Following deposition and lithification, tectonic activity folded the mineral rich formations into a tight western plunging synclinal structure. A strong slatey cleavage sub parallel with the synclinal axis further deforms the mineralisation. 

Approximately 3 kilometres to the southwest of Browns in the same host rocks is the Area 55 deposit.  This deposit is dominated by copper, cobalt and nickel although some lead silver mineralisation is also present. 

Total resources for the Browns, Browns East and Area 55 deposits are quoted in the 2001 Annual Report as 81.8 million tonnes<sup>(1)</sup> -

###### **5.   RESERVES AND SCHEDULES** 

Reserves and mining schedules have been sequentially developed by utilising the resources developed by Snowdens using Datamine software.  These resources are fed into the Whittle 4X programme along with economic inputs developed for each processing option.  These have been further entered into a mine-scheduling programme Medsystem. 

The ore variability provides an opportunity for a wide variety of mining and processing scenarios.  Initial prefeasibility work suggested a large annual throughput to maximise both annual revenue, net present value and IRR.  The resultant capital cost for such a project is in excess of $A500 million. 

With the globalisation of the mining industry, the number of major mining companies has diminished and the size of project they require to warrant their participation in a joint venture has increased dramat

ically.  The pragmatic realisation is that without the support of a major mining house as a project sponsor it would be almost impossible to secure funding for a $A500 million project. 

Compass thus undertook a series of scaling studies looking at both lower annual throughputs, open cut and underground mining options and technologies which enabled an incremental project to start at a smaller scale and increase by adding processing modules as time progressed. 

The variability of the orebody both along strike and across strike lends itself to relatively simple selective mining of various ores at low tonnages.  This opens the opportunity for a relatively low capital cost smaller start up project expanding once a profitable operation is established through the addition of modules to double or triple production. 

The gas handling facilities associated with the fuming of lead in the Ausmelt process provide a practical bottom size limit to the use of lead fuming technology.  Below about 1 million tonne per annum throughput it is thus necessary to replace the pyrometallurgy technology with a hydrometallurgical technology.  The selective mining of various ore types initially by smaller tonnage open pit mining can be further augmented by the use of selective underground mining for specific ore types.
