###### **6.   MINERALOGY** 

The bulk of the Browns deposit is a sulphide deposit with an oxide surface outcrop and oxides/carbonates in the top 15 to 20 metres.  Oxide ore is primarily a mixture of malachite and cerussite with minor pyromorphite along with remnants of pyrite in a matrix of muscovite and quartz with smaller amounts of kaolinite, graphite, goethite and biotite.  The sulphide ore mineralogy is hosted in a fine grained graphitic schist with chloritic slates and associated schists.  The main sulphide association occurs with the graphitic material although some discrete coarse recrystaline sulphide assemblage is present.  There are two main sulphide lithologies. The stratigraphically lower lithology consists of a cupriferous black shale with the main copper minerals being chalcopyrite with lesser covelite bornite and digenite. Cobalt and nickel are present in this zone as the mineral siegenite.  This is concentrated in the upper hanging wall section of the copper rich zone.  The dark colouration is due to the presence of carbon at around 6-8%. 

The other main ore lithology is a grey shale. Galena is the dominant mineral in this lithology with cobalt and nickel again present as siegenite, mainly in the lower or footwall section of the lead zone. 

The deposit is a relatively low sulphide system with iron present as pyrite particularly in the principal copper zone.  The major gangue minerals are potash feldspar, mica (in the form of sericite and an iron rich muscovite), quartz and carbon. 

The ore grade is highest in the central portion of the deposit. Ore minerals show a marked zonation.  At the eas

tern end of the deposit and in the footwall copper mineralisation dominates. This gradually weakens as lead mineralisation becomes predominant towards the western end of the deposit.  The zones overlap in the central portion of the deposit with copper dominantly directly overlain by lead mineralisation. Cobalt tends to be pervasive both in the copper and through into the lead zone, although it weakens in the western 200 metres of the lead zone as zinc increases. 

###### **7. METALLURGY** 

The bulk of the value in the Browns deposit lies with cobalt, whereas the bulk of the mass of contained metals lies with lead. 

The metallurgical processes are thus designed to recover the bulk of the mass i.e. the lead at the earliest opportunity, concentrating the copper cobalt and nickel into as small mass as possible for more intensive treatment. 

Alternative metallurgical process routes have been considered and have been reported previously (ALTA 1998<sup>2</sup> ,  ALTA 1999<sup>3</sup> ). 

###### **FLOTATION** 

Bulk sulphide flotation has been adopted to maximise the recovery of all the sulphide minerals into a low mass concentrate.  The fine grained nature of the mineralisation led to early work incorporating fine and even ultra fine grinds.  After ultra fine grinding, oil agglomeration flotation was tested to maximise the recovery of the finely liberated sulphide particles.  This was phototyped, but subsequent circuit developments gave better results using a conventional flotation circuit. 

During these operations a build up of lead in the grinding circuit was noted to a grade of almost three times the feed grade.  Flash flotation was trialed on the cyclone underflow and was not successful.  Gravity separation of this material was trialed with encouraging

results.  Subsequently flash flotation on the whole of the SAG mill discharge at a grind P80 of 250 microns gave extremely good results. 

Most of the early bulk flotation work was conducted on composites of all the ore types typical of the first five years of mining operations.  Concentrate grades in the Amdel prototyping campaign assayed 28% lead, 6% copper, 1.2% cobalt, 1% nickel and 120 g/t silver.  The controlling gangue association in this concentrate was silica.  Silica is present in the ore as quartz, muscovite, and k-feldspars.  An evaluation of the effect of silica on the Ausmelt lead fuming and smelting indicated that the maximum silica in concentrate should be 15%.  This silica level then became the flotation control and, together with the presence of carbon floating, controlled the grade of the lead, cobalt, copper and nickel. 

With the advent of flash flotation at a coarse grain size (P80 of 250 microns) very clean galena concentrates assaying 60% lead were possible from the flash flotation.  Regrinding of the flash flotation tails and conventional flotation produced bulk concentrates of significantly higher grade, typically 35% lead w

ith less than 12% silica and reduced levels of carbon. 

Noting the different lithologies in the highly carbonaceous copper rich zones and the less carbonaceous lead rich ore zones, an assessment was made that these could be substantially individually mined.  Testwork on the flash flotation bulk sulphide flowsheet was thus tested on both the copper rich lithology and the lead rich lithology.  This work resulted in much higher concentration ratios of the lead rich lithology with typical concentrate grades of 60% lead,  0.2% copper,  7% silica.  Parallel flotation tests on the copper zone resulted in concentrates grading 18% lead, 18% copper, 6% silica and 5% carbon.   In combination this will give 51% lead **,** 7% copper, 8% silica and 5% carbon. With the opportunity of utilising a hydrometallurgical process for the recovery of lead at a very small annual throughput work concentrated on producing a low lead copper concentrate which could be by-passed around the lead hydrometallurgical circuit.  This results in a flowsheet comprising parallel lead rich lithology ore and copper rich lithology ores going to separate SAG milling circuits and flash flotation.  The copper lithology flash flotation concentrate assays around 20% copper and contains only 3% of the total lead. This can by-pass the lead recovery circuit. 

The lead flash flotation concentrate is then be combined with the remainder of the concentrate produced after combining the copper flash flotation tailings and the lead flash flotation tailings into a common conventional flotation circuit.  This not only has the effect of by-passing copper and some of the cobalt and nickel around the lead recovery circuit but also increases flotation recoveries and reduces the amount of silica in the concentrates.

###### **LEAD EXTRACTION CIRCUIT** 

As previously reported, the fuming of lead from an Ausmelt furnace with the recovery of copper cobalt and nickel into the copper matt has been the preferred metallurgical option. This circuit has been extensively prototyped and proven.  The Ausmelt furnace recovers in excess of 98% of the lead directly to a lead sulphate fume which is then reduced to lead in a second Ausmelt furnace. 

Copper cobalt and nickel are collected into the matte with recovery of cobalt in excess of 95% being achieved by controlling the iron content of the matte and minimising the volume of slag made. 

The matte may then be leached in a conventional medium pressure autoclave with copper recovered by SX/EW to produce cathode copper.  After purification, the cobalt and nickel

The approach being taken is to advance an incremental project starting at a much smaller annual throughput and increasing the plant size by addition of modules at appropriate times.  This incremental approach enables a range of opportunities including the separate mining of the copper rich lithology and the lead rich lithology from the ore.  In this manner a viable project producing of the order of 30,000 tonnes per annum of lead is achievable in the early years, with the ability to scale this up in later years.  There is a limit below which the gas handling facilities required for the Ausmelt lead fuming becomes uneconomic. 

This in turn has dictated that Compass re-evaluate hydrometallurgical options for the recovery of lead.  With both Ausmelt and the Doe Run Company being 5% cornerstone investors in Compass Resources, our preference remains to use the Ausmelt technology as the primary lead recovery circuit.  However below its economic limit hydrometallurgical processes for the recovery of lead become necessary.  Doe Run have four years experience piloting the Engitec Flubor process whereby lead sulphide concentrate is dissolved in fluoboric  acid (HBF4).  The galena is dissolved preferentially to the other sulphide minerals and, after solid liquid separation, the lead is plated as sheets of lead cathode in an electrowinning cell.  Developments of the electrowinning technology produce a solid lead sheet cathode of 99.99% Pb purity which is then melted to produce refined lead. 

Elemental sulphur is recovered from the lead residue using an ammonium sulphide leach, and silver may be recovered using a cyanide leach.  The remaining copper, nickel and cobalt sulphides are then leached in a pressure acid leach at around 210°C.  The backend circuit for the recovery of copper cobalt and nickel is identical to the matte leach circuit described in the Ausmelt case.  Alternative leaching technologies using a combined atmospheric and pressure acid leach are also under evaluation.  The cobalt and nickel purification circuit may also be avoided by the use of iron exchange resins selective for iron, copper, cobalt and nickel.  This work is at an advanced stage of testing.

###### **ABSTRACT** 

Titan Resources NL, through its 100% owned subsidiary, Pacific Ore Technology Ltd, has made advances in the field of bacterial leaching using a thermophilic culture such that the bacterial treatment of primary sulphide minerals in a heap leach is now a practical reality. Results presented from laboratory testwork demonstrate rapid leaching kinetics on flotation concentrates without the need for ultra-fine grinding or other pre-treatment options. In addition to excellent reaction kinetics on concentrates the bacteria show equally impressive leaching rates on whole ores.  The results of the laboratory and pilot scale investigations, culminating in a 5,000 tonne BioHeap<sup>TM</sup> trial, are presented and discussed in this paper. 

###### **1. INTRODUCTION** 

For centuries bacteria have been used, be it intentionally or not, to leach base metals from their ores.  Ores containing minerals such as covellite and chalcocite have been found to be amenable to both heap leaching and dump leaching. The economic recovery of metals such as nickel and copper by heap leaching of primary sulphide ores, containing minerals

such as pentlandite and chalcopyrite, has not proven so easy however, and a lot of research has been undertaken to this end. Primary base metal sulphide ores are usually treated by froth flotation, with recovery from the sulphide concentrate by smelting, or roasting followed by acid leaching, and refining to produce finished metal. With everincreasing environmental awareness however, smelters are now, either voluntarily or through legislation, reducing the levels of sulphur dioxide gas emitted into the environment.  Additionally, sulphide ores normally contain trace levels of mercury, tellurium, selenium and arsenic. These impurities have been traditionally emitted into the atmosphere or alternatively, have entered the process gases used to make sulphuric acid. Processes have now been developed to cope with these hazards, eg. electrostatic precipitators and wet scrubbers, although these add significantly to the capital and operating costs of the smelters. 

Over recent years much research has been aimed at developing hydrometallurgical alternatives to the established pyrometallurgical processes. These include various autoclave based technologies such as the CESL process, the Activox process and the Mt Gordon process. Also falling into this category would be ammonia based leaching as typified by the Sherrit process. Non autoclave process include the Intec process in which the active leaching agent is a chloride-bromide complex, and various other leach alternatives have been investigated based on strong chloride or sulphate/chloride mixtures. Generally speaking however, the non-bacterial processes that are available, or have been put forward for the treatment of primary base metal sulphide concentrates or ores, are comparatively high-tech and involve the use of highly aggressive leaching conditions and/or chemicals. 

In general terms, there are four methods for bacterial leaching that might be considered for the recovery of base metals from primary sulphide minerals.  These are heap leaching, vat leaching, dump leaching and tank leaching. Although heap leaching is by far the most commonly utilised bacterial process for recovering copper from the more easily oxidised secondary copper minerals such as covellite and chalcocite, this approach has not been taken with the primary base metal sulphides such as pentlandite, chalcopyrite and sphalerite. This is presumably because of slow oxidation kinetics and/or poor extractions. This is certainly the case for chalcopyrite where it is commonly believed that due to a build up of insoluble reaction products at the surface of the mineral, the reaction rate is retarded, leading to the eventual passivation of the mineral. The mechanism by which the chalcopyrite is leached however, is widely held to be indirect with respect to the bacteria,

with the mineral coming under chemical attack from ferric ions that have been generated by iron oxidising bacteria. This explain

s why current developments in the bacterial leaching of primary sulphides, are centred around fine grinding of the leach feed, and developing bacteria that will operate at high temperatures. The aim is to make the ferric leach reaction go faster and further. Tank leaching is therefore the only alternative that will accommodate the ultra-fine grinding and high temperatures that have been perceived to be necessary. To this end, for example, the Billiton group, in conjunction with Codelco have developed the BioCop<sup>TM</sup> process which is being trialed at the Chuquicamata mine in Chile, and similarly, BacTech have developed a tank leach process which is being trialed at the Penolas mine in Mexico. 

Titan Resources, through Pacific Ore Technology, on the other hand, has developed a direct bio-leach process in which chemical attack by ferric does not play a significant role. As a result, the leach does not require extreme temperatures, nor does it require fine grinding.  As such the process is just as applicable to heap leaching as it is to tanks or any of the above alternatives. 

This paper describes the application of this process to the heap leaching of the Mt Sholl Cu/Ni orebody in the Pilbara region of Western Australia. 

###### **2. LABORATORY TESTWORK** 

###### **2.1 SAMPLE CHARACTERISATION** 

The Mt Sholl orebody is located about 25 km south of the town of Karratha, in the Pilbara region of Western Australia. The sulphide mineralisation is for the most part, quite finely disseminated within the host rock and sits at the base of a mafic-ultramafic layered intrusion. The laboratory scale testing was performed on a bulk sample of about 250kg of ore that was obtained from two HQ diamond drill cores. Mineralogical examination of this material showed the host rock to consist predominantly of clinopyroxene and calcic amphibole, with lesser sodium feldspar. Titanite, ilmenite, iron oxides, chloride, calcite and apatite were also present in minor amounts. Sulphide minerals comprised approximately 15% by volume of the total sample. These were predominantly pyrrhotite (40%), chalcopyrite (35%), and pentlandite (25%), with trace amounts of pyrite. The pentlandite mineralisation tends to be coarser than the chalcopyrite with typical grain sizes from 30um up to 1 or 2 mm in diameter. Coarse chalcopyrite is also present but the mineralisation overall tends to be finer, with some 60% to 70% of it being sub 100um and with over 50% of it being locked up in the un-reactive silicates, particularly the calcic amphibole.

. In order to affect a separation between Fe and the Cu and Ni in solution, it is common practice to reject the Fe by precipitation with limestone or a similar low cost neutralising agent. Bacterial oxidation using _Thiobacillus ferrooxidans_ (TF) was considered capable of providing a low cost method for achieving this and a biological contactor in the form of a separate, inert heap was envisaged. The ORP was checked on a regular basis and additional ferrous sulphate was added to the solution when it reached 600mV (Ag/AgCl) or more. In this way the rate of ferrous oxidation could be estimated. ###### **2. GEOLOGY, MINERALOGY, RESERVES AND MINING** 

The ICP deposits are situated within the Idaho Cobalt Belt, a mineral district characterized by stratiform occurrences of cobalt, copper, and gold. All of the important mineral deposits in the district occur within the Proterozoic age Yellowjacket Formation, which is composed of numerous sequences of moderately to strongly metamorphosed clastic sediments, with lesser volcanic and carbonate components. Numerous exploration targets have also been identified on the property. The Sunshine, East Sunshine, and Ram deposits occur associated with biotite-rich interbeds of volcanic origin within a series of coarsening-upward sequences of argillite, siltite, and quartzite of the middle unit of the Yellowjacket Formation. The mineralization has been characterized by Formation as syngenetic, stratiform, exhalative deposits. Mineralized zones typically occur as multiple stacked sulfide-rich beds (or horizons) and individual horizons, ranging from several inches to several feet in thickness, which are intimately associated with the biotite-rich tuffaceous exhalative interbeds.

###### **4. KEY HYDROMETALLURGICAL BULK CONCENTRATE TREATMENT TECHNOLOGIES** 

The cobaltite and chalcopyrite concentrates from the bulk flotation plant will be shipped and treated in an existing industrial hydrometallurgical nitrogen species catalyzed pressure (NSC) leach plant. The recovery of copper from chalcopyrite will rely on the use of nitrogen species catalyzed pressure leaching technology followed by conventional SX/EW. The recovery of cobalt from cobaltite will largely rely on the use of nitrogen species catalyzed pressure leaching technology and PSI Systems ion exchange technology. Gold may be recovered via alkaline sulfide lixiviation and recovery. A description of each innovative and proven technology is as follows. 

The NSC pressure oxidation system offers several definitive and industrially proven advantages. First of all it is the only proven industrial process over the long term for pressure leaching of precious metal bearing sulfides. Indeed the plant to be utilized by Formation Capital Corporation was the first and longest running copper concentrate leaching SX/EW industrial plant in the world.<sup>(2,3,4)</sup> Second, the rate of reaction is much faster and subsequent required reactor volume is thus smaller. Third, the process does not require excessively high temperatures or pressures. Fourth, the ORP is extremely high so it oxidizes almost any sulfide at low oxygen overpressures. Fifth, the materials of construction are readily available stainless steels so there is no need for titanium cladding or brick with lead liners. Thus, the capital and maintenance costs are less. Also, because of the simpler internal design, direct heat exchange can be utilized in-situ for optimal temperature control. Further, in a manner analogous to existing Ni/Co laterite HPAL systems, the energy from the in-situ heat exchange can be readily utilized for optimizing the plant heat balance or co-generating electrical power resulting in significant process operating cost savings. Sixth, there is no need for a dip tube or special design radial agitators with cowlings and the like. Oxygen transfer is innate with the enhanced nitrogen species chemistry. So

, with no titanium, and no titanium dip tube in particular, there is much less oxygen fire danger. Seventh, the design of the feed pump system is far less of a challenge as is the flash system and the choke system. Eighth, like a smelter, precious metals recovery can be high and direct. Ninth, there are no sophisticated chloride

Finally, there is both a minor amount of nitrogen species utilized and any sulfur produced is effectively utilized as both a gold lixiviant, and ultimately as a value added by-product so there are no major economic or environmental issues. 

The leach reaction mechanism is the heart of the leach process and has been recently characterized in detail and verified by independent research<sup>(5,6,7)</sup> . This work led to a patented change in the leach chemistry and significant improvements in recoveries. The elegant aspect of the leach chemistry is its use of low levels of nitrogen oxides, which are continuously regenerated within the reaction vessel.  The presence of the nitrogen species allows for a much higher redox potential than could be achieved with mild oxygen pressures. 

The original process utilized nitric acid as the catalyst at levels of only 2 grams per liter. The present chemistry, described by on site research efforts, now uses sodium nitrite at similar concentrations to bring about improved recoveries.  Broadly speaking, the chemistry is similar; but a close look at the nitrogen chemistry and the reaction mechanism will reveal the benefits attributed to the use of the nitrite ion over the nitrate ion.  Only a small amount of nitrogen species is required to drive the reaction. Silica gel materials have a long standing history of use as separation materials. These materials are traditionally used in chromatographic applications under mild conditions. Silica gel based materials have been avoided for use in large scale industrial separations of metals due to their inability to withstand the harsh conditions associated with these separations. The synthetic process developed by Purity Systems Inc. has led to the development of a silica gel based material that has overcome these problems. PEI has been tested through 3000 extraction cycles with less than 10% loss in capacity and PVA has been tested through 1500 cycles with negligible to no loss in capacity. Each cycle subjected the materials to loading with copper, elution of the copper with 4N sulfuric acid, and regeneration of the material with 4N ammonium hydroxide all at a flow rate of 10 column volumes per minute (cv/min). The capacity was checked periodically at a flow rate of 2 cv/min. To complement the long material lifetimes PEI and PVA hold the following characteristics as well, high capacities for many heavy metal ions, selectivity for heavy metal ions with no interference from alkali or alkaline earth metals, the ability to extract these metal ions at high flow rates to very low levels, and the ability to release these captured metals in highly concentrated solutions. PEI has copper (II) capacities of 0.93 mmol/g in batch tests and 0.84 mmol/g at flows of 2 cv/min. At flows of 2 cv/min PVA has a copper (II) capacity of ~1 mmol/g; it has not yet been evaluated under batch conditions. PEI modified with an ethyl sulfide group has reduced lead concentrations from 150 ppb to less than 2 ppb at flow rates of 40 cv/min. Strip solution fractions containing 32,000 ppm copper have been isolated from a 5 cm3 column of PEI. Large volumes (100 ml) of a

highly concentrated iron (II) strip solution (40,000 ppm) were collected as well by reusing the same strip solution repeatedly to strip the column after successive loadings. PEI and PVA have both been tested under a variety of real and simulated industrial and mine wastewater conditions extracting heavy metal ions from low pH solutions, solutions containing competing chelating ligands such as EDTA, and high temperature (96°-100° C) solutions.  In all cases these materials have suffered no adverse effects in performance. 

Silica-polyamine composite materials offer many advantages as a scaffolding from which to build many selective metal ion removal materials.  The structure of these materials is such that, if one were to look at a cross section of a single particle one would see the silica gel in the center surrounded by a polymer coating.  The large surface pores on the silica gel surface which increase the surface area of the silica gel particle also act as pockets which fill with polymer crating regions of high polymer density. The polymer itself offers many advantages in these types of applications: 1) The polyamines are water soluble, which makes the particle surface more hydrophilic than the surface of resin based materials.  2) The polymers contain the metal binding agents (chelating agents) as an integral part of their structure.  3) These chelating agents also offer sites for facile addition of ligands, molecules that can fine-tune the metal selectivity of the material. 

**Water Solubility** The water solubility of the polymer is important in two respects.  From an environmental standpoint it negates the use of highly toxic organic solvents in reactions involving the polymer.  Addition of the polymer to the treated silica gel and many of the ligand addition reactions carried out to date have been done in water, methyl alcohol or a mixture of the two.  Another critical environmental factor is that these materials can be used to extract the metal atoms, ions and complexes directly from aqueous media without first extracting them out into a highly toxic often flammable organic phase first. 

The performance of the material is also enhanced due to water-soluble nature of the polymer.  When the material is in an aqueous environment the polymer is able to float out into the aqueous solution.  The polymer reaches out from the silica gel particles to fill the void spaces between the particles thus as the contaminated water flows through a column it is forced through the polymer.  This allows more contact between the contaminating metal ions and the chelating elements of the polymer and hence more efficient extraction

**Integrated Chelating Agents** The polyamines used to synthesize PEI and PVA contain approximately 35% by weight amine nitrogens.<sup>1</sup> These nitrogens are incorporated into the polymer through chemically robust carbon - nitrogen bonds which have the abili

ty to withstand the conditions likely encountered during metal extraction processes.  The sheer density of the nitrogen atoms coupled with the conformational freedom afforded through their incorporation into a water soluble polymer makes this arrangement particularly effective at removing contaminant metals from aqueous solutions. 

**Ease of ligand addition** The unshared pair of electrons on the nitrogen offers another advantage besides its ability to form coordinate covalent bonds with metal atoms and ions. These electrons also allow facile nucleophilic substitution reactions to occur at 1° and 2° amine sites.  These amines react readily with aliphatic halogen containing molecules, as well as other electrophilic molecular substituents, to form chemically robust carbon - nitrogen bonds.  This is important for three reasons 1) the physical stability of the material is entirely dependent on the nature of the chemical bonds holding the material together, 2) many molecules which could be of interest as modifying ligands are already available commercially containing electrophilic aliphatic substituents, and 3) the relative ease with which most of these reactions takes place means that addition of the ligands to the polymer can usually be accomplished in one step and under mild reaction conditions.

For instance resin beads may perform well in an open bed application use in a column system is limited due to their fluctuating volumes.  Copper selective resin materials can lose up to 24% of their volume when converted from the protonated acid form to the deprotonated base form. They must also withstand the conditions associated with stripping and regenerating the material.  The polyamine - silica composites have been subjected to concentrated h

###### **6. SUMMARY** 

The Formation Capital Corporation Idaho Cobalt Project (www.formcap.com) currently hosts a potential 3 million ton cobalt-copper-gold reserve/resource established on two zones, the Sunshine and Ram deposits, both of which have significant potential for expansion. The main cobalt ore mineral is cobaltite while the main copper ore mineral is chalcopyrite. The potential for the Idaho Cobalt Project to host deposits totaling 10 million tons grading +0.5% cobalt is considered high. With the signing of a definitive Refinery Option and Sale Agreement in August of 2001 for an existing industrial nitrogen species catalyzed (NSC) pressure leach hydrometallurgical facility located in Idaho, USA, Formation Capital Corporation is quickly developing into an integrated cobalt miner and chemical refinery, unique to North America. This paper outlined the mi

ning project and the mineral processing required for bulk concentrate production. As well, the key technologies and methodologies utilized in the hydrometallurgical treatment of the bulk cobaltite, chalcopyrite and gold bearing concentrate in the existing, industrial nitrogen species catalyzed (NSC) pressure leaching plant to produce cobalt metal, cobalt oxide, cobalt hydroxide, cobalt carbonate, copper sulfate, copper metal and gold were elucidated.

###### **3. ALTERNATIVE REFINING PROCESS SELECTION CRITERIA** 

Nickel refining offers the largest variety of processes of all metallurgical industries. In fact almost every refinery operates its own specific circuit rejecting sulphur in every possible valency state from –2 through 0, +4 to +6 as primary sulphur product. Obviously the primary products might be further converted to economically favourable compounds, usually sulphuric acid. 

A number of requirements were imposed on process selection. The alternative process should be: 

- (1) compatible with slow cooling and magnetic separation 

- (2) largely independent on reagent cost or/and sulphur by-products markets (3) similar to the existing process 

- (4) in commercial operation 

Considerable impact of the reagent/product price differential on the economy of refining has been indicated above. An ideal process should not require reagents for sulphur removal, or reagent cost should only be a fraction of disposal product price. A disposal product could be dumped preferentially, or markets being so large, that extra quantity generated at RBMR would be easily absorbed on the local or international markets. The requirement (2) unambiguously indicated sulphur removal in the form of sulphur dioxide, further converted to sulphuric acid, as economically the most favourable. Reagents, air

Furthermore, long term experience with operation of the current plant led to build-up of a considerable expertise in hydrometallurgical processing across the entire labour complement. In combination with the requirement (2) the selection of non-oxidising pressure leach for the nickel leach circuit has been natural choice.

FUNDAMENTALS OF THE NICKEL LEACH CIRCUIT** A modern version of a hydrometallurgical process for treatment of Ni/Cu mattes utilising non-oxidising pressure leach was developed by OUTUKUMPU during the 70’s [4], but since then it has undergone numerous modifications. ###### **5.1. NON-OXIDISING LEACH** 

At elevated temperatures (>140<sup>o</sup> C) and in the absence of oxygen, nickel sulphides readily react with cupric ions in solution forming copper subsulphides. The mechanism of nickel substitution by copper is likely to be very complex, but overall reactions can be written as follows: 



Although the process is usually called “non-oxidising” leach, it is evident from equations that cupric ions act as oxidant being reduced to cuprous ions and simultaneously converting some sulphide sulphur to sulphate anion. Metathesis is a more appropriate term. 

The reactivity of individual nickel sulphides varies significantly. The monosulphide (millerite) is the most reactive, while the kinetics of Ni3S2 (heazlewoodite) and Ni3S4 (polydymite) conversion is at least an order of magnitude slower. Thus in order to minimise pressure reactor volume the Ni/Cu matte must be pre-treated to convert most of Ni3S2 to NiS, and prevent formation of Ni3S4. This is carried out in an oxidising atmospheric leach. 

The reaction rate of metathesis accelerates with increasing copper concentration, and our own testwork indicated that at initial Cu concentration >50 g/l even Ni3S4 can be efficiently

Even metallic copper can post-precipitate from solution by disproportionation of cuprous ions on cooling (BINDURA experience). ###### **5.2. ATMOSPHERIC LEACH STAGES** 

The Ni/Cu matte is usually pre-treated in a double-stage counter-current atmospheric leach under oxygen sparging. The overall function of atmospheric stages can be defined as follows: 

- (1) generation of neutral nickel sulphate rich solution with a minimum content of copper and iron (<10 mg/l). 

- (2) total conversion of Ni3S2 to NiS (ideally) (3) complete dissolution of alloy phase, if present 

The first stage is utilised for solution purification, i.e. copper and iron removal, whilst the second stage ensures almost complete decomposition of Ni3S2 to NiS and dissolution of alloy phase. Solution from the second stage is recycled to the first stage. The chemistry of both stages is largely identical. 

Below pH 2.5-3 free acid is neutralised by reaction with alloy and Ni3S2:

###### **5.3. IRON REMOVAL** 

In circuits with oxidising pressure leach, the iron is usually rejected from solution in the last pressure leach stage in the form of jarosite or hematite by controlling the discharge acid concentration (cf. the existing RBMR process). This is no longer possible in circuits with the non-oxidising pressure leach and a dedicated iron removal stage must be incorporated into the nickel leach circuit. 

Pressure iron hydrolysis is generally preferred as it produces a relatively very clean iron cake (Ni+Cu+Co <3%). Since nickel spent electrolyte, which contains a significant sodium sulphate concentration (80-120 g/l), is used as a source of acid for the nickel leach, a jarosite type compound is precipitated preferentially: 

6 FeSO4  +  Na2SO4  +  9 H2O  +  1.5 O2   =   2 NaFe3(OH)6(SO4)2  +  3 H2SO4    (16) 

The iron removal can be carried out on non-oxidising leach solution directly (BINDURA, HARTLEY). However, at a high iron concentration, some iron will precipitate even during the non-oxidising leach. During roasting of copper sulphide residues with a high iron content (>3%), refractory copper ferrites might be formed, decreasing available copper extraction. DYNATEC thus incorporated an acid wash of the 2<sup>nd</sup> stage atmospheric leach

This treatment dissolves re-precipitated basic sulphates only, copper and nickel instantaneously, and slow iron dissolution might be accelerated by  addition  of  reducing  agents (sulphur dioxide). Solution from this stage is then subjected to pressure iron hydrolysis at 150<sup>o</sup> C. The required extent of iron removal in both schemes can be controlled, if necessary, by partial neutralisation of free acid in the feed solution. 

Iron precipitates are known to be an excellent collector for dissolved amphoteric impurities and PGM. This stage thus provides a very good control of these elements in the nickel leach circuit. Iron cake can be recycled to electric furnaces of the smelter. 

A separate iron removal does offer some advantages vs. removal with final base metals leach residue, particularly when final residue must be subjected to residual PGM recovery. Base metals residue is only a fraction of iron precipitate mass, eliminating a large stage, e.g. iron dissolution and associated solution disposal, from the residual PGM recovery process. ###### **5.4. CONTROL OF SULPHUR REJECTION** 

About 85% of sulphur entering the nickel leach circuit in non-magnetic Ni/Cu matte is rejected in the form of copper subsulphides  (Cu9S5 being the major species) at average Cu/S mass ratio of 3.7-3.8 : 1. In order to facilitate this rejection the copper and sulphur in the circuit must be matched at the same ratio, however, subtracting the mass of matte sulphur being oxidised through the process. 

The non-magnetic fraction of converter matte has an average composition of 43% Ni, 29% Cu and 24% S, i.e. with Cu/S ratio of 1.2. Additional copper enters the nickel leach circuit in magnetics leach solution giving overall Cu/S (S<sup>2-</sup> ) ratio of ~1.6, i.e. far out of the required value. There are two fundamental routes to correct this ratio: 

- (1) blow down the sulphur content of non-magnetic Ni/Cu matte 

- (2) add additional copper to the nickel leach circuit from external sources or internal recycles 

The extent of sulphur elimination or copper addition is strongly dependent on Ni/Cu ratio in converter matte. For an average converter matte ratio of 1.65 calculations indicate that non-magnetic Ni/Cu matte has to be blown down to ~12% S. Requirement for the additional copper in route 2 has been calculated at 1.2 times the copper content in the converter matte.

###### **7. NICKEL LEACH CIRCUIT FOR TREATMENT OF HIGH SULPHUR (24%) MATTE** 

The nickel leach circuit with a high sulphur (~19%) matte feed has been operated by the HARTLEY refinery in Zimbabwe (currently defunct). However, copper for the nickel leach circuit was generated in a fully oxidising leach of copper sulphide residue, thus defeating the purpose of the non-oxidising nickel leach. DYNATEC has carried out exploratory tests for other clients and has shown that such a process is feasible. The following process feasibility study is based on detailed analysis of theoretical mass balance flowsheets generated at RBMR. 

###### **7.1. METHODS OF COPPER ADDITION** 

Addition of copper from external sources has been rejected as being uneconomical. Copper can only be added in sulphur free materials (e.g. copper oxide or copper scrap) with limited supply in South Africa. External copper addition would more than double the size of copper tankhouse, which would be very capital intensive. 

Two options of internal copper recycle are feasible: 

- (1) recycle of calcine, preferably to the atmospheric leach 

- (2) partial leach of copper from copper subsulphide residue 

The recycle of calcine to the atmospheric leach appeared to be operationally advantageous since it provided a convenient neutralisation reagent for acid generated in non-oxidising leach and iron hydrolysis. However, RBMR testwork on calcine leach indicated that a significant proportion of the tellurium and arsenic is solubilised, selenium being largely rejected to flue gas in a roaster. Calcine recycle may thus lead to accumulation of these impurities in the nickel leach circuit with a high risk of impurity breakthrough to the nickel recovery circuit.

On the other hand a partial copper leach (~52% was indicated in mass balances) can be accomplished in atmospheric oxidising leach (residence time ~6-8 hours) or a low temperature (110-120<sup>o</sup> C) pressure oxidising leach (residence time ~1-2 hours) at a minimum sulphide to sulphate oxidation (<10%). Without attacking sulphide sulphur, dissolution of amphoterics should also be negligible. This scheme offered a further very significant advantage over calcine addition. In option (1) the size of the roaster would have to be double of that for low S matte. In option (2) not only would the size of the roaster stay the same, but due to a very high sulphur content of residue (~35%), the roasting would be autogenous; in fact, cooling would have to be provide

d. This is conveniently done by injection of water slurry of residue considerably simplifying the roaster feeding mechanism (FALCONBRIDGE operation). 

Thus further process analysis was carried out for option (2) only. 

###### **7.2. PROCESS PROBLEMATIC AREAS** 

An analysis of flowsheet mass balances indicated several very problematic areas: 

- (1) Mass of NiS entering the non-oxidising leach would be ~2.6 times the mass of NiS for low sulphur matte option 

- (2) The non-oxidising leach generates a very significant quantity of free acid equal to 2/3 mole of acid per each mole of NiS converted (cf. equation 2, chapter 5.1). Further acid is generated in the iron hydrolysis. 

- (3) In the absence of alloy, the capability of the atmospheric leach stages to neutralise this acid is severely diminished: 12% S matte should neutralise 560 kg acid/t matte, 24% S matte is limited to 110 kg acid/t matte. 

- (4) In spite of a high matte sulphur content, the nickel leach circuit is acid deficient, i.e. any internally generated acid, which has not been utilised for the nickel leach, has to be supplied from other sources (e.g. Ni anolyte). 

- (5) Acid concentration in solutions available for copper leach is relatively low (Ni anolyte ~50g/l, non-oxidising leach solution ~25g/l), thus generating a very large volume of copper leach solution required in the non-oxidising leach. 

In overall, these points translate into a huge operating volume of non-oxidising autoclaves: 

- (1) excess acid above the requirement for atmospheric leach stages is neutralised by caustic in the iron hydrolysis stage:  autoclave operating volume ~1500 m<sup>3</sup> 

- (2) excess acid is utilised in the copper leach and ALR acid wash:  autoclave operating volume ~1200 m<sup>3</sup> 

- (3) low sulphur matte leach:  autoclave operating volume ~400 m<sup>3</sup> 

all figures being related to 40 000 t Ni/annum production capacity. 

The above process analysis indicated that no capital cost saving would be realised in a high sulphur matte leach without a significant reduction of autoclave operating volume. 

###### **7.3. REDUCTION OF NON-OXIDISING LEACH AUTOCLAVE OPERATING VOLUME** 

Analysis of nickel concentration changes during the non-oxidising leach indicated that the nickel extraction rate roughly follows first order kinetics, i.e. extraction rate decays proportionally to logarithm of reaction time. In actual terms, about 2/3 of the atmospheric leach residue nickel is solubilised during the initial 2 hours of leach, whilst the extraction of remaining 1/3 of nickel will require additional 6 hours. One would expect such behaviour naturally: in initial phases of leach, the surface area of NiS particles exposed per unit of volume is the largest, and the copper concentration in solution, determining the diffusion rate, is the highest. With progressing leaching time, the value of both kinetic factors rapidly decrease, which results in fast decay of the nickel extraction rates. The e

THE COPPER RECOVERY PROCESS** ###### **8.1. SELECTION** Non-oxidising pressure leach of Ni/Cu mattes generates a very clean copper sulphide residue containing ~75% Cu, <1% Ni,Fe and ~20% S on average, and carrying ~80% of matte sulphur content. A number of commercial processes for treatment of copper sulphide materials operate in similar or identical applications. These processes can be

divided into 3 principal groups: 

- (1) pressure/atm. leach  - electrowinning 

- (2) converting – anode casting – electrorefinning 

- (3) roast – atm.leach – electrowinning 

In addition, a clean copper sulphide residue would be ideal material for toll refining or sale. This would eliminate sulphur directly and reduce capital cost of a new refinery associated with production of a relatively cheap metal. Although this option is still being considered, sufficient credits for contained PGM (3-4% reports to non-magnetic fraction) are the major stumbling block. 

Pressure leach of copper sulphide residue was practised by HARTLEY refinery in Zimbabwe (currently defunct). Unfortunately, in order to attain a high copper extraction, most of the contained sulphur is oxidised to sulphate, negating the original process selection requirement. 

On the other hand an atmospheric leach with elemental sulphur generation appeared to be very attractive. Laboratory tests at RBMR indicated ~80% sulphide to sulphur conversion at >95% copper extraction. However, no such process operates on commercial scale and this scheme was rejected for reasons indicated by process selection criteria. Nevertheless its later incorporation in future plant is still feasible. 

The copper electrorefining route has been practised by BINDURA refinery in Zimbabwe. The residue sulphur is eliminated as sulphur dioxide during conversion to blister copper. Although the operating cost of copper electrorefineries is generally very low, this is achieved by the scale of operation (commonly >100 000 t/a) and full tankhouse automation. For RBMR size of operation (~20 000 t Cu/a) the capital and operating costs were estimated to be the highest of all considered options.

The roast – leach – electrowinning route is employed by the FALCONBRIDGE refinery in Norway for treatment of a copper sulphide residue generated in chlorine leach of Ni/Cu matte [16]. The residue sulphur is almost totally eliminated as sulphur dioxide in roasting stage. The process appears to be very robust and easy to control. A moderate capital cost and a low operating cost led to the selection of this option for RBMR operation. 

During roasting, selenium is almost totally volatilised as SeO2 and reports to flue gas. The other amphoterics (Te,As,Sb) are oxidised but remain in residue. Amphoteric oxides are then dissolved in the leaching stage and have to be removed. The purification process has been developed and thoroughly tested at RBMR. The process is based on collection of amphoterics on freshly precipitated ferric hydroxide. Testwork indicated that amphoteric impurity concentration of < 1 mg/l can be attained from feed concentration as high as 10 mg/l Se, 50 mg/l Te and 20 mg/l As.

###### **10. CONCLUSIONS** 

The proposed new refining process with the non-oxidising leach as the key stage in nickel dissolution fulfils the major requirement of the planned refinery expansion, i.e. a significant reduction in sodium sulphate production estimated at 60-70% on the current process. The major proportion of the converter matte sulphur input is rejected as sulphur dioxide (7085%), which would be converted to sulphuric acid in the existing acid plant. Based on current prices of sodium sulphate and neutralisation reagents, a saving of R ~50 mil/annum is projected. This is achieved using overall process technology very similar to the current process, in fact, more than 50% of the existing refinery can be directly reemployed in the new operation. Newly adopted technologies (e.g. Ausmelt converter, fluidised bed roaster) have been in commercial operation for many years. 

In addition, the new process offers a number of outstanding features, which are summarised in the following points: 

- (1) Base metals solution from magnetics leach can be incorporated into the new flowsheet directly without affecting base metals refining process efficiencies. 

- (2) De-coupling of nickel and copper circuits allows to sell or toll refine the entire copper input in the form of a clean copper sulphide residue (<1% Ni,Fe). Credits for PGM content are decisive. 

- (3) It allows production of a significant quantity (up to 50% of total Cu input) of high quality copper sulphate crystal, carrying a high premium (>25%) over the LME copper price, by direct crystallisation of calcine l

each solution. 

- (4) A dedicated iron removal stage capable of absorbing a massive increase in the refinery iron input without affecting the overall process efficiency. This may apply for treatment of a high iron alloy matte from a slag reduction furnace. 

- (5) Combination of mild atmospheric leach stages, non-oxidising pressure leach and pressure iron hydrolysis would depress solubilisation of amphoteric impurity in the nickel leach circuit, which should result in production of a better quality of nickel cathodes. 

- (6) Elimination of a large proportion of iron from the final residue (calcine leach residue) would make recovery of residual PGM a much simpler and more efficient process. Direct separation of amphoterics from PGM in the copper circuit is feasible. 

The proposed process is a leading candidate amongst alternative refining processes, although it has to compete with the existing process modified by incorporation of alternative methods of sulphur removal, such as acid solvent extraction, electrodialysis etc. The final decision will be based on a detailed capital and operating cost analysis, which is expected to be completed at the end of 2002.
